full_judgment:
In this revision Rule was issued calling upon the opposite party No. 1 to show cause as to why the impugned judgment and decree dated 25.10.2004 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, 1st Court, Cox’s Bazar, in Other Appeal No. 93 of 1998 dismissing the appeal and affirming the judgment and decree dated 07.06.1998 passed by the learned Senior Assistant Judge, Cox’s Bazar in  Other Suit No. 28 of 1997 decreeing the suit should not be set aside and/or pass such other or further order or orders as to this Court may seem fit and proper. 

Facts relevant for disposal of this Rule, in short, are that the opposite party No. 1, as plaintiff instituted Other Suit No. 28 of 1997 against the petitioners, as defendant Nos. 1 and 2, and opposite party No. 2, as defendant No. 3, on the following prayers; 
ক) বাদী ও ১নং বিবাদীর মধ্যে সৃজিত বিগত ১৩/০৩/১৯৮৫ ইংরেজী তারিখের ১৭৫৬ নং রেজিঃ যুক্ত এওয়াজনামা দলিল খানা ফেরবী, অবলবৎ, অকার্যকর ও যোগসাজসী উচ্চারন ক্রমে তাহা বাতিল করতঃ তদ্বারা নালিশী ১নং তপশীলের জমি ও বাদী বাধ্য নহে উচ্চারনের ডিক্রি দিতে। 
খ) বাদী কর্তৃক ১নং বিবাদীর বরাবরে প্রদত্ত ১নং তপশীলের জমি স্থিত বাদীর অনুমতিতে নির্মিত গৃহে থাকার অনুমতি ও নালিশী ১নং তপশীল���র জমির দখল বাতিল ক্রমে ১নং তপশীলের জমি ও তদস্থিত গৃহের খাস দখল বাদীর বরাবরে বুঝাইয়া দিতে।
গ) ৭/১০/৭৪ইংরেজী তারিখ হইতে অদ্যাবধি ও পরবর্তীতে মামলা নিষ্পত্তি কালতক নালিশী ১নং তপশীলের জমিস্থিত গৃহের মাসিক ১,০০০/- (এক হাজার) টাকা হিসাবে ভাড়া প্রদানের জন্য ১/২ নংবিবাদীদ্বয়ের প্রতি নির্দেশ প্রদান করিতে।
ঘ) মোকদ্দমার তাবৎ ব্যয় প্রতিদ্বন্দিকারী বিবাদীগনের বিরুদ্ধে ডিক্রী প্রদান করিতে।
ঙ) আদালতের ন্যায় বিচারে বাদী অন্যান্য যে যে প্রতিকার পাইতে পারেন তাহাও ডিক্রি দিতে হুজুর আদালতের বিহিত মর্জি হয়।

The case of the plaintiff, inter alia, is that the plaintiff was the owner of the land in schedule-I (hereinafter referred to as the suit land), defendant No. 1 is the distant relative of the plaintiff and defendant No. 2 is the husband of the defendant No. 1. In the 1st part of 1985, the defendant No. 2 told the plaintiff that he needs the suit land for extension of his dwelling house and proposed to exchange the same with the land of schedule II belonging to defendant No. 1. The plaintiff agreed and accordingly, on 13.03.1985 a deed of exchange was executed and registered between the plaintiff and the defendant No. 1 and the plaintiff delivered possession of the suit land to the defendant and it was agreed that the defendants would deliver possession and handover title deeds of the schedule-II land on 14.03.1985, but till now the defendant did not deliver possession to the plaintiff on different pleas. The plaintiff being an old man has been suffering from different types of ailment could not communicate with the defendant. Failure of the defendant to deliver the possession of the land of schedule-II created suspicion in the mind of the plaintiff regarding ownership of defendant No.1 in the suit land. On enquiry the plaintiff came to know that the defendant No. 1 has/had no title in the schedule-II land, but got the deed of exchange executed by false representation. On 20.12.1996, the plaintiff asked the defendant to deliver possession of the suit land but the defendant refused, hence, the plaintiff filed the present suit.     

The petitioners, as defendant Nos. 1 and 2, contested the suit by filing written statement denying material allegations made in the plaint contending inter alia, that the suit is not maintainable in its present form; the suit is hopelessly barred by limitation. The case of the defendants in brief, is that the total area of the suit plot is 30 decimals, out of which the plaintiff was the owner of 7 decimals land and his brother Mustaque Ahmed was owner of 6 decimals who by giving possession on 20.06.1967 orally and subsequently, by a written instrument on 07.10.1974 allowed the defendant No. 2 to live on the land with family by constructing house on 13 decimals of land. Subsequently, Mostaque  Ahmed being in need of money, sold his 6 decimals of land to the defendant by kabala dated 21.09.1967. 

The land of schedule-II along with other lands originally belonged to Abdur Rashid Chowdhury who settled the same in favour of one Mahfuzur Rabbi by Patta dated 19.05.1936. Mahfuzur Rabbi died leaving Jamaluddin and others as his heirs, accordingly, B.S. khatian (the latest records of right) stands recorded in the name of Jamaluddin and others, who by two kabalas dated 08.11.1978 sold the same to the brother of defendant No. 1, Md. Shawkat Alam. Subsequently, Shawkat Alam sold 10 decimals of land to the defendant No. 1 by kabala dated 16.06.1984. Said land is situated near Chakaria College. The plaintiff was looking for a piece of land in the said area to construct a house in order to provide accommodation to his children and grand children who were studying in Chakaria College and having come to know that the land of schedule II belonged to the defendant No. 1, was considered by him suitable to construct house and proposed the defendant to sell the said land to the plaintiff. The defendant considering the balance of convenience and inconveniences agreed to transfer the said land (schedule-II) by way of exchange with the suit land, accordingly, the plaintiff and the defendant No. 1 without being influenced or misrepresented by anybody executed and registered the deed of exchange on 13.03.1985 and delivered possession of their respective land to each other. The defendant by consolidating the land with the non-suited land (earlier purchased from Mostaque Ahmed) constructed semi pucca house thereon and planted fruit bearing trees and has been living thereon beyond the statutory period of limitation on payment of rents to the Government and Municipal taxes. On the other hand the plaintiff also having got the land of schedule-II bounded the same by fence and has been possessing by growing fruit bearing trees thereon. Since, the price of the suit land increased the same fell into the greedy eyes of the relatives of the plaintiff who with a view to grab the suit land managed the plaintiff to file the suit. The suit is false and frivolous and gambling in litigation, as such, prayed for dismissal of the suit.

The trial court framed 5 (five) issues for determination of the dispute. During trial the plaintiff examined as many as 4 witnesses and filed certain documents which were marked as exhibits-1 and 2. The defendants on the other hand, to substantiate their claim examined as many as 5 witnesses as DWs and filed documents which were marked as exhibits- Ka series (rent receipts), exhibit-‘Kha’ (Municipal Holding Tax receipts), exhibit-‘Ga’ (copy of B.S. khatian No. 608), exhibits-‘Gha’ and ‘Gha(1)’ kabala dated 08.11.1978 and 21.09.1979, exhibit-‘Uma’ (kabala dated 14.06.1984), exhibit-‘Cha’ (deed of exchange dated 13.03.1985) and exhibit-‘Chha’ (kabala dated 08.11.1978).

The learned trial court after hearing the parties, found, inter alia, that the suit is not barred by limitation, title and possession of the defendant No. 1 in respect of land of schedule-II has not been proved, consequently, she could not deliver possession to the plaintiff and accordingly, decreed the suit by judgment and decree dated 07.06.1998 declaring the Exchange deed No. 1756 dated 13.03.1985 voidable and cancelled and directed the defendants to surrender possession of the suit land to the plaintiff within 90 days. 

Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the judgment and decree dated 07.06.1998, the defendant-petitioner preferred Other Appeal No. 93 of 1998 before the District Judge, Cox’s Bazar, which was transferred to the 1st court of Joint District Judge, Cox’s Bazar for hearing and disposal, who after hearing concurred with the findings of the trial court and dismissed the appeal affirming the judgment and decree of the trial court by its judgment and decree dated 25.10.2004. At this juncture, the petitioners moved this Court by filing this revisional application under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure and obtained the present Rule and order of stay.  

Mr. Md. Nurul Amin, Senior Advocate with Mr. Sayed Misbahul Anwar, learned Advocates appearing for the petitioner at the very outset submit that the deed of exchange in question admittedly executed and registered on 13.03.1985 and the plaintiff claimed that the defendant No. 1 had to deliver possession of the property and handover all the title documents to him on the following day i.e. on 14.03.1985, but taking various pleas the defendants delayed delivery of possession and documents such statements amply proves that the plaintiff knowing fully well about title of the defendants in suit executed and registered the deed of exchange, exchanging the suit property with the defendant No. 1. He further argued that since there is no allegation of fraud and misrepresentation on the part of the defendant, the plaintiff ought to have filed the suit for cancellation of the deed within three years from 14.03.1985 as provided in Article 91 of the Limitation Act, but the suit was filed after near about 12 years beyond the prescribed period of limitation, as such, both the courts below fell in serious error in not finding that the suit is hopelessly barred by limitation. 

He further submits that in the impugned deed of exchange no stipulation was provided for cancellation of the deed for any defect in title or any fault, but there was a stipulation that the plaintiff would be entitled to claim market value of the property with compensation from the defendants and in the event of refusal by the defendants to pay the same could have filed a suit for recovery of market value of the property with compensation, but the plaintiff filed the suit praying for cancellation of deed of exchange and recovery of possession which is absolutely beyond the terms and conditions of the deed of exchange and section 119 of the Transfer of Property Act. 

He further argued that both the courts below utterly failed to find the stipulation contain in the deed of exchange and the observations of both the courts below in this regard is contrary to the provision of section 119 of the Transfer of Property Act. It is also argued that the defendant No. 1 by producing chain of documents and adducing evidences proved her title in the schedule-II land and there being no allegation or evidence to the effect that anybody disputed the title of the defendant No. 1 in the schedule-II property and the plaintiff was prevented by anybody or threatened with dispossession from the schedule-II land, both the courts below ought to have considered the evidences both oral and documentary in record. 

He submits that in the absence of any allegation of fraud in obtaining the deed of exchange, under the terms and condition of impugned deed the same is not at all liable to be cancelled, moreover, the plaintiff did not seek a declaration of title and has given boundary of the property in the plaint for specification, as such, the suit is liable to be dismissed on that counts also. 

It is also submitted that Erfan Uddin Chowdhury, one of the sons of plaintiff, Fayez Ahmed Chowdhury as constituted attorney of the plaintiff deposed in the suit before the trial court and represented the plaintiff respondent before the appellate court who after disposal of the appeal by a Nadabinama No. 1294 dated 03.04.2016 gave up his claim in the suit property, another son of the plaintiff named Fakhruddin Chowdhury by a registered deed No. 2024 dated 02.05.2016 transferred his share in schedule-II property to one Humayun Kabir son of Mahfuzul Islam, and one of the daughters of plaintiff named Jawhra Begum Chowdhury by a registered deed No. 5339 dated 18.07.2012 transferred her share in schedule-II property in favour of one Rezaul Karim admitting validity of deed of exchange in question and acquisition of title by inheritance from their father Fayez Ahmed Chowdhury and before fransfer all the heirs got their names mutated in khatian No. 1813 and by annexing all the three deeds, the petitioner filed an application for taking additional evidence and submits that those may be considered as additional evidences as nothing contrary could bring by the opposite party, meaning thereby, those documents are admitted by them.  In support of his submissions he has referred to a catena of cases: Noor Mohammad Khan and others vs. Government of Bangladesh and others reported in 42 DLR 434, Md. Zillur Rahman vs. Mst. Hosne Ara Begum reported in XII ADC, 338, Abu Naser Mohammad Wahidun Nabi and another vs. Md. Balai Roy and others reported in 15 BLT (AD) 27, Md. Naimuddin Sarder vs. Md. Abdul Kalam Biswas reported in 39  DLR (AD) 237, Md. Sorboddi Miah vs. Md. Serajul Haque and another reported in XII ADC 413, Kanchan Mallik and others vs. Saleha Begum and others reported in 9 ALR (AD) 115, Ratan Chandra Dey and others vs. Jinnator Nahar and others reported in 13 MLR (AD) 168 and Kanchan Mala Bepari Vs. Ananta Kumar Bepari & others reported in 6 DLR 254.  

Mr. Taposh Kumar Dutta, learned advocate appearing for the Added Opposite Party No. 3, Md. Rianul Haque against whom no rule was issued, submits that after disposal of the appeal and pendency of this revision the Plaintiff Fayez Ahmed Chowdhury by a registered deed of gift No. 929 dated 06.04.2007 gifted the suit schedule-I property to the added opposite party No. 3 as grandson and after making gift in his favour all the rights, title and interest devolved upon him and he is the right person to defend the rule as principal opposite party. 

He argued that the trial court as well as the appellate court concurrently observed and found that the defendant No. 1 had no title and possession in the suit property to be exchanged with Fayez Ahmed Chowdhury and as per terms and conditions of deed of exchange, the defendant could not deliver possession of the schedule-II property and could not produce any papers or documents showing that after purchase of the schedule-II property she got her name mutated in the khatian, paid rents to the government and also failed to prove delivery of possession to the plaintiff by giving specific boundary of the schedule-II property. Referring to Article 91 of the Limitation Act he submits that this is a suit for cancellation of deed of exchange and recovery of possession which is guided by Article 144 of the Limitation Act, providing 12 years of limitation, accordingly, the suit was filed within 12 years as provided in Article 144 of the Limitation Act and Article 91 prescribed three years limitation from the facts known to the plaintiff requiring cancellation of the deed and in the instant suit the plaintiff categorically stated in the plaint that the plaintiff on 20.12.1996 along with the witnesses mentioned in paragraph 8 of the plaint went to the house of defendant Nos. 1 and 2 and demanded possession of the exchanged property, in the alternative to pay market price of the property and being refused by the defendants on 25.12.1996, the plaintiff has become compelled to file the present suit on 27.02.1997, within three years as provided in Article 91 of Limitation Act and both the courts below concurrently found that the suit is not barred by limitation. 

He further submits that the defendant No. 1 could not prove by producing any document that she had title in the property, or she got possession of the property after purchase by giving definite boundary with specification. Both the courts below while decreeing the suit and disallowing the appeal concurrently found that in the deed of the defendant No. 1 dated 14.06.1984 as well as in the deed of exchange dated 13.03.1985 no boundary of the schedule-II property has been mentioned. In the absence of any boundary in the deeds, mutation in the khatian after purchase and payment of rents to the government she acquired no title and possession in the schedule-II property to be exchanged, resultantly, the defendant failed to deliver possession of the exchanged property to the plaintiff and handover all the title deeds in original, as such, both the courts below rightly held that title of the defendant in schedule-II property is defective which calls for cancellation of the deed in question. 

It is also argued that in a suit for cancellation of any document there is no need for seeking declaration of title of the plaintiff and giving any boundary in the schedule to the plaint. He further submits that concurrent findings of both the courts below cannot be disturbed in revision unless the petitioners can show there is any misreading and non-appreciation of evidence both oral and documentary, misconstruction of law and non-consideration of any important document, but in the instant case the petitioner could show nothing as such, the Rule is liable to be discharged. In support of his submissions he has referred the cases of Shamshad Ali Shah and others vs. Syed Hassan Shan and others reported in LEX/SCPK/0012/194 Supreme Court of Pakistan and Kanchan Mala vs. Ananta Kumar Bepari and others reported in 6 DLR 254.                   

Mrs. Fawzia Karim Firoze with Mr. Khandaker Aminul Haque, learned Advocates appearing for the opposite party Nos. 1(ii)(a)-1(ii) 1(iii), 1(iv), 1(v), 1(vi), 1(vii), 1(viii), 1(ix) and 1(x) adopting submissions of Mr. Taposh further submits that non-compliance of obligation on the part of the defendants by delivery of possession of the exchanged property and title document in original to the plaintiff vitiated the whole purpose of the exchange deed calling for cancellation of the same.  

She further argued that the suit is not barred by limitation because of the fact that for cancellation of a deed entire facts stated in the plaint have to be considered which entitles a person requiring cancellation of the deed and the plaintiff specifically and clearly stated in the plaint that the defendant on various pleas took time to deliver possession to the plaintiff and finally refused to the demand in the year 1996 and the suit was filed on 27.02.1997 within two months from the date of refusal, as such, the suit is not barred by limitation under Article 91 of the Limitation Act. 

She further submits that the suit is not only for cancellation of a deed, but also for recovery of possession. Article 144 of the Limitation Act provides 12 years for recovery of possession. If the time begins to run from the date of execution and registration of the deed on 13.03.1985 in that case also the suit has been filed within 12 years, as such, the suit is not at all barred by any Article of the Limitation Act. In support of her submissions she has referred to a catena of cases: Abdul Matin Chowdhury vs. Chapala Rani Sen and others reported in 37 DLR (AD) 205, Abdul Mannaf Khan and others vs. Bangladesh and another reported in 38 DLR (AD) 201, Nasimuddin Mia vs. Monindra Kumar Maloo and others reported in 2 BLC 83, and 6 MLR, 224, Irangauda Fakir Gauda Patil vs. Ningappa Bin Gopappa Gopagawda reported in AIR 1924 Bombay 517, Md. Mahbubul Haque vs. Md. A. Kader Munshi reported in 20 BLD (AD) 82, Jamaluddin vs. Rabeya Begum reported in 32 DLR 63 and Barand Sundari Paul and others vs. The Assistant Custodian , Enemy Property, Comilla and others reported in 15 BLD (AD) 95.   

Mr. Syed Hasan Zobair, learned Advocate appearing for the opposite Party Nos. 1(ix)(a), 1(ix)(b), 1(ix)(c), 1(ix)(e), (ix)(g) and 1(ix)(h) submits that predecessor of these opposite parties named Jawhra Begum transferred her share to one Rezaul Karim son of Monir Ahmed by a registered deed No. 5339 dated 18.07.2012, similarly her brother Fakhruddin also transferred his share to one Humayun Kabir son of Mahfuzul Islam by registered deed No. 2024 dated 02.05.2016 in the schedule-II property and Erfan Uddin Chowdhury relinquished his claim in the suit property in favour of petitioner by a deed of Disclaimer No. 1294 dated 03.04.2016 and the purchasers of the property duly delivered with the possession of the same, as such, they have no claim in schedule-1 property.    

Heard the learned Advocates for the parties, have gone through the revision application, counter affidavits, plaint, written statement, application for taking additional evidence, objection thereto, evidences both oral and documentary available in lower court records and impugned judgment and decree of both the courts below.

Admittedly, schedule-I property belonged to Fayez Ahmed Chowdhury, who exchanged the same with defendant No. 1 taking schedule-II property by a deed of exchange No. 1756 dated 13.03.1985 (exhibit-Cha and exhibit-2). It is also not denied that defendant No. 1 was in possession of schedule-I property as permissive possessor since 1967 and subsequently, on the basis of an agreement executed by plaintiff Fayez Ahmed Chowdhury in her favour dated 07.10.1974 and continued possession of the same till execution of deed of exchange on 13.03.1985. The plaintiff in his plaint claimed that on the following day of execution of deed of exchange, defendant No. 1 was supposed to deliver possession of the property to the plaintiff and handover all the title documents relating to schedule-II property, but the defendant on various pretext failed to deliver possession of the schedule-II property and related title document to the plaintiff. Thereafter, the plaintiff on several occasions requested the defendant and demanded possession of the schedule-II property. Since the defendant was delaying delivery of possession of schedule-II property, the plaintiff apprehended about title of the defendant No. 1 in the property and came to know that the defendant Nos. 1 and 2, misrepresenting the plaintiff and taking advantage of his good faith exchanged the schedule-II property with the schedule-I property of the plaintiff having no title at all, consequently, the defendants failed to deliver possession of the schedule-II property on repeated demands. Finally, he went to the house of defendant Nos. 1 and 2 with the witnesses on 20.12.1996 and demanded delivery of possession of the schedule-II property, in the alternative to pay market price of the property to the plaintiff, but the defendants through their relatives informed the plaintiff on 25.12.1996 that they will not deliver possession of the property and handover title documents to him. 

The trial court observed that schedule-II property under B.S. khatian No. 608, plot No. 2246 measuring 1.24 acres originally belonged to Jamal Uddin and others from whom brother of the defendant No. 1 named Md. Shawkat Alam purchased the same by registered deed Nos. 5609 and 5610 both dated 08.11.1978 (exhibits-‘Gha’ and ‘Gha-2’). Thereafter, Shawkat Alam by a registered deed No. 4828 dated 14.06.1984 transferred 10 sataks of land to his sister defendant No. 1 (exhibit-‘Umo’), without any boundary to the schedule specifying the property sold, moreover, both of them did not get their names mutated in the khatian and paid rents to the government and for those reasons the defendant No. 1 acquired no title in the schedule-II land and also observed that none of the D.Ws. could prove that the defendant No. 1 delivered possession of schedule-II property to the plaintiff but curiously enough to mention that it is not the case of the plaintiff that anybody raised any objection about title of defendant No. 1 or his brother Shawkat Alam in the schedule-II property or the plaintiff was threatened by any other persons with dispossession of the property or questioning title of the plaintiff in schedule-II land given by exchange, moreover, DW4 has deposed saying delivery of possession to the plaintiff. Mere absence of boundary in a sale deed, absence of mutation in the name of the purchaser, non-payment of rents cannot make the defendant No. 1 titleless in the property. The trial court in a suit for cancellation of an exchange deed instead of finding the reasons and circumstances for cancellation of a deed tried to decide the matter of title of defendant No. 1 wrongly in the manner mentioned above. 

The trial court found the suit is not barred by limitation under Article 91 of the Limitation Act, holding that cause of action is not a single fact but it’s a bundle of facts started from 13.03.1985 and continued on all subsequent dates till filing of the suit on 27.02.1996 and observed that to cancel or set aside an instrument not otherwise provided for, is three years, arises when the facts entitling the plaintiff to have the instrument cancelled or set aside become known to him relying on the statement made by the plaintiff at paragraph 8(eight) of the plaint, but failed to notice and give any reasons what has prevented the plaintiff to demand possession of the property and why he waited about 12 years to have the delivery of possession of the schedule-II property and failed to give any cogent reason whether the long waiting of the plaintiff for delivery of possession can extend the period of limitation from 1985-1996.

Moreover, it is the definite case of the plaintiff that he was supposed to get delivery of possession of the property on the following day of execution of deed of exchange, i,e, on 14.03.1985 as stated in paragraph 3 of the plaint. It is not the case of the plaintiff that the deed was obtained by the defendants by practicing fraud or he came to know about fraud on 20.12.1996, the only allegation brought against the defendants is non-delivery of possession and title documents of the property to the plaintiff which cannot be construed in any way that the defendant No. 1 had no title in the schedule-II property. 

The trial court further held that section 119 of the Transfer of Property Act entitles the plaintiff to get the deed of exchange cancelled by reason of any defect in the title of the other party deprived of the thing or any part of the thing received by him in exchange and herein, since the defendant No. 1 had no title in the property, the plaintiff rightly instituted the present suit and it is quite maintainable in the light of the decision report in 44 DLR (AD) 86 and on the above findings decreed the suit. The views taken by the trial court is not well founded. 

Section 119 of the Transfer of Property Act provides that:
 “If any party to an exchange or any person claiming through or under such party is by reason of any defect in the title of the other party deprived of the thing or any part of the thing received by him in exchange, then, unless a contrary intention appears from the terms of the exchange, such other party is liable to him or any person claiming through or under him for loss caused thereby, or at the option of the person so deprived, for the return of the thing transferred, if still in the possession of such other party or his legal representative or a transferee from him without consideration.” 

From perusal of Deed of Exchange No. 1756 dated 13.03.1985, it appears that there is a stipulation which runs as follows: 
"যদি ভবিষ্যতে এওয়াজপ্রাপ্ত জমিতে স্বত্ব দখলে কোন প্রকার বিঘ্ন সৃষ্টি হয় তাহা হইলে আমরা ঐ সময়ে বাজার ভাও মূল্য ও তৎক্ষতিপূরণ দিতে বাধ্য থাকিব।"

As per terms of the exchange, the plaintiff is entitled to claim market price of the property prevailing at that time along with compensation, by reason of any defect in title of the defendant No. 1 in schedule-II property but the plaintiff is not entitled to get the deed of exchange cancelled or return of the property, moreover, in the present suit the plaintiff could not prove any defect in the title of the defendant No. 1 in schedule-II land.

Another point to be taken note of is that the principle of section 119 of the Transfer Property Act, can be applied so long as the property is lying in the hands of the person to whom it was given in exchange. If however, the said person has parted with that property further on in favour of a third person, then the case goes out of the mischief of the said section. In the instant case the plaintiff parted with the suit property by executing a deed of gift in favour of opposite party No. 3, his heirs transferred the schedule-II property to third persons and one of the sons relinquished his claim in the suit property in favour of defendant No. 1. The plaintiff in these circumstances can neither succeed on the terms of the covenant hereinbefore reproduced not on the principle of section 119 which was sought to be invoked in this case.  

The appellate court while disallowing the appeal nothing held and observed new other than the observations made by the trial court. The appellate court also concurrently observed that for absence of boundary in the schedule to the deed of the defendant No. 1, absence of mutation in the name of Shawkat Alam as well as in the name of defendant No. 1 and non-payment of rents to the government proved that the defendant No. 1 had no title and possession in the schedule-II property to be exchanged with the plaintiff and also found that the suit is not barred by limitation under Article 91 of the Limitation Act as well as the plaintiff is entitled to get the deed of exchange cancelled under section 119 of the Transfer of Property Act.

Article 91 of the Limitation Act provides that to cancel or set aside any instrument not otherwise provided for--three years, when the facts entitling the plaintiff to have the instrument cancelled or set aside become known to him. In the instant case the exchange deed was not obtained by practicing fraud and it was well known to the plaintiff on the date of execution and registration of the deed on 13.03.1985 and it was also known to him that the defendant No.1 was supposed to deliver possession of the schedule-II property on the following day i.e. on 14.03.1985. Therefore, beginning of computation of limitation starts from 14.03.1985 and the plaintiff ought to have filed this suit within three years under Article 91, but filed the suit after about 12 years. Both the courts below though rightly found that the cause of action for the suit arose from 13.03.1985 but did not address the situations stated in the plaint and failed to give any findings about the legal effect on the period spent and consumed by the plaintiff from 1985-1996. In this regard case of Md. Zillur Rahman vs. Most. Hosna Ara Begum, reported in 12 ADC 338 can be referred to	Present suit has been filed for cancellation of exchange deed, if the limitation begins to start from 14.03.1985 the suit is barred as regard to cancellation of deed in that case there is no question of granting relief as to recovery of possession after about 12 years as held in the case of ANMW Nabi vs. Balai Roy and others reported in 15 BLT(AD)27.  

In the case of Kanchan Mala Bepari vs. Ananta Kumar Bepari, 6 DLR 254, the question raised primarily on limitation and maintainability of suit. It was filed after 15 years claiming that the deed dated 14.12.1925 was a void and fraudulent document and for a declaration that said document was a Jaisudi mortgage and it has been extinguished by lapse of 15 years from the date of the bond. So, question is when the period of limitation begins to run. Here the plaintiff stated that he executed the deed on good faith believing that the defendant No. 1 has title over the property and she will deliver possession of the same, but in the year 1996 he came to know that the defendant No. 1 had no title. Both the courts below concurrently held that because of absence of boundary in the schedule to the deed of the year 1984, in the exchange deed, absence of mutation in the name of defendant No. 1, non-payment of rents to the government, the defendant No. 1 acquired no title in schedule-II property, such observations are not correct in view of the established principles of law that title transferred to the transferee with the deed and non-payment of rent does not affect the title as held in the cases of Abdun Noor and others vs. Aziruddin and others, reported in 21 BLT (AD) 161 and Abdul Mannan Bhuiya and others vs. Md. Nasir Hossain and others reported in 18 BLC(AD) 44, observing that “the registered document prevail upon record of right. S.A. and R.S. records were not an evidence of title and that a registered document would prevail upon the records of rights and remain in force unless the same was concelled by an appropriate civil court.”

In the schedule to the plaint, there is no specific boundary to identify from which portion of the suit plot the plaintiff prayed for khas possession where the trial court criticized the boundary contain in the schedule-I of the property in the exchange deed to be vague and confusing. Plaintiff having failed to comply with the mandatory requirement of law in giving clear description or boundary to indentify the suit land, is not entitled to any decree for defect in the plaint as held in the case of Md. Sorboddi Miah vs. Md. Serajul Haque and another, reported in 12 ADC 413 and Noor Mohammad Khan and others vs. Bangladesh and others, reported in 42 DLR 435.

In the cases of Ratan Chandra Dey and others vs. Jinnator Nahar and others, reported in 13 MLR (AD) 168, Sanjib Kumar Bose and another vs. Syed Shamsuddin Ahmed and another, reported in 1 BCR (AD) 273, Mst. Sahara Khatun and another vs. Mst. Anwara Khatun and others, reported in 1 BCR (1981) 126 held that, a suit for cancellation and declaration that the deed of exchange is fraudulent, not binding upon the plaintiff is not maintainable without declaration of title. The present case also filed by the plaintiff without declaration of his title in the suit property. 

On the other hand, cases cited by the opposite parties are not related to the fact of the present case, those are relating to allegations of obtaining the document by practicing fraud and regarding concurrent findings of the courts below. 

The case of A. Mannaf vs. Bangladesh, reported in 38 DLR (AD) 201 referred by the opposite parties, in fact, helps the petitioner wherein it has been held that;
“Rule as to concurrent finding of fact is not so rigid that it might not be departed from if such a state of things existed as facts appearing from some undisputed document which are completely destructive of the finding of fact by the courts below. That was not the case here. It is not the error of fact but the error of law which is the requirement of law that call for exercise of jurisdiction.”   

	In the present case both the courts below committed error both in law and facts by misconstruction of evidence and documents as discussed above.

In Nasimuddin Mia vs. Manindra Kumar Maloo and others case, the plaintiff filed the suit for cancellation of an exchange deed by which defendant No. 1 got schedule-1 property in Bangladesh in exchange of schedules-2 and 3 property in Assam, subsequently, the plaintiff came to know that the defendant No. 1 had no title in schedules-2 and 3 property as he fransferred the property earlier, hence practiced fraud, but in the present case no allegation of fraud has been alleged and proved. Facts stated in the plaint and evidence led cannot constitute any fraud and defect of title of the defendant No. 1 in the schedule-II property. Therefore, application of provision of Article-91 of the Limitation Act, depends on the fact of each individual cases like the present one. 

Facts of Irangauda Fakir Gauda Patil vs. Ningappa Bin Gopappa Gopagawda case, 1924 AIR (Bomb) 517 is totally different from the fact of the present case and it was not a case for cancellation of any document, as such, not relevant in the instant suit.

During hearing of the Rule, the petitioner filed an application for taking additional evidence annexing some documents praying for accepting those as additional evidence which are mutation khatian No.1813 in the name of heirs of original plaintiff Fayez Ahmed Chowdhury (though the opposite parties without any proof claimed that subsequently, this mutation khatian was cancelled), true copy of deed No. 5339 dated 18.07.2012 executed by Alhaj Jawhra Begum daughter of the plaintiff in favour of one Rezaul Karim, sale deed No. 2024 dated 02.05.2016 executed by Fakhruddin Chowdhury son of the plaintiff infavour of one Humayun Kabir transferring their shares in plot No. 2246, schedule-II to the deed of exchange and plaint, admitting validity of the exchange deed dated 13.03.1985 and Deed of Disclaimer No. 1294 dated 03.04.2016 executed by Erfan Uddin Chowdhury son of Fayez Ahmed Chowdhury relinquishing his title in the schedule-I land to the deed of exchange and plaint in favour of defendant No. 1 who represented and deposed in the suit as attorney of original plaintiff Fayez Ahmed Chowdhury.

Apart from this the plaintiff Fayez Ahmed Chowdhury during pendency of this rule transferred the schedule-1 land to the added opposite party No. 3 by a deed of gift who got no possession, meaning thereby, the plaintiff gifted the property without delivery of possession of the schedule-1 property, which is a paramount condition of a gift.

Now, the question has come, had the deed of exchange not acted upon and possession of schedule-II property not delivered to Fayez Ahmed Chowdhury and the defendant No. 1 had no title in the property to be exchanged with Fayez Ahmed Chowdhury how the daughter and sons of Fayez Ahmed Chowdhury, after his death can transfer the property to other persons admitting validity of the exchange deed and delivered possession of their share in the land to the purchasers Rezaul Karim and Humayun Kabir, but all those documents are found to be executed and registered after disposal of the appeal by the appellate court and during pendency of the present Rule which did not enter into evidence by way of additional written statement or producing any witness. To give specific findings on long waiting of the plaintiff coupled with law of limitation, maintainability of the present suit and validity of deed of exchange and for proper adjudication of the matter in dispute legal effect and consequences of subsequent incidences and events occurred, as appearing from those deeds are required to be taken into consideration. In that view of the matter it requires recording of evidence to bring those documents on record. 

It is true that any transfer by any party during pendency of any suit is hit by section 52 of the Transfer of Property Act, but in the instant case the situation is otherwise, here the transfers made by the claimants of schedule-1 property in suit, not by the defendant. In the absence of proper adjudication of the whole matter in dispute, transfers made by the heirs of original plaintiff Fayez Ahmed Chowdhury will give rise to multiplicity of proceedings. To avoid multiplicity of proceedings and to get the dispute effectively adjudicated for all intents and purposes, this court thinks that for the interest of justice the suit is required to be sent back on remand to the appellate court to consider and record additional evidence affording the appellant petitioner an opportunity to file additional written statement and to adduce evidence in respect of documents filed and the Respondent-opposite parties shall get opportunity to cross examine the witnesses adduced, accordingly, application for taking additional evidence is allowed. 

Taking into consideration the above, this Court finds merit in the Rule and in the submissions of the learned advocates for the petitioner. 

In the result the Rule is made absolute, however without any order as to costs.

Judgment and decree of the appellate court is hereby set aside. To save time and unnecessary expenses of the parties and considering age of the litigation the appeal is sent back on remand to the appellate court for hearing and passing judgment afresh on the points specifically mentioned hereinbelow, as the appellate court has the same power like the trial court and directed to dispose of the appeal within six months from the date of receipt of this judgment positively.

Order of stay stands vacated. 

The petitioner is allowed to take back the documents submitted and annexed to the application for taking additional evidence providing photocopies of the same and to file those before the appellate court for the purpose of recording additional evidence. 

The appellate court should give clear findings in the light of the observations made in the body of the judgment on the point of (i) legal position of the period spent from 1985-1996 under Article 91 of the Limitation Act, (ii) application of section 119 of the Transfer of Property Act in the present case (iii) whether the situations stated in the plaint can call for cancellation of deed of exchange under the terms and conditions contain therein (iv) consequences of transfers made by the plaintiff by a gift and transfers made by his heirs to third parties and (v) maintainability of suit on the point of limitation, want of prayer for declaration of title and absence of boundary in the schedule to the plaint. 

Communicate a copy of the judgment and send down the lower court records to the concerned court at once.       

End.

case_source: (From the judgment and order dated 4-6-2009 passed by the I HO Court Division in First Appeal Nos.349, 350 and 351 of 2002)
full_judgment:
Md Nuruzzaman J: These 3(three) Civil Appeals, by leave, have arisen out of the judgment and order dated 4-6-2009 passed by the High Court Division in First Appeal Nos. 349, 350 and 351 of 2002 disposing of the appeals without any order as to costs.
2. All these civil petitions for leave to appeal arising out of common judgment and order between the same parties, and involving common question of law and fact, having been heard together are being disposed of by this single judgment.
3. Facts, leading to filing of this civil appeal, in short, are that:—
The sole plaintiff, Mosammat Hilufa Hanum Joarder filed Title Suit No. 302 of 1976 for declaration of her title, recovery of possession and also for mesne profits in respect of 0.29 acre of suit property including the building and structures standing thereon know as 'Acharya Lodge' along with mesne profit of Taka 7,06,000. The above title suit was lastly renumbered as Title Suit No. 73 of 1984.
4. The sole plaintiff also filed Title Suit No. 51 of 1970 for declaration that, order of requisition dated 26-5-1964 passed by the Extra-Assistant Commissioner and Land Acquisition collector, Kushtia in LA Case No. 12/63-64 in respect of 0.29 acre of suit property with building and structures thereon at Chuadanga town, and dispossession of the plaintiff therefrom were illegal and also for directing the defendants to restore her the suit property and possession along with payment of adequate co-operation for damages. The above title suit was lastly re-numbered as Title Suit No. 117 of 1981, and thereafter, Title Suit No. 24 of 1988 respectively.
5. The plaintiff also filed Title Suit No. 88 of 1972 for declaration that, the order of permanent acquisition dated 8-6-1966 relating to the plaintiff's 'Acharya Lodge' is illegal, Mak fide, collusive, fraudulent, inoperative, and not binding upon the plaintiff and also for direction to restore the vacant possession of the same. The above title suit was lastly re-numbered as Title Suit No. 141 of 1984.
6. The plaintiff is the owner in possession of the building and other structures standing on 0.29 acre of the land in CS Plot Nos. 2203 and 2210 under Khatian Nos. 218 and 298 of Mouza Chuadanga in Chuadanga town in the District of Kushtia. The plaintiff acquired the property and obtained possession over it firstly on the basis of a Bainapatra dated 18-12-1963 and subsequently, by Kabala dated 16-1-1964 from the owner Md Mahbub Hossain, the lawful owner in possession, who had acquired the same by exchange from the heirs of CS recorded tenant Upendra Nath Acharjee. In such position, defendant No. 2, the Extra-Assistant Commissioner issued an order of requisition of the suit property dated 25-5-1964 for providing accommodation to the branch office of the National Bank of Pakistan in the Town of Chuadanga District, addressing the plaintiff's husband, who was an officer of the then Government of East Pakistan, and had been working as a Circle Officer in different outlying areas of the country. In 1964, the plaintiff's husband was serving at Kishoregonj Sub-Division. Though the Bank had its existing office in a proper place in the town, yet requisition and acquisition was done with ulterior motive without serving any notice to the plaintiff. No sooner had the plaintiff come to know the matter, than he raised objection to defendant No. 2, and preferred an appeal to the Commissioner, lamina Division, and thereafter, to the Government through the Secretary, Revenue Department on 26-12-1964, but, they did not give any reply. After that, the plaintiff filed an application on 1-1-1966 to the Minister-in-Charge of Revenue where the plaintiff's application for vacating the order of requisition was rejected, and she was intimated through a letter dated 23-9-1965. Lastly, the plaintiff's prayer for review was also rejected by a letter dated 12-11-1965. After that, the plaintiff had submitted her original unregistered 'Bainapatra' in support of her transaction following the subsequent possession from its lawful owner and title holder of the suit property by exchange within the knowledge of defendant Nos. 1-3. But no notice was ever served on either of them under the provisions of East Bengal (Emergency) Requisition of property Act, while the plaintiff was thrown out of her own property most arbitrarily. The Order of permanent acquisition dated 8-6-1966 was disclosed for the first time on 7-11-1970, and the defendant in their written statement in Title Suit No. 51 of 1970 admitted the same, and following the requisition order, defendant No. I forcibly took possession of the suit property on 21-11-1965 after evicting the plaintiff, and in that aspect, the cause of action in Title Suit No. finally arose on 12-11-1965, when the defendants refused to interfere with requisition order made by defendant No.3's Head Office at Dhaka, and also filed Title Suit No.
7. Defendant Nos.1-3, contested the suit by filing written statement denying all the material statements made in the plaints. Their cases, in short, are that, the plaintiff was not the owner of the suit property, requisitioned under HR Case No. 12/63-64, and permanently acquired through LA Case No. 13/65-66 which was requisitioned for accommodation of the National Bank of Pakistan, Chuadanga Branch, where the plaintiff failed to produce any documents of her ownership. The acquisition notices under section 3 was issued on SA recorded tenant. The acquisition notices under section 5(1A) and 5(3) were issued, and served on 8-6-1966 and 9-6-1966 respectively, where advance payment was offered on 31-5-1966, but the owners did not appear to receive the advance payment as they were Indian nationals. The plaintiff has no locus standi or right, title and possession over the suit property. The permanent acquisition of the suit property is neither illegal nor void. The suit is not maintainable as the LA proceeding has been finalized long before, and no suit against an order passed or any action taken under Emergency Requisition Property Act was maintainable.
8. Defendant No.4, National Bank Limited, also contested the suit by filling written statement denying the material statements made in the plaint. Its case, in short, is that there is no cause of action against the defendant, and the suit is barred by limitation. The defendant does not admit the title of the plaintiff, and also of her predecessor Mahbub Hossain. The property was requisitioned on 26-5-1964 for public interest, and public purpose. The plaintiff failed to prove her title over the suit property, where the requisition notice was also issued on SA recorded tenants, and the said notice was also served upon the husband of the plaintiff as he had possessing the house at the time of requisition. The defendant No.4 got possession on 21-11-1965. The suit is not maintainable under section 14A of the Emergency Requisition Act, 1948, and, as such, the defendant prayed for dismissing the suit.
9. On conclusion of the trial, the Trial Court upon hearing the suits analogously, and on consideration of the evidence and materials on record, by its judgment and order dated 15-6-2002 dismissed the suits.
10. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the judgment and decree of the Trail Court, the plaintiff had been filed the First Appeal Nos. 349, 350 and 351 of 2002 before the High Court Division.
11. In due course, a Division Bench of the High Court Division upon hearing the parties disposed of all the appeals with observations by the impugned judgment and order dated 4-6-2009.
12. Feeling aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the impugned judgment and order passed by the High Court Division, the defendants as the leave-petitioners have filed these instant Civil Petitions for Leave to Appeal before this Division, and obtained leave, which, gave rise to the instant appeal.
13. Mr Sk Md Morshed, the learned Additional Attorney-General appearing on behalf of the appellants in all the appeals, submits that, the plaintiff not being the owner of the property requisitioned under HR Case No. 12/63-64 and permanently acquired through LA Case No.13 of 65-66 which was requisitioned for accommodation of National Bank of Pakistan (now Sonali Bank Limited), Chuadanga Branch, the High Court Division erred in modifying the decree of the Trail Court regarding title of the property. He further submits that, the requisition notice under section 3 was issued on SA recorded tenant and acquisition notices under sections 5(IA) and 5(3) were issued, and served on 8-6-1966 and 9-6-1966 respectively, and advanced payment was offered on 31-5-1966 and the owners failed to appear to receive the advance payment as they were Indian Nationals, and, as such, the High Court Division erred in law in modifying the decree of the Trial Court regarding reassessment of compensation according to the present market value. He then submits that, the plaintiff having no right, title, interest and possession in the suit property, and having no locus standi, and the LA proceeding having been finalized long before, and no objection having been taken against the said acquisition under Emergency Requisition of Property Act, the High Court Division erred in law in modifying the decree of the Trial Court. He lastly submits that, the suit of the plaintiff not being maintainable under section 14A of the Emergency Requisition of Property Act, 1984, and the plaintiff having failed to establish her ownership of the suit property, the High Court Division erred in law in modifying the decree passed by the Trail Court, and, as such, the impugned judgment of the High Court Division being not sustainable, and, the same is liable to be set-aside. Hence, he prayed that, the instant appeals may kindly be allowed.
14. Mr Bivash Chandra Biswas, the learned Advocate-on-Record appearing on behalf of the respondent No. 1 in all the cases submits that, the plaintiff acquired valid title by virtue of a deed of agreement, and by subsequent Kabala, and, as such, she became the owner of the property in question, then the finding and observation passed by the High Court Division in decreeing in the Title Suit No. 302 of 1976 may be sustained, and, hence, the High Court rightly passed the impugned judgment. He further submits that, the High Court Division passed an order directing the defendant appellants herein to reconsider the compensation on the assessment of the same for the purpose of permanent acquisition, but, to that, expect to judgment and order dated 4-6-2009 by the High Court Division was correct, and, legal. He finally submits that, the judgment and decree passed by the High Court Division was legal as the instant suit was maintainable as per provision of Section 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure, and, therefore, he prays for dismissal of the instant appeals.
15. Mr MA Sobhan, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the respondent No. 2 in Civil Appeal No. 194 of 2014 submits that, the plaintiff not being the owner of the property requisitioned under HR Case No.12/63-64, and permanently acquired through LA Case No. 13 of 65-66 which was requisitioned for the accommodation of National Bank of Pakistan (Now Sonali Bank Limited), Chuadanga Branch, Proforma Respondent No. 2 (defendant No. 4), and who got possession on 21-11-1965, and requisition notice under section 3 was issued on SA recorded tenant, and the acquisition novice under section 5(IA) and 5(3) of the Act, 1948, and served on 8-6-1966 and 31-5-1966, and owners failed to appear to receive the advance money as they were Indian Nationals. He further submits that, suits of the plaintiff are misconceived not being maintainable under section 14A of the Emergency Requisition of Property Act, 1948. He finally submits that, the plaintiff failed to prove her title over the suit property where the requisition notice was also issued on SA recorded tenants, and the said notice was also served upon the husband of the plaintiff as he had been possessing the house at the time of requisition. The impugned judgment passed by the High Court Division is illegal and not maintainable. Hence, the same is liable to be set-aside.
16. We have heard Mr Sk Md Morshed, the learned Additional Attorney-General for the appellants in all the cases, and Mr Bivash Chandra Biswas for the respondent No.1 in all the cases, and Mr MA Sobhan, the learned Advocate for the respondent No. 2 in Civil Appeal No.194 of 2014. Perused the impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division and other connected materials on record.
17. Leave was granted to examine the submissions made by the learned Deputy Attorney-General for the appellants as quoted below:—
"Mr Abdus Salam, learned Deputy Attorney-General, appearing on behalf of the leave-petitioners in all the petitions for leave to appeal, submits that the plaintiff not being the owner of the property requisitioned under HR Case No..12/63-64 and permanently acquired through LA Case No. 13 of 65-66 which was requisitioned for accommodation of National Bank of Pakistan (now Sonali Bank Limited), Chuadanga Branch, the High Court Division erred in modifying the decree of the Trial Court regarding title of the property. He further submits that the requisition notice under section 3 was issued on SA recorded tenant and acquisition notices under sections 5(1A) and 5(3) were issued and served on 8-6-1966 and 9-6-1966 respectively and advance payment was offered on 31-5-1966 and the owners failed to appear to receive the advance payment as they were Indian Nationals and, as such, the High Court Division erred in law in modifying the decree of the Trial Court regarding reassessment of compensation according to the present market value. He then submits that the plaintiff having no right, title, interest and possession in the suit property and having no locus standi and the LA proceeding having been finalized long before and no objection having been taken against the said acquisition under Emergency Requisition of Property Act, the High Court Division erred in law in modifying the decree of the Trial Court. He lastly submits that the suit of the plaintiff not being maintainable under section 14A of the Emergency Requisition of Property Act, 1948 and the plaintiff having failed to establish her ownership in the suit property, the High Court Division erred in law in modifying the decree passed by the trial Court."
18. At this moment let us weigh up the materials on record as to whether judgment and order of the High Court Division is justified or erred which calls for interference by this Division.
19. This Division in the case of Bangladesh and others vs Nawab Abdul Malik Jute Mills Ltd. reported in 60 DLR (AD) 7 pointed out that:—
"Once the property is acquired and gazette notification is published under section 5(7) of the Emergency Requisition of Property Act, 1948 (Act XIII of 1948), the right, title and interest if any of the owners are extinguished and preparation of Khatian or payment of rent does not improve the position of the original owners in respect of acquired land."
<u>20. In this case there is dispute of title as well as non-acceptance of compensation as assessed by the Deputy Commissioner concerned. However, there are provisions for settling these sorts of disputes as per section 7 of the (Emergency) Requisition of Property Act, 1948. As per sub-section (aaa) read with sub-section (b) these disagreements should be resolved by the Arbitrator appointed for these purposes and against the Arbitrator's Award, an appeal could be preferred to the High Court Division. The section is as follows:—</u>
<u>"7. Compensation for Immovable Property-Whenever any immovable property is requisitioned or acquired under this Act, there shall be paid compensation the amount of which shall be determined in the matter, and in accordance with the principles, hereinafter set out, that is to say,—</u>
<u>(a) where the amount of compensation can be fixed by agreement, it shall be paid in accordance with such agreement;</u>
<u>(aa) where no such agreement can be reached, the Deputy Commissioner shall, having regard to the provisions of clause (e), assess compensation for the immovable property, and shall after obtaining the approval of the Government thereto, give immediate notice of the assessment to the person or persons interested;</u>
<u>(aaa)(i) any person interested, who has not accepted the assessment made under clause (aa), may make an application to an arbitrator appointed under clause(b), for an award,</u>
<u>(ii) the application shall state the grounds on which objection to the assessment is taken: Provided that every such application shall be made within six weeks of the service of the notice by the (Deputy Commissioner) under clause (aa)</u>
<u>(b) the arbitrator referred to in sub-section (1) of clause (aaa) shall be a judicial officer not below the rank of a Subordinate Judge and shall be appointed by the Government by notification in the Official Gazette;</u>
<u>(bb) Application hereto filed and pending with the Government for making reference to an arbitrator for awards shall stand transferred to the arbitrator concerned appointed under clause (b);</u>
<u>(c) the Government may, in any particular case, nominate a person having expert knowledge as to the nature of the property requisitioned or acquired, to assist the arbitrator, and where such nomination is made the person to be compensated may also nominate an assessor for the said purpose; See sub-rules (5), (6), (7) & (15) of rule 9 of the Rules).</u>
<u>(cc) On receipt of an application under clause (aaa) the arbitrator shall give notice of such application to the Deputy Commissioner who shall forward a copy thereof to the requiring person, if any;</u>
<u>(d) at the commencement of the proceedings before the arbitrator, the Deputy Commissioner, the person to be compensated and the requiring person, if any, shall state what, in their respective opinions, is a fair amount of compensation and shall produce all the documents in their possession or power on which they intend to rely;</u>
<u>(e) the arbitrator in making his award shall have regard to the provisions of sections 23 and 24 and sub-section (2) of section 35 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, so far as the same can be made applicable: Provided that—</u>
<u>(i) the market-value of any immovable property for the purpose of this section shall be the "weighted average value, calculated in the manner prescribed by the rule made by the Government and after excluding abnormally high and low sale figures" of the properties of a similar description and, with similar advantages in the vicinity, during the (twenty-four months) preceding the date of the service of notice under sub-section (la) of section 5;</u>
<u>(ii) where the public purpose, for which the immovable property is acquired under section 5, is the establishment of an industry by a person other than the Government, the arbitrator shall, in addition to such market value of the immovable property, award a sum of twenty-five per centum on the market value, instead of fifteen per centum as provided in sub-section (2) of section 23 of the Land Acquisition Act (I of 1894), in consideration of the compulsory nature of the acquisition; and</u>
<u>(iii) in awarding compensation for the requisition of any immovable property to which the provisions of the Premises Rent Control Ordinance, 1961, (Ordinance XXV of 1961) or any other law for the time being in force, for the control of house-rent, apply, the arbitrator shall have regard to those provisions, so that the compensations awarded may not exceed the amount of rent allowable in respect of such property under those provisions.</u>
<u>(f) an appeal shall lie to the High Court against an award of an arbitrator except in cases where the amount thereof does not exceed an amount specified in this behalf by rule made by the Government;</u>
<u>(g) save as provided in this section and in any rules made thereunder nothing in any law for the time being in force shall apply to arbitrations under this section."</u>
21. All of the 03 suits are not maintainable under section 14A of the Emergency Requisition of Property Act; 1948. The relevant laws are as follows:—
"14A. Bar to jurisdiction of Civil Court—
Except as expressly provided in this Act, no Civil Court shall entertain any suit or application against any order passed or any action taken under this Act and all suits and appeals pending in any such Court against any order passed or any action taken under this Act shall abate with effect from the date of coming into force of the (Emergency) Requisition of Property (Amendment) Ordinance, 1963."
22. Accordingly, we find merit in submissions of the learned Additional Attorney-General for the appellants.
23. Hence, our considered view is that the High Court Division erred in law in modifying the decree of the Trial Court.
Accordingly, these appeals are allowed. The impugned judgment and order passed by the High Court Division is set-aside.
End.

parties:
Abdus Salmi Murshedy and others -------- Petitioners
vs
Envoy Textiles Limited and others ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
By filing an application under section 233 of the Companies Act, 1994 (hereinafter referred to as the Companies Act), the petitioners raised a number of allegations of mismanagement of Envoy Textiles Limited (hereafter referred to either as the Company or the respondent No. 1) by the majority Directors of the Company's present Board of Directors, and sought for a declaration to the effect that the activities of the majorities in the Board of Directors of the Company were illegal and prejudicial to the interest of the petitioners. 2. The petitioners are mainly aggrieved by (1) the minutes of the EGM held on 12-5-2022 (mistakenly stated as 18-4-2022 in the prayer which is the date of the notice of EGM convened on 12-5-2022) whereat certain articles of the Company's Articles of Association were amended, (2) minutes of the Board Meeting held on 8-6-2022 whereat three Additional Directors, one Vice-Chairman and one Independent Director vide agenda Nos. 5, 6 & 7 were appointed and (3) the Notice of the 13th NRC meeting, which was scheduled to be held on 12-6-2022 (so far as it relates to the said meeting's agenda Nos. 2 & 3) by which cessation of the service of Mr Abdus Salam Murshedy ( the petitioner No. 1) from the post of the Company's Managing Director was undertaken vide agenda No. 2 and Mr Tanvir Ahmed (the respondent No. 4, who happens to be the son of the respondent No. 2-Mr Kutubuddin Ahmed) was in the consideration for appointment as the replacement of the petitioner No. 1 by the agenda No. 3. 3. And, at the time of admission of this case, an Order staying the minutes of the Board Meeting dated 8-6-2022 made with reference to its agenda Nos. 5, 6 & 7, decisions of the Extraordinary General Meeting (EGM) dated 12-5-2022 taken on the basis of its agenda Nos. vii, viii, xiii and xiv and the agenda Nos. 2 & 3 of the Notice of 13th Nomination and Remuneration Committee (NRC) meeting, which was scheduled to be held on 12-6-2022, was passed by this Court. 4. The background facts of approaching this Court by the parties of this case are that the Company was incorporated under the laws of Bangladesh in the year 1995 with objective to carry on the businesses of, among others, manufacturing and exporting denim fabric. Even though the Company was incorporated in 1995, it was not in operation until 2009 when the Company was converted into a Public Limited Company. The Company, thereafter, was enlisted with the stock exchanges in 2012. The petitioners together are holding a total of 13.86% shares of the Company. The authorised share capital of the Company is Taka 400,00,00,000 (Taka four hundred crores) divided into Taka 40,00,00,000 (Taka forty crores) shares comprising Taka 27,50,00,000 (Taka twenty seven crore fifty lacs) ordinary shares of Taka 10 (Taka ten) each with rights, privileges and conditions attached thereto. The petitioners are holding 2,32,44292 paid up shares, the respondent Nos. 2-5 are holding 7,25,29555 shares. As per the latest audited Financial Statements, the current total assets of the Company are valued at Taka 19,719,935,768 and the total liabilities are at Taka 6,729,934,040. The Board of Directors (hereinafter referred to as the "Board") was initially consisted of four members each from the family of the petitioner No. 1 and the respondent No. 2. Eventually two Independent Directors were appointed by the respondent No. 2 in order to comply with the requirements of Bangladesh Securities and Exchange Commission (BSEC) and, after these two Independent Directors' appointments, whenever the petitioners voted against various agenda to protect interest of shareholders, they could not validate their remarks because of minority voting. Recently, the petitioners have taken over the entire Envoy Group along with its subsidiary companies and since then, the respondent Nos. 2-7 have started to create complications in the affairs of the Company, which are evident from the minutes of the EGM dated 12-5-2022, minutes of the Board Meeting dated 8-6-2022 and agenda Nos. 2 & 3 of the Notice dated 12-6-2022 of the 13th NRC Meeting. 5. It is stated that on 18-4-2022 a notice of the EGM was circulated to the effect that an EGM will be held of the shareholders of the Company on 12-5-2022 in which the proposed amendments of the articles were being laid down to be approved by Special Resolution by the share-holders and, subsequently, on 12-5-2022 the respondents, being the majority shareholders of the Company, approved the aforesaid alteration of Article of Association and, thereafter, on 22-5-2022 a notice was served for the meeting of NRC to discuss the matter of appointment of Additional Directors and Independent Director and selection of a Vice-Chairman of the Company and, subsequently, on 30-5-2022, the said meeting was held in presence of petitioner No. 2, respondent No. 3 and respondent No. 6. During the meeting the petitioner No. 2 raised strong objection in regard to the aforesaid agenda but, respondent No. 3 and respondent No. 6, paying no heed to the objections raised by the petitioner No. 2, recommended appointment Additional Directors and Independent Director and also recommended selection of Mr Sheikh Bashir as the Vice-Chairman of the Company. Subsequently, on 30-5-2022, the petitioners received notice of the Board Meeting mentioning the agenda of appointment of the Additional Directors, appointments of a Vice-Chairman and an Independent Director. Dismayed, the petitioners Nos. 1 & 2 sent letters to the Chairman. on 5-6-2022 and requested to take necessary action in relation to the decision of appointment of Additional Directors by calling of the agenda Nos. 5, 6 & 7 of the meeting scheduled to be held on 6-8-2022 for securing the best interest of the Company. However, the respondent Nos. 2-7 without considering the letters and objections raised by the petitioner Nos. 1 & 2 on 8-6-2022 held the Board Meeting. On 11-6-2022 the respondent No. 2 issued a letter to the NRC directing them to recommend the method of cessation of the employment of the current Managing Director and consider the respondent No. 4 as replacement in the place of Managing Director. Based on that, the NRC issued a notice dated 12-6-2022 to the effect that the committee will consider and recommend cessation on any other course of action with regard to the Managing Director i.e. the petitioner No. 1 and the next agenda implies recommendation for the appointment of a new Managing Director. The said notice was served to the petitioner No. 2 on 16-6-2022 late afternoon though the petitioners and the respondent Nos. 2-5 have their official address at the same building and they stay at their official address during office hours, but with ulterior motive of deprivation from taking any legal resort, the respondent No. 2 did not let' the notice to be served accordingly on time. Thereafter, on 16-6-2022, the petitioner No. 2 sent an email to the Company Secretary requesting him to reschedule the said NRC meeting considering her medical issues, and after series of email, the Company Secretary confirmed that 13th NRC meeting would be held on 22-6-2023 at 4.30 p.m. 6. It is stated that in the last Annual General Meeting (AGM) dated 28-12-2021, though it was decided and approved that respondent No. 2 will be continuing as .the Chairman till 27th AGM to be 'held in 2023 and the petitioner No. 1 will be continuing as the Managing Director till 30th AGM to beheld on 2025, however, by the above-mentioned impugned decisions of the NRC, EGM and Board Meeting, when the respondents were in the process of appointing Mr Tanyir. Ahmed (respondent No. 4) as the Managing Director of the Company, Mr Sheikh Bashir Ahmed (respondent No. 10) as the Vice-Chairman of the Company and Mr Rezaur Raharnan Sohag (respondent No. 7A) as an Independent Director of the Company, the petitioners having invoked section 233 of the Companies Act filed the instant application for redress. 7. By filing an affidavit-in-opposition, supplemented by a number of subsequent affidavits, the respondent Nos. 1 to 7 state, amongst others, that the petitioner No. 1 and the respondent No. 2 together had common share-holding in certain RMG Companies and Textile Companies and recently it was mutually decided with the understanding that the most of the RMG companies would be owned and managed by the petitioner No. 1 and his family, whereas the Textile businesses would be managed by the respondent No. 2 and his family and, accordingly, vide agreement dated 29-11-2021, the said understanding was executed; that after the division, it was revealed that petitioner No. 1 imported chiller machine in the name of the respondent No. 1-Company by declaring them to be the capital machinery of this Company, but actually those were imported for the purpose of installation in his personal commercial building located in Uttara; that the petitioner No. 1 is functioning as the Managing Director in another company; that the petitioner No. 1 has never professionally discharged his duties as the Managing Director of the Company as he hardly visits the factory and Head Office of the Company; that two Independent Directors were appointed as per the requirements of BSEC following the Corporate Governance Code, 2018; that the operating Board in the Board Meetings dated 22-3-2022 and 18-4-2022 proposed amendments to certain articles of the Articles of Association of the Company, including Articles 128, 129, 137, 140, 145 and 147, following which, an EGM was held on 12-5-2022, wherein the proposed amendments to the Articles of Association of the Company were approved by a Special Resolution by the shareholders of the Company and, on 22-5-2022, a notice was served to the NRC for a meeting regarding the appointment of Additional Directors and Independent Director and selection of a Vice-Chairman of the Company pursuant to the amended Articles of Association; that the meeting duly took place on 30-5-2022 whereupon recommendations were made regarding the appointment of Additional Directors, Independent Director and Vice-Chairman; that the appointments of the recommended members of the Board were subsequently completed in the Board Meeting dated 8-6-2022 and, accordingly, Form IX (consent to act as a Director) and Form XII (Particulars of Directors) were submitted before the RISC which were duly recorded and, pursuant thereto, certified copy of the Form XII was issued by the RJSC recording the changes in the Board of Directors; that on 11-6-2022, the respondent No. 2 issued a letter to the NRC requesting a recommendation regarding the method of cessation of the employment of the position of Managing Director of the Company; that on the following day (i.e., 12-6-2022), the NRC issued a notice calling a meeting for the committee to consider and recommend cessation or any other course of action with regard to the Managing Director, but petitioner No. 2 through emailing the Company Secretary rescheduled the NRC meeting, claiming to have medical issues and being unable to attend on the scheduled date and, accordingly, the NRC Meeting was rescheduled to 22-6-2022. But before the scheduled meeting took place, the instant application under section 233 of the Companies Act was filed by the petitioners allegedly for protection of minority shareholders. 8. Mr Mohammad Mehedi Hassan Chowdhury, the learned Senior Advocate appearing for the petitioners, by placing the provisions of sub-section (1) of section 233 of the Companies Act and, side-by-side, taking me through the latest Schedule-X of the Company, contends that the petitioners jointly hold more than 10% shares in the Company and, hence, they are well-competent to file the instant application. By referring to the cases of (1) Vijoy Krishan Jaidka vs Jaidka Motor Comp. Ltd. [1997] 1 Comp. LI 268, 285 and (2) KN Bhargava vs Trackparts Indian Ltd. & others (2001) 104 Cornp. Case 611, CLB, he submits that mismanagement of the company and usurpation of the office of Managing Director of the company named in the Articles and, also, the burdensome, harsh and wrongful conduct of the majority members of the company that lacks degree of probity which they are entitled to expect in the conduct of the company's affairs are covered under section 233 of the Companies Act. 9. He next submits that all the changes were made in the Articles of Association with an ulterior motive of removing the petitioner No. 1 from the post of Managing Director and, hence, the same are illegal. By referring to the cases of ABS Safdar and others vs Bangladesh, 52 DLR 249 and Syed Al-Nesar Ahmed vs Nafisa Chowdhury and others 53 DLR (AD) 83, he submits that taking any resolution for changing the Articles of a company with an ulterior motive by the majorities are not permissible. He submits that in the case of a public company if it is seen that it is a family company with two identifiable groups of shareholders who are in the management of the company, then, in such a case, removal of any such Director from the management with ulterior motive could be considered to be an act of oppression. He submits that creation of the posts of Additional Directors by incorporation of Article 124 is a sheer violation of the provisions of section 91 of the Companies Act and, as such, appointments of three Additional Directors and Mr Sheikh Bashir as the Vice-Chairman of the Company are illegal. He, then, places minutes of the NRC meeting dated 30-5-2022 in tandem with the provisions of Code 1(3) of the Corporate Governance Code, 2018 and submits that recommendations made by the NRC for appointments of Mr Sohag as an Independent Director and approval thereto given by the BSEC have been done in violation of the conditions stipulated in Code 1(3) of the Corporate Governance Code and, hence, the said appointment is illegal. He next submits that NRC cannot be dictated by the Chairman of the Company in the appointments of the Managing Director or any other Director or top executives of the Company. 10. By referring to the case of Re Company (No.00477 of 1986) 11986] BCLC 376, he submits that the Directors may act as per the terms of the Companies Act and yet again such actions could be prejudicial to the interest of the minority shareholders who had more than ten percent of the shares issued and, thus, a member of the company has a legitimate right to take part in the management of a quasi-partnership company if he had a legitimate expectation to continue to be a Director of the company. By referring to the case of Nurul Hoque Chowdhury vs Mrs. Mahzabin Chowdhury, 2004 (12) BLT (I-1CD) 261, he submits that the acts of a Director must pass the test of reasonableness and fairness and, in this case, since the timeline 'of the alteration in the Articles and modification in the managerial position is absolutely not reasonable, it was not bon fide. By referring to the case of MA Gafur vs RISC, 64 DLR 547, he submits that even if all members of the Board adopted a unanimous resolution that can also be prejudicial to the 3rd parties or even in doing or ratifying an ultra-vires act and, in such circumstances, section 233 of the Companies Act gives the Court wide powers to pass appropriate Orders. 11. By making the above submissions, the learned Advocate for the petitioners prays for cancellation of the minutes of the Board Meeting dated 8-6-2022 made with reference to its agenda Nos. 5, 6 & 7, decisions of the EGM dated 18-4-2022 taken on the basis of its agenda Nos. vii, viii, xiii and xiv and the decisions corresponding to agenda Nos. 2 & 3 of the 13th NRC meeting held on 12-6-2022 and, further, prays for appointment of an Independent Chairman to fairly carry out the responsibilities of the Company, to chair meetings and perform all other necessary incidental and consequential responsibilities in place of the respondent No. 2 and also to appoint an Independent Auditor to carry out a special audit of the Company for the purpose of ascertaining the true and correct financial affairs of the Company. 12. Per contra, Mr Tanjib-ul Alam, the learned Senior Advocate appearing on behalf of the respondent Nos. 1 & 2, takes this Court through section 233 of the Companies Act and submits that the instant case is not maintainable under section 233 of the Companies. Act as it fails to satisfy any of the following requirements of section 233 of the Companies Act: either (i) the affairs are being conducted in a prejudicial manner to the shareholders or (ii) any action taken by the company is discriminatory to the shareholders or (iii) a resolution is passed which is discriminatory to the interest of the shareholders. By placing before this Court the Judgments passed in the cases of (1) Re Saul D Harrison & Sons Pls [1995] 1 BCLC 14, (2) Marikar (Motors) and another vs MI Ravikumar and others 52 Comp Cases (1982) 362 and (3) ASM Shamsul Islam Reashedi vs Satellite Fishing Ltd., 54 DLR 28, he submits that in addition to fulfilling the requirements of section 233 of the Companies Act, the petitioners must satisfy that the conduct of the respondents were both prejudicial and unfair; but none of the elements, let alone both the elements as are required by the principles laid down in the afore-cited cases, is present in this case.
