He submits that if any person is potentially to be affected by the proposed cessation of the Managing Director, it is the petitioner No. 1, and since he does not personally have the qualification-shares to file an application under section 233 of the Companies Act, his family members, petitioner Nos. 2-4, have joined the instant proceeding in total disregard of the law. 13. With regard to the petitioners' submissions that the instant application is maintainable even though the same has been filed by the persons from management of the Company, for which the petitioners have relied on the case-laws of (1) Vijoy Krishan Jaidka and others vs Jaidka Motor Co. Ltd. 11997] 1 Comp LJ 268 (CLB) and (2) KN Bhargava and others vs Tracparts of India and others 2001 104 CompCas 11 CLB, the learned Advocate for the respondent Nos. 2-7 submits that such contention is misdirected. In a bid to elaborate his submissions, he contends that in Vijay Krishan Jaidka and others vs Jaidka Motor Co. Ltd. [19971 1 Comp Li 268 (CLB), only one family was involved as the father of the petitioner No. 1 and the respondent No. 2 were consanguine brothers and incorporated the company which was not a listed company, but in the instant case, the Company has been incorporated by two families who have parted their ways through an Agreement dated 29-11-2021 and the Company is a publicly listed company and, as such, the ratio of the aforecited cases is not applicable in the instant Company Matter; and in the case of KN Bhargava and others vs Tracparts of India and others 2001 104 CompCas 11 CLB, although the company in question was a publicly listed company, the shareholders were from a single family and, furthermore, the petitioners of the said case filed the application under sections 397 and 398 of the Indian Companies Act, 1956 for specific performance of the Family Agreement between the parties and, in the instant Company Matter, the petitioners and the respondent Nos. 2-5 are from. different families and also parted their ways through an Agreement dated 29-11-2021. 14. Mr Alam, then, submits that the first relief that has been prayed for by the petitioners is to cancel the minutes of the Board Meeting dated 8-6-2022 taken/made on the basis of its agenda Nos. 5, 6 and 7, which are about appointments of Additional Directors, Vice-Chairman and Independent Director in the Company, but inclusion in the management of a publicly listed company is not a right qua member and no shareholder's rights are being prejudiced and /or facing unfairness by the conduct of the majority shareholders of the Company and, hence, the superfluous apprehension of the petitioners that they will be minority in the Board is nothing but a sweet will of the petitioners to remain in the Board of the Company and, more importantly, since the appointments have been made pursuant to Articles of Association of the Company and as per the Companies Act and Code of Corporate Governance, no question can be raised by the petitioners about these appointments. He submits that the second relief that has been prayed for by the petitioners is to cancel the decisions of EGM dated 12-5-2022 made on the basis of its agenda Nos. vii, viii, xiii and xiv which are amendments to the Articles of Association of the Company through inclusion of Article 128A, amendments to Articles 128, 129, 145 and 147, but the petitioners have patently failed to raise any specific allegation as to how the said amendments are unfair and/or prejudicial to their interest in the Company. He argues that since prior to the appointment of the Additional Directors in the Board, there were 4(four) Directors from each of the families of the petitioner No: 1 and the respondent No. 2, and the respondent No. 2, as the Chairman of the Company, having got casting-vote under Article 133 of the Articles of Association of the Company, the petitioners were always minority in the Board and, as such, arguing that the petitioners have become minority in the Board by the appointment of the Additional Directors is a poor and desperate attempt to grasp at straws by misleading the Court. 15. Mr Alam next submits that the scheme of the Companies Act is to provide the shareholders of a company to run and manage as per the decision of the majority shareholders, which has been confirmed by a long line of case-laws of different jurisdictions, including Bangladesh. By referring to the case of Nurul Hoque Chozodhury vs Mahzabin Chowdhury 2004 (12) ELT (I-1CD) 261, the case of Foss vs Harbottle (1843) and the case of Marikar (Motors) and another vs MI Ravikumar and others reported in 52 Comp Cases (1982) 362, he submits that the Court will not interfere with the decision of the majority shareholders at the objections of the minority shareholders unless the same falls under the exceptions as mentioned in the aforecited cases. 16. By putting forward the above submissions, the learned Advocate for the respondents prays for rejecting the instant application under section 233 of the Companies Act with an exemplary cost. 17. The learned Advocate for the respondent No. 4 Mr Mustafizur Rahman Khan, in making his submissions mostly adopted the submissions advanced by Mr Tanjib-ul Alam, the learned Advocate for the respondent Nos. 1-2, but he added that since the respondent No. 4 has been working as the Managing Director of the Company by virtue of an interim Order passed by this Court on the basis of the consent given by all the parties before this Court, he should be allowed to continue to serve as the Managing Director in the greater interest of the shareholders and other stakeholders of the Company and, further, since the Additional Directors have been appointed in compliance with the provisions of Regulation 86 and Article 124 of the Articles of Association of the Company, they should be allowed to be in the Board. 18. Mr AM Masum, the learned Advocate appearing for the respondent No. 9, the Bangladesh Securities and Exchange Commission (BSEC), places the different provisions of Securities and Exchange Ordinance, 1969, BSEC Rules, (Public Issue), 2006, BSEC Rules (Public Issue), 2015 and Corporate Governance Code, 2018 and submits that it is mandatory for all the listed companies to comply with the provisions of the Corporate Governance Code promulgated by the BSEC from time to time. By taking this Court through the Consent Letter dated 5-6-2012 issued by BSEC in favour of Envoy Textiles Limited, he submits that Part-D Clause-2 of the said Consent Letter mandatorily requires the Company to comply with BSEC (Public Issue) Rules, 2006, as, in order to make an application for public offer of its securities, the issuer has to comply with the provisions of Corporate Governance Guidelines as per Rule 3(2)(i) of the BSEC (Public Issue) Rules, 2015 and, as per its Rule 16, if any issuer violates the provisions of these Rules, the BSEC can take appropriate actions under the Securities and Exchange Ordinance, 1969. He next submits that Regulation 7(2)(vii) of Dhaka Stock Exchange Listing Regulation, 2015 makes it mandatory for the issuer of listed securities to comply with the provisions of the Corporate Governance Guidelines as prescribed by BSEC from time to time and, as per Regulation 36 of the Regulations, 2015, the issuer of listed securities has to include a compliance certificate upon compliance of the conditions of the Corporate Governance Code in its Annual Report and Regulation 51(1)(c) of the Regulations, 2015 has provision to delist an issuer if there is a failure to comply with the Corporate Governance Code. 19. By placing the present and previous versions of Articles 128 and 129 of the Articles of Association, he contends that since the previous Articles 128 and 129 of the Articles of Association of the Company were in violation of Code 3(1)(b) and Code 1(4)(a), (b) and (e) of the Corporate Governance Code, as under no circumstances and at no junction the Chairman and the Managing Director can be the same person. He submits that the previous Article 145 of the Articles of Association of the Company allowed the petitioner No. 1 to remain as the Managing. Director of the Company till his death or until he resigns which is a direct violation of section 110 of the Companies Act as well as Code 3(1) of the Corporate Governance Code. He submits that pursuant to section 1.30 of the Companies Act it is incumbent upon every Director who is directly or indirectly concerned or interested in any contract or arrangement entered into by or on behalf of the company to disclose his personal interest at the meeting of the Directors and, that is why, if at any given time it transpires that the Managing Director hasn't disclosed his connection in any contract entered into by or on behalf of the company, and if at that point of time due to the absence of the Chairman, the Managing Director presides over the Board Meeting, then the agenda to remove the Managing Director shall not get any approval as removal of Managing Director from the Board is not possible without approval of the Board as per Code 3(1)(e) of the Corporate Governance Code. He contends that the petitioner No. 1 has previous record of violating the Code 1(5)(vi) of the Corporate Governance Code as well as section 130 of the Companies Act when he did not disclose the fact of importing the chillers for his personal business using the Company's name. He alleges that Code 9 of the Corporate Governance Code requires the Company to obtain a certificate, which needs to be affixed in the Annual Report from a practicing Professional Accountant or Secretary regarding the compliance of the Corporate Governance Code, but the petitioner No. 1 committed non-compliance with the Code in the past as the Managing Director. 20. He next submits that the Nomination and Remuneration Committee (NRC) of the Company consisting of one Independent Director and two non-executive Directors, one of which is the petitioner No. 2, has resolved that Mr Sohag qualifies with the conditions of the Corporate Governance Code to be appointed as an Independent Director since he has equivalent academic qualification and professional experiences as per Code 1(3)(b)(v) of the Corporate Governance Code and since it was earlier agreed to by the petitioner No. 2 in the NRC that his appointment as an Independent Director will make meaningful contribution to the business and, hence, the appointment of Mr Sohag was consented to by the BSEC h wing found his qualifications in accordance with Code 1(3) of the Corporate Governance Code. 21. Upon hearing the learned Advocates for all the sides, on perusal of the application as well as the affidavit-in-opposition filed by the respondents together with their annexures and reading the relevant statutory laws and case-laws cited from the various Law Journals of home and abroad, it appears to this Court that the following issues are to be adjudicated upon by this Court; (1) whether the instant petition is maintainable, (2) whether the changes in the Articles of Association of the Company were made bonafide, and whether amendments in the Articles of Association of the Company have been done legally, (3) whether creation of the posts of Additional Directors are permissible in the law, (4) whether, in making recommendations to the post of Managing Director, the NRC performed its functions in compliance with the provisions of the Corporate Governance Code, (5) whether recommendation by the NRC for appointment of Mr Rezaur Rahaman Sohag as an Independent Director was lawful and whether BSEC's approval thereto was proper, (6) whether the petitioner No. 1 has any legitimate expectation to remain in the post of the Managing Director of the Company, and whether the decision taken in the last AGM held on 28-12-2021 as to keeping the petitioner No. 1 as the Managing Director of the Company till 2025 is binding upon the Company, and whether in a publicly listed company, its Managing Director can preside over the meeting of Directors in absence of the Chairman of the company, and (7) whether the petitioner No. 1 has earned any disqualification to act as the Managing Director of the Company? 22. For the sake of brevity and ease of understanding, the issue No. 1 (i.e. the issue of maintainability) will be taken up after examining the rest of the issues of the case, as framed by this Court and, accordingly, let me now take up the issue No. 2, namely, whether the changes in the Articles of Association of the Company were made bonafide, and whether amendments in the Articles of Association of the Company have been done legally. 23. Since the petitioners are questioning the purpose and mode of amendments of Article. Nos. 128, 129, 137, 140, 145 and 147 of the Articles of Association of the Company, it would be useful to look at the previous and amended versions of the above-mentioned articles upon reproducing them serially. Article 128 in the past contained the following provisions: "Mr Kutubuddin Ahmed shall be the first Chairman and on his retirement the Board of Directors shall elect a Chairman from amongst themselves who shall be paid such remuneration as may be decided by the Board." 24. The amended version reads as follows: "Mr Kutubuddin Ahmed shall be the first Chairman and on his retirement the Board of Directors shall elect a Chairman from amongst themselves. 25. Though no significant amendment has been made in the afore-quoted Article 128 of the Articles of Association of the Company, however, an addition thereto has been made by inserting a new article, being Article 128A, which is quoted below: "128A. The Board of Directors shall elect a Vice-Chairman from amongst themselves who shall be a non-Executive Director. In the absence of Chairman, the Vice-Chairman shall preside over the meetings and shall perform such other functions as may be decided upon by the Board from time to time." 26. The previous Article 129 refers to: "All meetings of Directors shall be presided over by the Chairman and in his absence, the Managing Director and in the absence of them; the Directors present shall choose another Director to preside over the meeting". 27. This Article 129 has been substituted as: "All meetings of Board of Directors shall be presided over by the Chairman and in his absence, the vice-chairman. If both the Chairman and Vice-Chairman are absent from the meeting, the Directors so present shall elect one among themselves to act as the Chairman of the meeting and preside over the same" 28. On these changes in Articles of Association, Mr Mohammad Mehedi Hassan Chowdhury, the learned Senior Advocate appearing for the petitioners, contends that through the insertion of Article 128A and the amendment of Article 129 of the Articles of Association of the Company, the Managing Director's right to preside over a meeting in absence of the Chairman has been replaced by constituting a new post called "Vice-Chairman" who will be presiding over the meeting instead of the Managing Director. He contends that this new position has been created entirely with an ulterior motive of curtailing the power of the petitioner No.1 as the Managing Director, so that he cannot raise his voice in the interest of the Company. 29. On the other hand, Mr Tanjib-ul Alam, the learned Senior Advocate appearing for the respondent Nos. 1-2, submits that Clause 1(4)(a) of the Corporate Governance Code, 2018 does not permit the Managing Director of a company to chair a meeting of a Board of Directors and requires the positions of Chairperson and Managing Director to be filled by different individuals, and since, the Chairman of the Company is the respondent No. 2, in his absence, it will not be possible for the petitioner No. 1 to chair the Board Meeting of the Company as per the Corporate Governance Code and, that is why, in order to avoid such an issue, Article 128A was included in the Articles of Association of the Company, and since previously as per Article 129, the Managing Director could fill in the position of Chairman in the absence of the Chairman, as such, amendments to the Article 129 has also been made to be in line with the Clause 1(4)(a) of the Corporate Governance Code and providing the opportunity to fill in the position of Chairperson by the Vice-Chairman. Mr Tanjib-ul Alam submits that the aforesaid amendments to Articles of Association of the Company were made with full consent of the petitioners. 30. At this point, Code 1(4)(a) and (c) of the Corporate Governance Code may be quoted for examination of the contentious arguments advanced by the learned Senior Advocates from the petitioners' side and respondents' side. "(4) Duality of Chairperson of the Board of Directors and Managing Director or Chief Executive Officer.— (a) The positions of the Chairperson of the Board and the Managing Director (MD) and/or Chief Executive Officer (CEO) of the company shall be filled by different individuals; (b) .............. (c) The Chairperson of the Board shall be elected from among the non-executive Directors of the company." 31. From a plain reading of the afore-quoted law, this Court finds that the BSEC has amply made it clear for the public limited companies that the Managing Director and Chairman of a public limited company must not be the same person; meaning that two different persons must be appointed for the posts of the Managing Director and the Chairman. In other words, while the Managing Director of a public company cannot perform the functions of the Chairman of the same public company, vice versa, the Chairman of a public company cannot serve as the Managing Director of a public company at a time. It follows that since the Managing Director of a public company cannot hold the post of the Chairman of the same public company at a time, there is no scope for the Managing Director of a public company to chair the meeting of the same public company. 32. Thus, from a concurrent reading of the present and previous versions of Article Nos. 128 and 129 of the Company's Articles of Association in tandem with the provisions of Code 1(4)(a) and (c) of the Corporate Governance Code, it appears to this Court that that by inserting Article 128A and by amendment of Article 129 of the Articles of Association of the Company, the Company introduced a Vice-Chairman to preside over the Board Meetings in the absence of the Chairman. Previously Article 129 had allowed the Managing Director to perform the duties of the Chairman of the Company when the Chairman is to be found absent, which is a clear violation of Code 1(4)(a) & (c) of the Corporate Governance Code and, thus, this alteration in the Articles of Association of the Company appears to this Court to be for the purpose of bringing the provisions of the said Articles 128 and 129 of the Company's Articles of Association in line with the Companies Act, conditions of the Corporate Governance Code as well as Regulation 54 of the Schedule-1 of the Companies Act, so that the same person cannot function as the Managing Director and Chairman of the Company at a time. This is all the more relevant in the context that whenever an occasion will arise to remove the Managing Director because of violation of section 130 of the Companies Act or for any other reason during the incumbency of the said Managing Director, and he presides over the meeting as the Chairman of the Company due to absence of the Company's regular Chairman, it shall not be possible to remove him. Hence, this Court finds the purpose of insertion of Article 128A and the amendment of Article 129 to be bonaficle. 33. The previous Article 137 and the amended one are quoted below: "Three Directors present in person shall form quorum for a Directors meeting of the Company". The change reflects as; "Five Directors present in person shall form quorum for a Directors meeting of the Company". 34. The present version of Article 140 of the Articles of Association is as follows: "A resolution in writing, signed by all the Directors for the time being in Bangladesh (not being less than three Directors) shall be as valid and effectual if it had been passed at a meeting of the Directors duly called and constituted". 35. The amended version of Article 140 runs as follows: "A resolution in writing, signed by all the Directors for the time being in Bangladesh (not being less than five Directors) shall be as valid and effectual if it had been passed at a meeting of the Directors duly called and constituted". 36. Regarding the afore-quoted changes in the Articles, Mr Mohammad Mehedi Hassan Chowdhury, the learned Senior Advocate for the petitioners, submits that the majority Directors have acted in breach of their duty inasmuch as they have changed Article 137 of the Company with an ill-motive of depriving the opinion and assessment of the petitioners, for, because of increasing the requirement of Directors to 5(five) from 3(three) being present in the meeting for fulfilling quorum, the petitioners being a 4(four) family members will never be able to form quorum at any meeting of the Company, while the respondent No.2 would easily in co-operation with his close acquaintances i.e. respondent Nos. 6 & 7, would form quorum and will establish any decision. He submits that the words "not being less than three Directors" have been substituted by "not being less than five Directors" to deprive the petitioners from giving validity of a resolution. 37. Per contra, Mr Tanjib-ul Alam, the learned Senior Advocate for the respondent Nos. 2-7, contends that the Board of the Company consists of 10 (ten) members out of -which 2 (two) of the members are appointed as Independent Directors and the remaining 8 (eight) members are the petitioner Nos. 1 to 4 and respondent Nos. 2-5 and, therefore, since both the petitioners and the respondents have equal voting right, there is always scope for the petitioners to raise their voices. However, given that the Chairman of the Company is empowered by Article 133 of the Company's Articles of Association to cast a casting-vote, in the past also the petitioners were minority in the Board, Mr Alam adds to this count of submission. 38. At this juncture, it would be useful for the Court to look at the wordings of Article 133 of the Company's Articles of Association which runs as follows: The Directors may meet together for the dispatch of the business of the Company and may adjourn and otherwise regulate their meetings as they think fit. Questions arising at any meeting shall be decided by a simple majority of votes. In the event of an equality of votes, the Chairman shall have a second or casting vote. 39. From a perusal of the provisions of Article 133 of the Company's Articles of Association, it is apparent that the Chairman is empowered to cast a second vote in a scenario where votes are found to be equal for and against an agenda and, therefore, the petitioners were always minority in the Board because of Chairman's casting-vote. Furthermore, the Company being a public limited company, there shall always be required number of Independent Directors to form quorum as well as to give validity to a resolution in conjunction with the petitioners' attendance and, thus, even if all the family members of the respondent Na. 2 remain absent in attending a meeting, the petitioners along with the Independent Directors are competent to form quorum for the meeting. Therefore, this Court does not find any malafides in the amendment of Articles 137 and 140 of the Company's Articles of Association. 40. The previous Article 145 of the Articles of Association of the Company states: "Mr Abdus Salam Murshedy shall be the first Managing Director of the Company for a period of five years from the date of incorporation of the Company and after expiration of his tenure, he will be eligible for re-election and in case of death or resignation of the Managing Director, the Directors shall elect a new Managing Director. His remuneration shall be fixed by the general meeting from time to time". 41. The amended version of Article 145 refers as: "Mr Abdus Salam Murshedy shall be the first Managing Director of the Company for a period of 5 (five) yeas from the date of incorporation of the company. The Board of Directors may from time to time appoint a Managing Director from amongst the Board of Directors for such term at such remuneration as the Board thinks fit. A retiring Managing Director shall be eligible for re-election, provided that no such re-appointment, re-employment or extension of term of office shall be made without the consent of the company in a general meeting". 42. With regard to the above-mentioned amendments, Mr Mohammad Mehedi Hassan Chowdhury, the learned Senior Advocate for the petitioners, contends that while the previous Article 145 endowed clear power to the Board to re-elect the petitioner No. 1 as the Managing Director for a further tenure, as per the new Article 145, the Board retained power for appointment of a Managing Director as time-to-time required and, further, in order to make the process burdensome for the petitioner No. 1 as the Managing Director, the respondent Nos. 2-5 imposed an additional requirement of confirmation in general meeting and, in the long run, after the expiry of the current tenure of the Managing Director, his re-appointment will entirely depend on the Board as well as shareholders of the Company, which clearly shows that the motive of the respondents is not fair. 43. Mr Tanjib-ul Alam, on the other hand, submits that the previous Article 145 was not in compliance with the Companies Act, as section 110(3) of the Companies Act requires the re-appointment of a continuing Managing Director with the consent from the shareholders of a company and, as such, in line with section 110(3) of the Companies Act, the amendment was made to Article 145 of the Articles of Association of the Company and, furthermore, the post of Managing Director being subject to the contract of employment and its renewal being dependent on the consent of the shareholders, no changes between the old and the current Article 145 can be seen and considered as prejudicial or unfair to the minority shareholders of the Company. 44. For the purpose of an effective adjudication of the contentious arguments made by the learned Senior Advocates of the rival groups, let me look at the provisions of section 110 of the Companies Act, which is quoted below: 110. Managing Director not to be appointed for more than five years at a time. — (1) No company shall, after the commencement of this Act, appoint or employ any individual as its managing director for a term exceeding five years at a time. (2) Any individual holding, at the commencement of this Act, the office of the Managing Director in a company shall, unless his term expires earlier, be deemed to have vacated his office immediately on the expiry of five years from the commencement of this Act. (3) Nothing contained in sub-section (1) shall be deemed to prohibit the re-employment or the extension of the term of office of any person as Managing Director for a further period not exceeding five years on each occasion. Provided that no such re-appointment, re-employment or extension of term of office shall be made without the consent of the company in general meeting. 45. From a plain reading of the afore-quoted provisions of section 110 of the Companies Act, it appears to this Court that a company is competent to appoint its Managing Director for a maximum period of 5 (five) years which can be extended for a maximum further period of 5 (five) years subject to the nod of the members in the company's general meeting. So, it is not difficult to understand that the provisions of section 110 of the Companies Act is about 'maximum period' of appointment of the Managing Director of a company and, thus, it is not the proposition of law that appointment of a Managing Director of a company cannot be for 1 (one) year or for less/more than a year. In other words, while a company is allowed to employ its Managing Director for any fixed period upto maximum 5 (five) years, for example, a company may appoint its Managing Director for a period which may be more than 1 (one) year or less than 1 (one) year or for maximum 5 (five) years, however, in case of extension of the tenure of the incumbent Managing Director, the company is under an obligation to have it approved in a general meeting of the company. 46. Even, for appointment of the new Managing Director in a public company, the consent of the members in the company's general meeting is mandatory as per the Proviso to section 109(1) of the Companies Act, which is quoted below: 109. Restriction on Managing Director — (1) No public company and no private company which is a subsidiary of public company shall, after the commencement of this Act, appoint any person as Managing Director, if he is a Managing Director or manager of another company. Provided that no appointment under this section shall be made without the consent of the company in a general meeting. (2) Notwithstanding anything contained in sub-section (1) the Government may, by order, permit any person to be appointed as a Managing Director of more than two companies if the Government is satisfied that it is necessary that the companies should, for their proper working, function as a single unit and have a common Managing Director. 47. From a bare perusal of the afore-quoted provisions of section 109 of the Companies Act, it appears that no public company is allowed to appoint a person as its Managing Director who is serving in another company as the Managing Director and, secondly, the appointment must be approved by the members in the company's general meeting. In other words, employment of the Managing Director in a public company must be made with the consent of the company's members in general meeting and the Managing Director of a public company cannot serve as another company's Managing Director simultaneously, unless permission in writing from the Government is obtained by the company. 48. So, the underlined portion of the amended Article 145 "The Board of Directors from time to time appoint a Managing Director from amongst the Board of Directors for such term at such remuneration as the Board thinks fit." appears to be in conflict with the statutory provisions of sections 109 and 110 of the Companies Act which requires that appointment of the Managing Director of a public company shall not be made without the consent of the members of the company in a general meeting. However, this Court is of the view that in this advanced era, where time is the most important essence of the businesses, there may be exigencies/urgencies to appoint an acting (i.e. in-charge) Managing Director in a public company and, that is why, the Board should be empowered to appoint an acting Managing Director till the regular Managing Director is appointed by the company in its general meeting. Further, an additional provision should be incorporated to appoint a Deputy Managing Director, who may be anyone either from the shareholder-Directors or from the independent Directors. 49. Former Article 147 of the Articles of Association refers to: "The Managing Director with the approval of the Board may delegate all or any of his powers to such other Director or persons as he may think fit and proper" 50. The newly substituted Article 147 portrays as: "The Managing Director may delegate his power under Article 146 so far as it relates to taking care of legal proceedings by or against the Company, to any employee or any other director as he deems fit and proper. Notwithstanding above, the Board may delegate all or any of his powers to such other Directors or persons as they may think fit and proper" 51. About the afore-quoted amendments, the learned Senior Advocate for the petitioners, Mr Mohammad Mehedi Hassan Chowdhury contends that Article 147 of the Company has been changed to curtail the Managing Director's power of delegation inasmuch as before the alteration of the Article, the Managing Director had all the power and could delegate his powers to any other Director, but after the amendment, he can only delegate the power of handling legal proceedings. 52. Per contra, Mr Tanjib-ul Alam, by taking this Court through the present and old Article 147 of the Articles of Association of the Company, argues that the delegation of power by the Managing Director has always been subject to the approval of the Board of the Company; rather, the current Article 147 has provided the Managing Director with the authority to delegate his powers to any employee or to any other Director to initiate or defend legal proceedings by or against the Company without the approval from the Board and, hence, it can never be argued that amendment to Article 147 of the Articles of Association of the Company has curtailed the power of the Managing Director and for the same reason, any shareholder of the Company has been prejudiced or is facing unfairness. 53. From a conjoint reading of the present and previous Article 147 of the Company's: Articles of Association, it appears to this Court that the amended version of Article 147 is sounder and more practical being conducive to the businesses of the modern-day public company and, thus, this Court does not find any malafides in the amendment of Article 147 of the Company's Articles of Association. 54. Now comes the aspect of the mode of amendments of all these articles in question, to see whether there has occurred any procedural illegality. For that purpose, relevant law, namely, section 20 of the Companies Act needs to be adverted to section 20 of the Companies Act provides the following provisions: 20. Alteration of Articles by special resolution: —Subject to the provisions of this Act and to the conditions contained in its memorandum, a company may by special resolution alter, exclude from or add to its articles: and any alteration, exclusion or addition so made shall be as valid as if originally contained in the articles, and be subject in like manner to alteration, exclusion or addition by special resolution. 55. From a plain reading of the above-quoted provisions, it is easily understandable that by a special resolution, a company is empowered to amend its articles in any form. That is to say, either by alteration or exclusion or addition of a company's Articles of Association through adopting a special resolution, the company can change its articles at any time. And, a special resolution means when a company convenes a general meeting upon giving 21 (twenty one) days' notice specifying certain special agenda and a resolution is passed at the said general meeting by a majority of not less than three-fourth of the votes cast by the shareholders who voted in respect of the resolution or the resolution is signed by all the shareholders entitled to vote on that resolution, as provided in section 87 of the Companies Act. 56. In the case in hand, it is evident from the annexed papers that, at first, the Board of Directors passed resolutions for amendments of the articles in question upon fixing the date for issuance of notice of the EGM containing the agenda and also by fixing the date of EGM. Thereafter, 21 (twenty one) days’ notice was given to the members of the Company articulating the agenda for amendments in the Articles of Association and the special resolutions were passed with more than 75% of votes. It is further evident from the annexed papers that the petitioners did not raise any objection against the proposed amendments either in the Board Meetings held on 22-3-2022 and 18-4-2022 nor in the EGM held on 12-5-2022. Therefore, the amendments in the Articles of Association of the Company appear to this Court to have been made upon observing the required legal procedures laid down in the Companies Act and, thus, are held to have been done legally, save and except the portions of the amendments made in article 145 which requires modification by this Court under section 233(3)(a) and (c) of the Companies Act. 57. Let me examine the issue No. 3, namely, whether creation of the posts of Additional Directors is permissible in the law. 58. On this issue, the learned Senior Advocate for the petitioners, Mr Mohammad Mehedi Hassan Chowdhury submits that the Board of Directors violated the provisions of section 91 of the Companies Act in taking a resolution for inserting Article 124 in the Articles of Association of the Company, for, no provision in an article of a company's Articles of Association can be incorporated which is inconsistent with the provisions of the Companies Act. He contends that there is no apparent need for appointment of Additional Directors in the Company; rather it will subjugate the interest of shareholders as a whole because such appointment would bring nothing but increase the Board size unnecessarily and would incur huge financial loss to the shareholders. He raises a question that the business of the Company in the past 4 months has not been expanded so much or there has nothing been so dramatically changed that the management needs 3 (three) Additional Directors, 1 (one) Vice-Chairman and 1 (one) Independent Director. By referring to the case of JK Paliwal vs Paliwal Steel Ltd. (2007) 80 CLA 180, he submits that it is the settled proposition of law that new Directors appointed for the purpose of creating new majority in the Board of Directors constitutes oppression and mismanagement entitling the petitioners to relief for attaining substantial justice between the parties. He further contends that no discussion took place in the Board expressing need for amendments of the Articles for appointments of Additional Directors and respondent Nos. 2-7 did not provide any reason whatsoever as to why and how these appointments of Additional Directors would help the Company. By referring to the case of Shahadat Hossain vs Base Textile Ltd. 54 DLR 583, he submits that it is a settled principle of law that the Board shall first address the issue in the Board meeting and come to a clear finding that such amendments are necessary and only then an EGM can be called to amend the Articles. 59. However, the learned Senior Advocate for the respondent Nos. 1-2, Mr Tanjib-ul Alam, submits that the Company's Board of Directors was not in violation of section 91 of the Companies Act in view of Regulation 86 of Schedule-I to the Companies Act, which empowers the Board to appoint Additional Directors. He submits that the Additional Directors were duly appointed by the Board of the Company in compliance with the Companies Act and Article 124 of the Articles of Association of the Company, by which the Directors are made competent to appoint a person as an Additional Director who shall retire from office at the next following ordinary general meeting but shall be eligible for election by the Company at that meeting as an Additional Director. He submits that the provisions of Regulation 86 has the force of law as it is part of the Companies Act duly passed by the Parliament and, as such, while interpreting the provisions of section 91 of the Companies Act, the provisions of the Regulations will have to be interpreted harmoniously. Mr Alam submits that Additional Directors are merely an addition to the Board for a brief period, which in the instant case till the upcoming Annual General Meeting as per the resolution passed in the Board Meeting held on 8-6-2022 and, as such, the Additional Directors being not regular Directors, section 91(1)(b) of the Companies Act is not applicable to the appointment of such Directors. He submits that there is no case law which has negated the provisions of Regulation 86 on the ground that it is inconsistent with section 91 of the Companies Act. He submits that since the Board has been empowered tb appoint Additional Directors until the next AGM in pursuance of Regulation 86 and Article 124 of the Articles of Association, negating such right and power under section 91 of the Companies Act would amount to putting an undue restriction on the rights of the Board to meet business exigency. 60. In order to resolve the issue, it is necessary for this Court to look at the provisions of Article 124 of the Articles of Association of the Company, Regulation 86 of the Schedule-1 to the Companies Act and, side by side, the provisions of section 91 of the Companies Act. 61. Article 124 of the Articles of Association of the Company runs as follows: "The Directors shall have power at any time and from time to time, to appoint any person, who may be a nominee of an institutional shareholder, to be a Director either to fill a casual vacancy or as an addition to the Board, but so that the total number of Directors shall not at any time exceed the number fixed by the Article 117. Any Directors so appointed shall hold office only until the following Annual General Meeting and shall then be eligible for re-election." 62. Regulation 86 of the Schedule-I to the Companies Act states as follows: "The Directors shall have power at any time, and after the expiry of a specified period, to appoint a person as an Additional Director who shall retire from office at the next following ordinary general meeting but shall be eligible for election by the company at that meeting as an Additional Director." 63. Now, let me see whether the provisions of Regulation 86 of the Schedule-1 to the Companies Act is inconsistent with the provisions of sections 91 of the Companies Act. Section 91 of the Companies Act states as follows: "91. Appointment of Directors: — (1) Notwithstanding anything contained in the articles of a company- (a) the subscribers of the memorandum shall be deemed to be the Directors of the company until the first Directors are appointed. (b) the Directors of the company shall be elected by the members from among their number in general meetings and (c) any casual vacancy occurring among the Directors may be filled in by the other Directors but the person appointed shall be a person qualified to be elected to be elected a Director under clause (b) and shall be subject to retirement at the same time as if he had become a Director on the day on which the Director in whose place he is appointed was last appointed a Director." 64. From a concurrent reading of Article 124 of the Articles of Association of the Company and Regulation 86 of the Schedule-1 to the Companies Act and, side-by-side, the provisions of section 91 of the Companies Act, it appears to this Court that there is no inconsistency between the provisions as to filling the casual vacancy by the Board of Directors contained in Article 124 of the Articles of Association and the provisions of section 91 of the Companies Act, as the provisions of section 91(1)(c) of the Companies Act clearly empower the Board to appoint a person with required qualification in the vacant post of Director for the remaining period of the Director against whose vacancy the new appointment is given with a nomenclature of an Alternative Director. However, the provisions contained in Article 124 of the Company's Articles of Association stating "or as an addition to the Board, but so that the total number of Directors shall not at any time exceed the number fixed by Article 117" are apparently in conflict with the provisions of section 91(1)(b) of the Companies Act, for, while provisions of the aforesaid Act of Parliament requires that the Directors of the company shall be elected in general meeting, the provisions of Article 124 of the Articles of Association and Regulation 86 of the Schedule-1 to the Companies Act empower the Board to appoint a Director, as an Additional Director. It is a settled principle of law that provisions of a sub-ordinate legislation cannot exceed or override the provisions of the parent statute, and if it is ever found that a local authority or any other legal body by exercising its delegated power has incorporated a provision in a subordinate legislation exceeding or overriding the scope of an Act of a Parliament, in that scenario, it is the duty of the Court of law, at first, to give a harmonious meaning of both the provisions and if such meaning cannot be imputed, to ignore the provisions of the subordinate legislation. 65. To this end; it is pertinent to know the legal status of the Regulations contained in Schedule-1 to the Companies Act as well as the legal status of the Articles of Association of a company. And, for this purpose quotations of sections 2(1)(a), 17, 18 and 22 of the Companies Act would be useful. Section 2(1)(a) of the Companies Act runs as follows: 2(1)(a) "articles" means the articles of association of a company including so far as they apply to the company, the regulations contained in schedule I to this Act.: Provided that the articles of association of a company framed under any law relating to companies at any time in force before the commencement of this Act shall, so far as they are not inconsistent with the provisions of this Act, be deemed to be the articles of association of that company framed in accordance with the provisions of the Act; 66. Section 2(1)(a) seeks to provide definition of Articles of Association by stating that when an incorporated company frames some canons for operating the said company, either by incorporating the necessary provisions of its own choice upon excluding the provisions of the Schedule-1 to the Companies Act or by adopting the Schedule-1 to the Companies Act entirely or partly, without being inconsistent with any provisions of the Companies Act, the said canons shall be regarded as the constitution or the Articles of Association of the company. 67. Sections 17 and 18 of the Companies Act run as follows: 17. Articles of Association: - (1) A company limited by guarantee and an unlimited company shall, and a company limited by shares may have an article of association wherein provision shall be made for regulating the affairs of the company; and the articles shall be signed by the subscribers of the memorandum and be registered together with the memorandum. (2) Articles of association may adopt all or any of the regulations contained in Schedule-1 and shall in any event be deemed to contain regulations identical with or to the same effect as regulation 56, 66, 71, 78, 79, 80, 81, 82, 95, 97, 105, 108, 112, 113, 114, 115 and 116 contained in that Schedule. 18. Application of Schedule I:-In the case of a company limited by shares and registered after the commencement of this Act, if articles are not registered, or, if articles are registered, in so far as the articles do not exclude or modify the regulations in Schedule 1, those regulations sha1l so far as applicable be the regulations of the company in the same manner and to the same extent as if they were contained in the duly registered articles. 68. As per section 17(1) of the Companies Act, while it is optional for a company limited by shares to have its Articles of Association either by incorporating the wordings and the provisions of its choice or by adopting the part/entire provisions of the Schedule-1. to the Articles of Association, however, section 17(2) and section 18 of the Companies Act conjointly state that a company limited by shares having its own Articles of Association must make the Regulations 56, 66, 71, 78, 79, 80, 81, 82, 95, 97, 105, 108, 112, 113, 114, 115 and 116 as the integral part of its Articles of Association. In other words, when a company declares in its Articles of Association that Schedule-1 to the Companies Act shall not be applicable, in that scenario as well, the compulsory provisions of the Schedule-1 to the Companies Act shall form part of its Articles of Association and if the said company does not draft an Articles of Association with its chosen wordings and provisions, Schedule-1 to the Companies Act shall be deemed to be its Articles of Association. 69. Section 22 of the Companies Act provides the following provisions; 22. Effect of memorandum and articles: - (1) A memorandum and articles shall when registered bind the company and the members hereof to the same extent as if they respectively had been signed by each member, and contained a covenant on the part of each member, his heirs and legal representatives to observe all the provisions of the memorandum and of the articles subject to the provisions of this Act. 70. As per the provisions of section 22 of the Companies Act, all the provisions of a registered Articles of Association must be regarded and observed by the company and its members like a contract between them 'subject to the provisions of the Companies Act'; meaning that the provisions of the Articles of Association of a company will operate as the company's Regulations so long as they are not found to be inconsistent with any of the provisions of the Companies Act. 71. So, from the examinations of sections 2(1)a, 17, 18 and 22 of the Companies Act, it can be held that Schedule-1 to the Companies Act is basically a template or specimen copy of an ideal Articles of Association of an incorporated company, applicability of which depends upon the adoption of the same by the promoters of a company at the time of incorporation of the company. While there is no gainsaying that Schedule-1 to the Companies Act is the part of the Companies Act, however, by the provisions of section 17, 18 and 22 of the Companies Act, the Legislature clearly intended to regard it as a secondary legislation. Therefore, if any provision of the Schedule-1 to the Companies Act surfaces to be inconsistent with any of the provisions of the main part of the Companies Act, the latter shall prevail and, similarly, if the provisions of any article of the Articles of Association of a company are found to be in contradiction with the provisions of the Companies Act, the provisions of articles are to be considered as repugnant to the extent of inconsistency with the provisions of the Companies Act. 72. In this case, Regulation 86 of the Schedule-1 to the Companies Act is not relevant, for, the Company, vide article 1 of its Articles of Association, has specifically excluded the application of the entire Schedule-1 to the Companies Act and, consequently, Regulation 86 has no application in this case and only the compulsory Regulations, namely, Regulations 56, 66, 71, 78, 79, 80, 81, 82, 95, 97, 105, 108, 112, 113, 114, 115 and 116 shall be deemed to be the part of Articles of Association of the Company. 73. Reverting to the issue in hand as to whether creation of the posts of Additional Directors by the Company by its Article 124 is permissible in law or not, this Court is of the view that given the current trend of fast-growing business of our country, a company might require appointment of some further Directors in addition to the present number of Directors, and since no provision of the Companies Act prohibits to appoint an Additional Director and, on the other hand, since the provisions of section 91 of the Companies Act require appointment of a Director to be made in a company's general meeting, the provisions of Article 124 may be modified by this Court by exercising its power under section 233(3)(a) and (c) of the Companies Act to the extent that the proposal of the Board as to appointment of Additional Director shall be required to have approval in the general meeting to be held immediately after holding the said Board Meeting by giving 21 (twenty one) days' notice. It may be pertinent to mention here that in India, section 161(1) of the Companies Act 2013 provides the following: "The articles of a company may confer on its Board of Directors the power to appoint any person, other than a person who fails to get appointed as a director in a general meeting, as an additional director at any time who shall hold office up to the date of the next annual general meeting or the last date on which the annual general meeting should have been held, whichever is earlier." 74. But, there being no such enabling provision in our Companies Act, a clause in the Articles of Association should not be included empowering the Board to appoint any Additional Director. Such a clause can only be included if it also requires taking approval from the company in general meeting, in line with the requirement contained in section 91(1)(b) of our Companies Act. 75. Now, comes issue Nos. 4 and 5, namely, (4) whether in making recommendations in the post of Managing Director, the NRC performed its functions in compliance with the provisions of the Corporate Governance Code, and (5) whether recommendation by the NRC for appointment of Mr Rezaur Rahaman Sohag as an Independent Director was lawful and whether BSEC's approval thereto was proper. 76. Both the 2 (two) issues are taken up together for convenience, as both the issues involve examinations of the Codes of Corporate Governance Code. 77. On the issue No. 4, the learned Senior Advocate for the petitioner, Mr Mohammad Mehedi Hassan Chowdhury by taking this Court through the letter dated 11-6-2022 written by the respondent No. 2 to the NRC and notice dated 12-6-2022 issued by the NRC pursuant to the aforesaid letter and, side-by-side, Code 6(5)(iii) of the Corporate Governance Code, submits that the duty of the NRC is merely to identify persons who are qualified to become Directors and who may be appointed in top level executive position in accordance with the criteria laid down and recommend their appointment and removal to the Board and, therefore, the respondent No. 2 has no authority to issue letter by recommending his son i.e. respondent No. 4's name for the post of Managing Director, and the aforesaid interference clearly shows that the respondent No. 2 is not only controlling the Board but also the NRC. On the issue No. 5, Mr Chowdhury submits that the recommendation for appointment of the proposed Independent Director, Mr Rezaur Rahaman Sohagh, can be found ludicrous with a simple vigilant observation that a journalist being a Special Correspondent of the Daily Inqilab can in no way make a meaningful contribution to the welfare of the Company, as a plain reading of his Curriculum Vitae Would reveal that the recommended person has no special knowledge who is able to ensure compliance with financial laws, regulatory requirements and corporate laws as required under Code No. 1(3)(a) of the Code of Corporate Governance, 2018. Also, as Mr Chowdhury continues to submit, the BSEC has utterly failed to perform its duty in giving its consent to the proposed appointment of Mr Rezaur Rahaman Sohag as an Independent Director. 78. Per contra, Mr Tanjub-ul Alam, the learned Senior Advocate for the respondent Nos. 1-2, submits that there is no provision in the Corporate Governance Code prohibiting the Chairman or Director of the Board to recommend a name for the appointment of Managing Director or other Directors or for appointment of any officer. He submits that while the NRC is independent to identify a qualified person for a top level position of the company towards recommending the said person to the Board, there is nothing wrong for a member of the Board to supply a suitable person's name to the NRC for their consideration. 79. And, Mr AM Masum, the learned Advocate for the BSEC, submits that BSEC has not committed any wrong in consenting to the appointment of Mr Sohag as he has been working as a journalist for decades having an academic certificate of a Masters Degree. 80. Let me adjudicate upon the issues with reference to the relevant Codes of the Corporate Governance Code. Role of the NRC has been provided in Code 6(5) of the Corporate Governance Code, upon cataloging at length the provisions under a number of Paragraphs and sub-Paragraphs, quotation of which here will make this Judgment somewhat cumbersome and, hence, avoided. From a minute perusal of the entire provisions of Code 6(5) of the Corporate Governance Code, it appears to this Court that all the provisions are meant to allow the NRC, on the one hand, to perform its functions independently and, on the other hand to remain accountable to the Board and shareholders of the company. Out of numerous functions of the NRC, one function is- "Identifying persons who are qualified to become directors and who may be appointed in top level executive position in accordance with the criteria laid down, and recommend their appointment and removal to the Board" (Code 6.5 of the Corporate Governance Code) 81. However, nowhere in the Corporate Governance Code it is provided as to what/who are the sources for obtaining the names of the persons whom the NRC may identify as qualified for the top level executive position for the purpose of recommending them to the Board. Therefore, in absence of having any such provision in place, if a member of the Board or Chairman of the Board forwards a CV to the NRC for its consideration for appointment in any of the posts in the Board or in the management, it cannot be said that the said action is illegal. But when the Chairman of a company sends a CV of his own son to the NRC with a recommendation to consider his appointment, eyebrows may be raised questioning whether it fairly fits in the scheme of the Corporate Governance Code. The very purpose of enactment of the Corporate Governance Code is to encourage (in fact, to compel) portraying the publicly listed companies to the general investors as being truly run in a manner more transparent than a private company or non-listed public company, securing the interests of the general investors upon compliance of all the laws of the land which can be evident from the conduct of the Directors. However, in a publicly listed company, Board of Directors of which is predominately consisting of the members of one family with Chairman of the said family in the Board, and if the Chairman finds any of his family members to be competent for a top level executive, there remains hardly any scope to condemn the said act as reprehensible. It follows that the action of the Chairman of the Company (respondent No. 2) in sending the name of the respondent No. 4 to the NRC for appointment in the post of Managing Director, though not befitting, cannot be termed as illegal. 82. For adjudication of the issue No. 5 (i.e. whether recommendation by the NRC for appointment of Mr Rezaur Rahman Sohag as an Independent Director), let me be acquainted with the legal criteria required to be fulfilled by an Independent Director, as enshrined in Code 1(3) of the Corporate Governance Code, which are quoted below: Qualification of Independent Director: — (a) Independent director shall be a knowledgeable individual with integrity who is able to ensure compliance with financial laws, regulatory requirements and corporate laws and can make meaningful contribution to the business; (b) Independent director shall have following qualifications: i) Business Leader ii) Corporate Leader iii) Former official of government iv) University Teacher v) Professional who is or was an advocate practicing at least in the High Court Division of Bangladesh Supreme Court or a Chartered Accountant or Cost and Management Accountant or Chartered Financial Analyst or Chartered Certified Accountant or Certified Public Accountant or Chartered Management Accountant or Chartered Secretary or equivalent qualification; (c) The independent director shall have at least 10 (ten) years of experiences in any field mentioned in clause (b); (d) In special cases, the above qualifications or experiences may be relaxed subject to prior approval of the Commission. 83. While Paragraph (a) of Code 1(3) of the Corporate Governance Code requires that an Independent Director shall possess knowledge on financial laws, regulatory requirements and corporate laws with integrity so that s/he can truly help the company in running its business sitting in the highest forum of the company, Paragraph (b) of the Code stipulates the academic qualifications and experiences to be possessed by an Independent Director. However, Paragraph (d) of the Code has empowered the Commission (i.e. BSEC) to relax the qualifications and experience in special cases. 84. From a careful scrutiny of the CV of Mr Rezaur Rahaman Sohag, it surfaces that he does not have the requisite academic qualifications and experiences in the relevant field. So, the NRC's recommendation to appoint Mr Sohag as an Independent Director in the Company was erroneous and, consequently, the BSEC fell in error in approving the appointment as evidently it was misguided by the Company in giving consent to Mr Rezaur Rahman Sohag's appointment as an Independent Director. It is evident from the annexed papers that BSEC has not approved Mr Sohag's appointment invoking Paragraph (d) of the Code No. 1(3) of the Corporate Governance Code and, in fact, Mr Sohag's CV does not disclose any special kind of qualification or experience for which the BSEC may decide to relax the qualifications and experiences set out in the said Paragraph (b) of the Code 1(3) of the Corporate Governance Code. It follows that since the NRC's recommendation to the appointment of Mr Sohag as an Independent Director was not lawful and the BSEC's approval thereto was erroneous, the final appointment of Mr Rezaur Rahman as an Independent Director by the company was illegal. 85. Let me now take up the issue No. 6, which is whether the petitioner No. 1 has any legitimate expectation to remain in the post of the Managing Director of the Company, and whether the decision taken in the last AGM held on 28-12-2021 as to keeping the petitioner No. 1 as the Managing Director of the Company till 2025 is binding upon the Company to implement it, and whether in a publicly listed company, its Managing Director can preside over the meeting of Directors in the absence of the Chairman of the company. 86. On the issue No. 6 the learned Senior Advocate for the petitioners, Mr Mohammad Mehedi Hassan Chowdhury submits that in a quasi-partnership type company where two families manage the affairs of the company, representation in the Board of Directors from each family should be made, and when they are promise-bound mutually to act as the Managing Director or Chairman of the company, legitimate expectation arises for them to perform their respective duties as per their promises. He argues that since the petitioner No. 1 was promised by the respondent Nos. 2-4 at the time of splitting their businesses vide agreement dated 29-11-2021 that the former shall be acting as the Managing Director and, accordingly, he was appointed as the Managing Director of the Company for 5(five) years in the last AGM held on 28-12-2021, it is the legitimate expectation of the petitioner No. 1 that he shall be next allowed to serve as the Managing Director of the Company. He submits that in the event of taking any action against the Managing Director, the Articles of Association may incorporate a provision to the effect that the Managing Director shall not be present in the Board, not to mention presiding over the Board Meeting even though at that point of time he might have been acting as the Company's Chairman due to absence of the regular Chairman. 87. Per Contra, Mr Alam submits that the Articles of Association of the Company and the Companies Act do not provide any exclusive right to the shareholders of the Company to be appointed in the office of Managing Director of the Company; nor is there any agreement between the shareholders regarding holding the position of the Managing Director. He submits that the Company is a publicly listed company and by claiming legitimate expectation, the petitioners are manifestly abusing the process going against the interest of the rest of the shareholders including the public shareholders of the Company and, as such, the petitioners cannot claim to be included in the management of the Company on the basis of an equitable remedy i.e. legitimate expectation. In an endeavour to substantiate his above count of submission, he refers to the cases Re Posgate and Denby (Agencies) Ltd. (1986) 2 BCC 99 and Re Blue Arrow 11987] BCLC 585. By referring to the case of Re Astec (BSR) plc [1998] 2 BCLC 556, Mr Alam submits that the concept of legitimate expectation cannot be considered in a publicly listed company, for, if the concept is introduced in the context of the publicly listed companies, then this would be a recipe for chaos. He submits that in the afore-cited case, the observation was made on the ground that the publicly listed companies shall be free from extraneous equitable considerations and constraints and, thereby, provide assurance to the public shareholders of a company that the Managing Director can be removed from the office as per the Articles of Association and the relevant laws of the land. He submits that the position of Managing Director in a company, be it a private or public listed company, is contractual in nature and, even if a person is appointed in the office of Managing Director for a period of 5(five) years as per section 110 of the Companies Act, he may be removed from such office by the Board of Directors and may be replaced by another person as the Board of Directors thinks fit, subject to the confirmation in an EGM and after such removal, the Managing Director may only seek compensation for loss of office and nothing else from the Company. 88. From a minute reading of all the provisions of the Companies Act governing the issues relating to competency, disqualifications, appointment, tenure, remunerations, removal and re-appointment of the Managing Director of a company, it appears to this Court that there is no law with reference to which a shareholder or a Director can claim legitimate expectation to become or to remain in the post of the Managing Director of a company. However, from a minute perusal of the case-laws of our jurisdiction as well as those of foreign jurisdiction, it appears to this Court that the interactions or conduct of the shareholders, such as, giving assurances to a shareholder to make him Managing Director or Chairman of the company either by incorporating a provision in the Articles of Association to that effect or by entering into a contract with the said person, an expectation may legitimately arise in the mind of the person so promised that s/he shall be acting as the Managing Director or Chairman of the company, subject to the condition that in mitigating the said claim of a legitimate expectation, no provision of law is infringed or subjugated. 89. In this case, it is an admitted position of the parties that the petitioner No. 1 and the respondent No. 2 started their business venture together in the year 1984 by establishing a number of companies and eventually they amicably split up by execution of an agreement dated 29-11-2021. Thus, this Court considered it pertinent to go through the entire agreement dated 29-11-2021 in a bid to find out as to whether any promise was made by the respondent Nos. 2-4 to keep the petitioner No. 1 as the Managing Director but nothing of that sort could be revealed from the said agreement; rather at page 3 (three) of the said agreement dated 29-11-2021, it is stated that— "Envoy Textiles Ltd. being jointly owned by the SELLER and the PURCHASER by dint of holding shares and as being the Public Limited Company listed with Stock Exchange will remain undivided. The curriculum and activities of the Company shall be operated under the provisions of the Companies Act, 1994 and other laws and regulations as applicable from time to time." 90. From the wordings and phrases employed in the above-quoted Para of the agreements dated 29-11-2021, it is crystal clear that the petitioners and the respondents have agreed to run the Company in compliance with the provisions of the Companies Act, the Articles of Association and other laws of the land (such as, Corporate Governance Code, Contract Act etc.) and, therefore, it signifies that both the parties agreed to run the Company devoid of any specific reserved right and, as such, the said agreement having negated any right to be in the post of Managing Director, this Court holds that no legitimate expectation arose from the Agreement dated 29-11-2021 with regard to participation in the management of the Company. However it is evident from the annexed papers that in the last AGM held on 28-12-2021, the petitioner No. 1 was appointed as the Managing Director of the Company for 5 (five) years and the respondent No. 2 was appointed as the Chairman of the Company for 2 (two) years by the shareholders of the Company, including the respondent Nos. 2-4 and, at this juncture, a pertinent question crops up as to whether the Company has been debarred to appoint a new Managing Director because of the decision taken in the last AGM held on 28-12-2021. In other words, whether by virtue of the aforesaid decision the petitioner No. 1 can claim the equitable right of legitimate expectation to continue in the post of the Managing Director. This Court's answer thereto is that since in the last AGM held on 28-12-2021, their appointments were given by the Company in its general meeting, the appointment of the Chairman appears to be completely valid being in consonance with the provisions of sections 109 and 110 of the Companies Act. However, the appointment of the petitioner No. 1 has been given in violation of the provision of section 109 of the Companies Act inasmuch as neither the petitioner resigned from the post of the Managing Director of other company before being appointed as the Managing Director of this public company nor the Company obtained necessary permission from the Government to allow the petitioner No. 1 to serve as the Managing Director of 2 (two) companies at a time. And, since the very appointment of the petitioner No. 1 as the Managing Director of this public listed company was illegally made by the Company in its last AGM held on 28-12-2021, he cannot claim a right of legitimate expectation on the basis of the said illegal appointment. Moreover, it is the established general principle of the Company law that the will of the majority shareholders of a company binds all the members including the members who voted against such decision of the majority and, that is why, when a company in its general meeting takes a decision regarding any of its businesses (i.e. about any purchase, sale, appointments etc.), it remains competent to overturn all or any of the said decisions by a subsequent resolution taken in the general meeting by the majority shareholders. However, if the person has already done something on the basis of the company's said decision taken in its general meeting, the principles of equity demand that for the purpose of jeopardizing the said person's interest, the company shall not invalidate its original decision by applying the rule of "the decision of the majority shareholders shall be binding upon all", unless the company subsequently finds it difficult to implement the said original decision as inconsistent with the laws of the land. 91. Regarding issue No. 7, namely, whether the petitioner No. 1 has earned any disqualification to act as the Managing Director of the Company, the learned Senior Advocate for the petitioners Mr Mohammad Mehedi Hassan Chowdhury submits that in last 3 (three) decades of the petitioner No. l's service as the Managing Director of the different companies of the Envoy Group, no allegation as to embezzlement of fund or inefficiency was ever brought against him and even after splitting the group, none of the members of the Company raised any allegation; rather being satisfied with his long years of experiences and integrity, the members of the Company in its last ACM decided to keep the petitioner No. 1 as the Managing Director of the Company and, now, bringing an allegation of embezzlement of the Company's fund or discharging its duties by the petitioner No. 1 improperly, are malafide. 92. On the other hand, the learned Senior Advocate for respondent Nos. 1-2, Mr Tanjib-ul Alam, submits that the petitioner No. 1 has lost his competency to be the Managing Director of the Company as he has committed an offence under section 156(1)(14) of the Customs Act, 1967 by giving a false declaration to the Customs Authority in violation of section 32 of the Customs Act that chillers were being imported as the capital machineries of the respondent No. 1-Company, though the said chillers were actually being imported and, then, have been installed for his personal commercial building situated in Uttara, Dhaka and, secondly, since the petitioner No. 1 is serving as the Managing Director of another company, therefore, as per the provisions of section 109 of the Companies Act, the petitioner No. 1 is disqualified to be the Managing Director of the Company. 93. In view of the contentions made by the respondents that the petitioner No. 1 is still acting as the Managing Director of the private companies owned by him which have not been disputed by the petitioners, and since as per section 109 of the Companies Act, no Managing Director of a public company is allowed to serve as the Managing Director of another company, thus, the petitioner No. 1 is not eligible to act as the Managing Director of a public company unless the Company obtains permission from the Government or the petitioner No. 1 resigns from the post of the Managing Director of other companies owned by him. From the annexures 2 series and 18 series (18 to 18-J), which are the customs papers, Letter of Credit, Bills of Entries and commercial invoices, it is evident that an LC with Pubali Bank Ltd was opened for an amount of USD 3,27,000, which subsequently was amended to an amount of USD 3,13,047, against which the petitioner No. 1 imported different equipment related to the Central Air Conditioner from Cord Engineering Pte Ltd in the name of the respondent No. 1-Company, but it has actually been installed in SIAAM Tower at Uttara, Dhaka owned by the petitioner No. 1. While the petitioner No. 1 admits that it has been installed in his personal tower upon payment of Taka 1,14,22,432 (Taka one crore fourteen lacs twenty two thousand and four hundred thirty two) to the respondent No. 1-Company against USD 3,13,047 which is equivalent to Taka 2,17,56,766 (Taka two crore seventeen lacs fifty six thousand and seven hundred sixty six), and thereby still leaving a dues to Cle respondent No. 1-Company of an amount of Taka 1,03,34,334 (Taka one crore three lac thirty four thousand and three hundred thirty four), however, by even full payment of Taka to the respondent No. 1-Company or by obtaining the consent of the Chairman of the Company as to installation of the Air Conditioner for the personal use of the petitioner No. 1, the commission of an offence under section 156(1)(14) of the Customs Act cannot be obliterated. And, for this reason, the petitioner No. 1 can be held ineligible to remain in the Board as a mere Director even, not to mention the Managing Director of the respondent No. 1-Company. 94. I may now take the issue No. 1, namely, whether the present application is maintainable. 95. On the issue of maintainability, it is the submission of the learned Senior Advocate Mr Mohammad Mehedi Hassan Chowdhury on behalf of the petitioners that since the petitioners jointly hold more than 10% shares and since the petitioners' interests have been prejudiced because of the whimsical resolutions and decisions taken in the Board Meetings and EGM, the instant petition squarely falls within the ambit of section 233 of the Companies Act. He submits that there is no requirement in section 233 of the Companies Act that the issue of removal of the Managing Director of a company cannot be challenged in a section 233 application or the challenge must be made by the Managing Director alone or for the purpose of challenging the majority's action of removal of the Managing Director, 10% shares are required to be held by the Managing Director alone or the other shareholders can not join the aggrieved Managing Director. 96. On the other hand, Mr Tanjib-ul Alam, the learned Senior Advocate for the respondent Nos. 1-2 submits that the petitioners have failed to satisfy that their case falls under any of the circumstances stated in section 233 of the Companies Act, inasmuch as they miserably failed to satisfy a single prejudice or unfair conduct on the part of the respondents. He submits that the petitioners have preferred the instant application under section 233 of the Companies Act merely to continue to be in the management of the Company, specifically to secure the office of the Managing Director in the Company, and in the absence of any specific allegation against the respondents as to how the amendments to Articles of Association or the appointments of Additional Directors, Independent Director and Vice-Chairman are prejudicial to their interest, the petitioners are only creating smoke out of nowhere to secure the position of the petitioner No. 1 as Managing Director. Mr Alam further submits that in an application under section 233 of the Companies Act, the petitioners i.e. the minority shareholders are required to prove that the actions taken by the majority shareholders are prejudicial to the interest of the minority shareholders. He submits that in this prejudice to the interest of the petitioners so far it relates to the amendments to the Articles of Association of the respondent No. 1 Company, firstly, the petitioners must prove that the amendments have been made to prejudice the interest of the petitioners and, secondly, it must be proved that such prejudicial amendments have been made without the consent of the petitioners. He submits that in the instant application, the petitioners have miserably failed to satisfy any of the stated hurdles; firstly, the petitioners have failed to show any cogent reasons as to how the amendments are prejudicial to their interest and, for the sake of argument, even if it is considered that the amendments are prejudicial to the interest of the petitioners, it is to be satisfied that such amendments have been made without the consent of the petitioners, but given the fact that the petitioners have consented to the amendments consecutively in the Board Meetings as well as in the EGM, the petitioners failed to cross the second hurdle as well and, therefore, it is apparent that the petitioners have taken a scattergun approach to show prejudice to their interest without having any basis to file the instant application. 97. From the submissions advanced by the learned Senior Advocates for the two sides with regard to issue of maintainability, the following questions (sub-issues) arise for adjudication by this Court: (i) whether a section 233 application can be filed for retaining the post of the Managing Director or becoming the Managing Director of a company and (ii) for engaging in legal battle for the purpose of remaining in the post of Managing Director, whether the said Managing Director is required to hold 10% shares alone in his own name or the other shareholders may also stand beside him as the co-petitioners towards fulfilling the requirement of 10% shares in the company and (iii) whether the interests of the petitioners have been or are being or are likely to be prejudiced in any manner. 98. For an effective and fair adjudication of the questions (i.e. sub-issues) derived from the issue No. 1, namely, whether the instant application is maintainable, it is necessary to quote the provisions of section 233 of the Companies Act, which run as follows: Protection of minority interest 233.
