Power of Court to give direction for protections of interest of the minority. — (1) Subject to fulfillment of the conditions of the required minimum as specified in section 195 (a) and (b), any member or debenture-holder of a company may either individually or jointly bring to the notice of the court by application that— (a) the affairs of the company are being conducted or the powers of the directors are being exercised in a manner prejudicial to one or more of its members or debenture holders or in disregard of his or their interest; or (b) the company is acting or is likely to act in a manner which discriminated or is likely to discriminate the interest of any member or debenture holder; (c) a resolution of the members, debenture holders or any class of them has been passed or is likely to be passed which discriminates or is likely to discriminate the interest of one or more of the members or likely to debenture holder: and pray for such order, as in his or their opinion, would be necessary for safeguarding his or their interest and also the interest of any other member or debenture holder. (2)………………….. (3) If after hearing the parties present on the date so fixed, the Court is of opinion that the interest of the applicant or applicants has been or is being or is likely to be prejudicially affected for reasons specified in the application, it may make such order as prayed for or such other order as it deems fit including a direction—(a) to cancel or modify any resolution or transaction or (b) to regulate the conduct of the company's affairs in future in such manner as is specified therein (c) to amend any provision of the memorandum and articles of the company. (4) ………………………………………….. (5) ……………………………………… 99. From a plain reading of section 233 of the Companies Act, it appears to this Court that while the first part of sub-section (1) of section 233 of the Companies Act delineates the qualifications of a section 233 application, the Clauses under it (namely, Clause a, b & c) stipulate the issues or subjects which can be brought to the notice of the Company Court, and sub-section (3) of section 233 of the Companies Act is the provision regarding the scope and extent of powers of the Company Court which can be exercised if the Court is satisfied about the grievances placed before it. Thus, while the main part of sub-section (1) of section 233 of the Companies Act, fixes the competency or qualifications of the members of a company limited by shares for approaching the Company Court to be 10% shares required to be held either individually or jointly, Clauses (a) (b) & (c) of sub-section (1) of section 233 of the Companies Act state that the petitioners need to show to the Court that (a) interests of one or more share-holders/debenture-holders are being prejudiced because of the manner of exercising the power by the Directors or the affairs of the company are being conducted in a prejudicial manner or (b) the manner of acting by the company is discriminatory for the shareholders/debenture-holders or (c) one or more share-holders/ debenture-holders has been discriminated or is going to be discriminated because of passing of a resolution by majority shareholders/ debenture-holders. Sub-section (3) of section 233 of the Companies Act invests the Court with a wide power of giving direction (i) to cancel or modify the resolution or transaction in question, (ii) to run the company in a manner suitable for all the shareholders and debenture-holders and (iii) if needed, to bring any change in the Memorandum and Articles of Association either by alteration of the existing provision or by inserting new provision/s, subject to the condition that the Court is satisfied about any or all of the grievances under Clauses (a), (b) & (c) of sub-section (1) of section 233 of the Companies Act. 100. In this case, at the time of admission hearing a number of grievances purported to have fallen under Clauses (a), (b) & (c) of section 233 (1) of the Companies Act were brought to the notice of this Court upon showing their holding of shares of more than 10% in the Company and, accordingly, the instant application was admitted. Now, at this final hearing, if this Court is satisfied about having qualification shares by the petitioners and also about the petitioners' grievances as to whether the grievances come within the ambit of the Clauses (a), (b) & (c) of section 233 of the Companies Act, this Court shall be competent to pass necessary Orders and Directions under section 233(3) of the Companies Act. 101. The first objection of the respondents is that since the instant petition is mainly about keeping the petitioner No. 1 as the Managing Director of the Company, the Managing Director himself has to hold 10% shares, without taking aid of other shareholders, namely, petitioner Nos. 2-4 in this petition. However, from a minute reading of the entire provisions of section 233 of the Companies Act as well as the case-laws of our jurisdiction and foreign jurisdiction, this Court does not find the basis of such submission; rather, this Court finds that the Managing Director of a company alone is, or together with some other shareholders are, very much competent to approach the Company Court for vindicating his grievances to become the Managing Director or to remain as the Managing Director of a company if s/he can satisfy the Court that as a part of the implementation of, and compliance with, the Articles of Association of the Company or as part of execution of the stipulations made in a contract entered into by the company with the Managing Director, s/he has acquired an equitable right, subject to the conditions :hat making/keeping the said petitioner as the Managing Director of the company shall not be a violation of any provisions of the law of the land and, further, service of the Managing Director is needed for the greater interest of the company, meaning that not only the shareholders, but also the other stakeholders of the company, including the creditors, shall be benefited by retaining the said Managing Director. Therefore, if the petitioner/s of a section 233 application, who may be the Managing Director him/herself or together with other shareholders or only a group of shareholders other than the Managing Director having 10% shares in the company, can show to the Company Court that the company has incorporated a provision in its Articles of Association or the company has entered into a contract breaking any law of the country, the application deserves consideration by this Court, for, conducting the affairs of a company either by incorporating a provision in its Articles of Association inconsistent with the law of the land or by adopting a resolution in violation of the law of the land shall be tantamount to prejudicial action against all the shareholders and debenture-holders of a company. 102. In this case, it has been found hereinbefore that a part of the provisions of Article 124 of the Articles of Association has been incorporated in violation of section 91 of the Companies Act and amendment of Article 145 has also been done upsetting the provisions of sections 109 and 110 of the Companies Act and, also, one Independent Director has been appointed infringing the provisions of Code 1(3) of the Corporate Governance Code, 2018. Hence, this Court is well competent to pass necessary Orders cancelling the resolutions of the Board Meetings and the EGM whereat the same were adopted and this Court, thereby, can amend the provisions of Articles 124 and 145 to the extent it is necessary and, then, direct the Company to conduct the Company's affairs in a manner to be specified hereinafter. Moreover, this Company, being a public listed company, there is another aspect of this case, namely, public interest. In a section 233 application, whenever, either directly from the statements made in the petition or from the queries made by the Court at the time of admission hearing, it transpires to the Company Court that the said Company's affairs are being run in a manner which is unsafe for the general investors, creditors and other stakeholders, it is incumbent upon the Company Court to admit the case towards final hearing and, if needed, to pass ad-interim Order/s exercising its power under section 233 (3)(b) in tandem with section 85(3) of the Companies Act, if applicable. 103. In this case, the Company has got a liability of Taka 672,99,34,040 (Taka six hundred seventy two crores ninety nine lacs thirty four thousand fourty) to different Banking and other companies and, also, the general shareholders have invested more than Taka 100,00,0000 (Taka hundred crores) by acquiring shares through stock exchanges in addition to the investments made by the promoters. Therefore, for protecting the interest of the general investors, Banks, Financial Institutions and other stakeholders, this Court requires to issue necessary Directions upon the Chairman, Managing Director, shareholder-Directors, Independent Directors, Bank and other companies of home and abroad with whom the company currently is transacting its businesses and will engage in business in future, so that because of the on-going tussle between the groups of Directors of the Company, the normal transactions of the Company are not hampered in any manner. Keeping the afore-stated consideration in view, this Court is of the opinion that the Company's affairs should be run and conducted by as many upright and competent Independent Directors as may be accommodated. Keeping the aforesaid purpose in view, this Court now appoints (i) Dr. Kazi Anowarul Hoque, PhD, a retired Additional Secretary to the Government of Bangladesh who possesses vast experience of working in different field, including External Resources Division of the Government and presently serving as an Advisor to the Asian Development Bank (ADB) and has been certified by his present and former colleagues to be a man of unquestionable integrity, (ii) Mr Muhammad Shafiqur Rahman, Barrister-at-Law, a regular practitioner in the Supreme Court of Bangladesh having specialisation in Company and Securities Laws, (iii) Mr Fakhruddin Ahmed, FCA, FCMA, an experienced Chartered Accountant and (iv) Ambassador Syed Shahed Reza, who previously served as the Ambassador of Bangladesh to Kuwait and is a former President of Dhaka Club and, presently, Secretary General, Olympic Association of Bangladesh and is known to have a good rapport with corporate and political bodies and figures of home and abroad, as the Independent Directors of the Company for 3 (three) years. Of them, Dr. Kazi Anowarul Hoque, will be acting as the Vice-Chairman of the Company. 104. Before passing the necessary Orders and Directions, it is to be noted down here that currently the Board of Directors is being run under the chairmanship of Justice (retired) Moyeenul Islam Chowdhury with his two 2 (two) comrades as the Independent Directors (Barrister Muhammad Shafiqur Rahman and Mr Fakhruddin Ahmed FCMA, FCA) together with 4 (four) family members from each of the families of Mr Abdus Salam Murshedy (the petitioner No. 1) and Mr Kutubuddin Ahmed (the respondent No. 2) on the basis of an Order passed by this Court on 25-8-2022. And upon taking consent from the learned Advocates of both the sides, while Mr Tanvir Ahmed (respondent No. 4, who is the son of Mr Kutubuddin Ahmed) was appointed as the Managing Director of the Company, Barrister Shehrin Salam Oishee (the petitioner No. 3, who happens to be the daughter of Mr Abdus Salam Murshedy, the petitioner No. 1) was appointed as the Deputy Managing Director of the Company. Thereafter, an endeavour was made by this Court to sort out the disputes amicably with the aid of the Court-appointed Independent Directors, but it did not see the light of success. 105. Accordingly, the following Orders and Directions are passed; Orders as to cancellations of the Board Resolutions dated 22-3-2022, 18-4-2022 and 8-6-2022 as well as the Decisions taken in the EGM held on 12-5-2022 and, thereby, formation of the Board of Directors: 106. It is hereby ordered that the Board resolutions dated 22-3-2022, 18-4-2022 and 8-6-2022 as well as the decisions taken in the EGM held on 12-5-2022 so far as they relate to creation of the posts of Additional Directors, appointments of three Additional Directors Mr Sunil Darlatram Daryanani, Mr Sheikh Bashir Ahmed and Mr Moin Uddin, appointment of Mr Sheikh Bashir Ahmed as Vice-Chairman and appointment of Mr Rezaur Rahaman Sohag as an Independent Director of the Company are hereby cancelled. And, (i) Dr. Kazi Anowarul Hoque, (ii) Barrister Muhammad Shafiqur Rahman, (iii) Mr Fakhruddin Ahmed and Ambasador Syed Shahed Reza are appointed as the Independent Directors of the Company for 3 (three) years. Of them, Dr. Kazi Anowarul Hoque will be acting as the Vice-Chairman of the Company. The Board of Directors are formed with the following structure:

The amended Articles 124 and 145 are replaced by the following wordings in Articles 124 and 145: Articles 124: "The Directors shall have power at any time, and from time to time, to appoint any person, who may be a nominee of an institutional shareholder, to be a Director as an addition to the Board, or to fill a casual vacancy but the total number of Directors shall not at any time exceed the number fixed by the Article 117. However, if the Company intends to appoint Additional Director/s under the modified provisions of Article 124; as it stands pursuant to the Order of this Court, in that event, the Company should get it approved either in any EGM or in the AGM for the calendar year an, for the reason that the present version of Article 124 will come into effect from the date of signing this Judgment. full_judgment:
Mahmudul Hoque, J: In this application under Article 102 of the Constitution Rule Nisi was issued calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the order No. 61 dated 7-8-2018 passed by the Judge of the Artha Rin Adalat No. 4, Dhaka (respondent No. 3) in Miscellaneous Case No. 17 of 2009 as evidenced by (Annexure-'F') to the writ petition allowing the application under Order 6, rule 17 and Order 1, rule 10(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure should not be declared to be without lawful authority and is of no legal effect and/or such other or further order or orders passed as to this Court may seem fit and proper.
2. Shorn of unnecessary details, fact of the case lies in a very short compus. Respondent Nos. 5-12, as petitioner, filed an application under Order 21, rules 58 and 90 of the Code of Civil Procedure read with sections 32(2) and 57 of the Artha Rin Adalat AM 2003, in Execution Case No. 105 of 2002 claiming title in the case property. The bank contested the case by filing written objection and additional written objection. The execution court heard the Miscellaneous Case No. 17 of 2009 and after hearing by its judgment and order dated 5-11-2009 dismissed the same.
3. Being aggrieved, the petitioners moved before the District Judge by filing Miscellaneous Appeal No. 312 of 2009 which was dismissed on 3-3-2009. Thereafter, the petitioner in Miscellaneous Case filed Civil Revision No. 1848 of 2010 before this Court in which the rule was made absolute. Against the judgment and order of this Court the bank preferred CPLA No. 1469 of 2011 and the auction purchaser preferred CPLA No. 1498 of 2011. In those appeals the Appellate Division set-aside the judgment and order of this Court and sent back the case to the execution court on remand for fresh trial by its judgment and order dated 24-1-2016. After arrival of record before the execution court the petitioners in miscellaneous case filed an application under Order 6, rule 17 of the Code of Civil Procedure praying for amendment of their application. The bank filed written objection against the application for amendment. The petitioners also filed an application under Order 1, rule 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure praying for adding the auction purchaser opposite party. The execution court heard the applications for amendment of original application and addition of party and after hearing by its judgment and order dated 7-8-2018 allowed both the applications. At this juncture, the auction purchaser moved this Court by filing this writ petition and obtained the present Rule Nisi and order of stay.
4. Mr Md Hasanat Parvez, learned Advocate appearing for the petitioners submits that proposed amendment has changed the nature and character of the main application as the petitioners introduced new facts contrary to the statements made in the application at the time of filing of the same. He further argued that law does not allow a petitioner or plaintiff to alter the nature and character of the plaint or application by introducing inconsistent and contradictory facts to the detriment of the other party, as such, the execution court has committed illegality in allowing the application for amendment of main application filed under Order 21, rules 58 and 90 CPC and sections 32(2) and 57 of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003. In support of his such submissions he has referred to a catena of cases Mollah Shahidul Islam vs Md Monsur Rahman and others reported in 57 DLR 164, Shahajadpur Central Co-operative Bank Ltd. vs Md Majibur Rahman and others reported in 1998 BLD (AD) 81 = 50 DLR (AD) 86, Nazrul Islam Majumder (Md) vs Tahamina Akhtar alias Nahid and another reported in 42 DLR 235, M/s City Ice and Cold Storage Ltd. vs Nitai Chandra Shah and others reported in 1983 BLD (AD) 268, Abdus Salam vs Korban Ali and another reported in 48 DLR 372 and Khaledur Reza Chowdhury vs Saleha Begum and others reported in 48 DLR (AD) 209.
5. Mr Mustafa Niaz Mohammad, Senior Advocate with Mr Md Khalilur Rahaman and Mr Mohammad Masum Billah, learned Advocates appearing for the respondent Nos. 5-12 submit that the decree holder bank did not come before this Court against the order passed by the execution court. The auction purchaser of the property who has no connection about title of the property mortgaged with the bank by the mortgagor, they only can claim that in response to an auction notice they participated in the auction and being highest bidder their offer was accepted by the bank and they purchased the property in auction upon payment of auction price. Had there been any grievance against the order of the execution court the mortgagee bank could have agitated the validity of the order.
6. He further submits that it is the settled principle of law that the plaintiff cannot file an application seeking amendment of plaint which may change the nature and character of the suit introducing inconsistent and contradictory fact, but in the present case the petitioners in miscellaneous case filed the application for amendment of their petition only adding some statement which are absolutely relating to the document filed before the court and it was filed pursuant to the direction and observations made by the Hon'ble Appellate Division in disposing CPLA Nos. 1498 and1469 of 2011, as such, the nature and character of the application in Miscellaneous Case No. 17 of 2009 has not been changed in any way. Moreover, the opposite party can agitate and deny the facts by filing written objection and by cross examining the witnesses at the time of hearing of the miscellaneous case.
7. It is also argued that admittedly that the proposed amendment brings some new facts which are necessary for disposal of the dispute between the parties, as such, the execution court committed no illegality in accepting the amendment of the main application. In support of his submissions he has referred to the cases of Abdul Wadud contractor and another vs Nazir Ahmed and others reported in 48 DLR (AD) 120, M/s Bangladesh Rubber Industries and another vs Begum Lutfunessa and another reported in 1983 BLD (AD) 220, Abdul Rouf (Md) alias Nayan vs State and another reported in 53 DLR 283 and Sunil Chandra Mondal and others vs Narayan Chandra Shil and others reported in 50 DLR (AD) 148.
8. We have heard the learned Advocates of both the sides, have gone through the impugned judgment and order passed by the execution court along with other annexures annexed to the writ petition.
9. The bank filed Execution Case No. 105 of 2002 for execution of the decree passed in Title Suit No. 27 of 2001 in favour of the bank in which the bank obtained a certificate under section 33(5) of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain to sell the property at their instance. Accordingly, the bank published an auction notice on 12-7-2009 for sale of the property fixing 30-7-2009 for submission of quotation and the property was sold in auction on 19-8-2009. The respondent Nos. 5-12 as petitioners filed Miscellaneous Case No. 17 of 2009 under Order 21, rules 58 and 90 of the Code read with sections 32(2) and 57 of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, which was dismissed by the execution court vide the judgment and order dated 5-1-2009. Thereafter, they preferred Miscellaneous Appeal No. 312 of 2009 before the District Judge which was also disallowed on 3-3-2010. Thereafter, Civil Revision No. 1148 of 2010 was preferred in which the Rule was made absolute. Against the judgment and order of this Division the bank and the auction purchaser preferred CPLA Nos. 1469 and 1998 of 2011 respectively before the Appellate Division in which the appeals was allowed on 24-1-2016 and sent back the case to the execution court on remand for fresh trial. Thereafter, the petitioners in Miscellaneous Case No. 17 of 2009 filed an application seeking amendment of their original application proposing some facts to be added and wanting deletion of some statements made in the application. The application was opposed by the bank as well as the present petitioner. The execution court by the impugned judgment and order dated 7-8-2018 allowed the application, hence, the present writ petition.
<u>10. It is true that the plaintiff or applicant in any proceeding cannot alter the nature and character of the suit or the application by introducing new, inconsistent and contradictory fact to the detriment of the other party. It is also settled that Order 6, rule 17 of the Code provides that the court may at any stage of the proceedings can allow either party to alter or amend their pleadings in such manner and on such terms as may be just and necessary for the purpose of determining the real questions in controversy between the parties. From perusal of application for amendment, we find that the petitioners in miscellaneous case wanted to add some statements as paragraph '1Ka"8Ka', and '8Kha' and to add a schedule describing the same as disputed land which was sold in auction and wanted to delete some statements in different paragraphs relating to knowledge of the auction and other admitted facts.</u>
11. From perusal of judgment and order passed by the Appellate Division in the above mentioned 2 (two) CPLAs, it appears that the court observed that present respondent Nos. 5-12, as petitioner, in Miscellaneous Case No. 17 of 2019 submitted some documents which were not filed before the execution court and observed that it is imperative on the part of the execution court to consider those documents. In the event of considering the documents so have been filed by the petitioners in miscellaneous case, statements in that regard should be made in the main application. Accordingly, the petitioners in Miscellaneous Case No. 17 of 2019 by filing an application wanted to introduce such facts relating to documents filed in court. We find that by way of amendment the nature and character of the main application has not been changed in any way rather those statements by way of amendment is necessary for the purpose of determining real questions in controversy.
12. In that view of the matter, the decisions referred by the petitioner regarding amendment of pleading has no application in the instant case, but facts remains whether some facts admitted by the petitioners in miscellaneous case in their main application can be deleted after a long time substituting a new facts which already created right in favour of the opposite party. In this case, the petitioner
in miscellaneous case at paragraph No. 2 clearly stated that:
"বিগত ২৩-৫-২০০৫ ইং তারিখে দৈনিক ইনকিলাব পত্রিকায় ১নং প্রতিপক্ষ বাদী কর্তৃক নালিশী সম্পত্তি বিষয়ে নিলাম সম্বন্ধে জানিতে পারেন যে, ৪ ও ৫ নং প্রতিপক্ষ আমেনা ও জামিনা বিবি নালিশী সম্পত্তি বিগত ২০-৮-১৯৯৭ তারিখে প্রতিপক্ষ বরাবরে ৬৩৪৬ নং মর্গেজ দলিল করিয়া দিয়া ২ ও ৩ নং প্রতিপক্ষকে ১নং প্রতিপক্ষ হইতে লোন পাওয়াইয়া দিয়াছে।"
<u>13. By the proposed amendment, the petitioner in miscellaneous case deleted the date of knowledge as mentioned in Clause-'s' of the proposed amendment and also deleted the statement in same paragraph "বিগত ২০০৩ ইং সনের ডিসেম্বর মাসের শেষ সপ্তাহে". This two dates stated in the main application relating to cause of auction for filing of the miscellaneous case and filing of the Title Suit No. 158 of 2005. By the amendment admittedly, we find that the nature and character of the original application has not been changed, but the petitioners in miscellaneous case once admitted the fact of their knowledge from "Daily Inailab" and also stated name of a month thereafter, so admission made by the petitioners in the original application about date of knowledge cannot be allowed to change the same by subsequent amendment giving a go bye to such admission, bringing a new date of knowledge. In the present case, the deletion of such fact as stated in Clause-'ঙ' and ‘চ’ of the application for amendment of their main application cannot be entertained.</u>
14. In the situation, we are inclined to maintain the order of the execution court allowing amendment except the statements proposed to be deleted from paragraph 2 of the main application mentioned in Clauses-'s' and of the amendment application.
15. Taking into consideration the above, we find no merit in the Rule Nisi issued as well as in the submissions of the learned Advocate for the petitioner except the proposed amendment in Clauses-'ঙ' and 'চ'. Therefore, we feel that the impugned order needs to be modified to that extent.
16. In the result, the Rule is disposed of with modification.
17. The execution court is directed to dispose of the Miscellaneous Case No. 17 of 2009 within 3(three) months excluding the amendment made in Clauses-'ঙ' and 'চ'.
18. The order of stay granted at the time of issuance of the Rule Nisi stands vacated.
Communicate a copy of this judgment to the parties concerned.
End.

lawyer:
Md Ahiya, Advocate—For the petitioners in both Civil Revisions. 
Md Hamidur Rahman, Advocate—For the opposite party No.1-8 in Civil Revision No.925 of 2006 and Opposite Party No.1 in Civil Revision No. 927 of 2006.
parties:
Sheikh Murad Hossain and others ------- Petitioner
vs
A. Gaffar Khan and others --------- Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
Sheikh Hassan Arif, J : Since the questions of facts and law involved in these two Civil Revisions are almost same and the said Civil Revisions have arisen out of the similar impugned orders in two miscellaneous appeals, the same have been taken up together for hearing and are now being disposed of by this common judgment.
1.1 At the instance of the respondents in Artha Rin Miscellaneous Appeal Nos. 16 of 2004 and 15 of 2004, Rules in the aforesaid Civil Revisions were issued calling upon the appellants therein to show cause as to why the orders dated 2-10-2005 passed by the First Court of Additional District Judge, Dhaka in the said appeals thereby reversing the judgment and orders dated 23-5-2004 passed by the Fourth Court of Artha Rin Adalat, Dhaka in Miscellaneous Case Nos. 27 of 2002 and 28 of 2002 arising out of Artha Rin Execution Case No. 59 of 1997, should not be set-aside.
2. Back Ground Facts:
2.1 The common facts, relevant for the disposal of the Civil Revisions, in short, are that in execution of Artha decree obtained by Uttara Bank Ltd. Hatkhola Road Branch, Dhaka, (opposite party No.9), the decree holder bank filed Artha Rin Execution Case No. 59 of 1997 before the Fourth Court of Artha Rin Adalat, Dhaka against the petitioners in these Civil Revisions. In execution process of the said decree, the Artha Rin Adalat concerned issued notice as regards attachment of the property of the petitioners, which they mortgaged in favour of the Bank to secure the credit facility obtained by them. During such execution process, the opposite party Nos. 1-8 in Civil Revision No. 925 of 2006 and opposite party No. 1 in Civil Revision No. 927 of 2006 filed two sets of applications under Order XXI, rule 58 of the Code of Civil Procedure for releasing the said properties from such attachment process claiming themselves to be the owners of the said property by way of purchase from the admitted original owner. Accordingly, the said applications were registered as Miscellaneous Case Nos. 27 of 2002 and 28 of 2002.
2.2 The common case of the said claimants before the executing Court is that they purchased the said property by way of registered purchase deeds either from the admitted owner, Sheikh Mozahar Ali or from the transferee of the said admitted owner. The said Miscellaneous Cases were contested by the heirs of the said admitted owner, namely the petitioners in these Civil Revisions as opposite parties by filing written objections mainly contending that the admitted owner Sheikh Mozahar Ali did not make any such transfer by way of sale, and that after the death of the said admitted owner, they (the petitioners) remained owners in possession of the said property by way of inheritance, and they muted their names in order to pay khajna etc. Their further case is that at one stage of such ownership and possession, they tried to sell the said property by way of agreement/baina in favour of one Mr Ahmed Ali Chowdhury, who published legal notice in the daily Ittefaq on 29-7-1988. But nobody raised objection about such proposal of sale or such ownership of the petitioners in respect of the land in question. However, the said sale agreement was later cancelled. That the petitioners then mortgaged the said property with the opposite party No.9-Bank on 16-5-1991 in order to obtain some credit facilities, and, accordingly, the Bank filed execution case for execution of the decree obtained against them wherein attachment proceedings commenced in respect of the said property. That the claimants created some forged deeds, and, accordingly, they do not have any right, title, and interest in the said property. The decree holder bank also opposed the said applications filed by the claimants by filing separate written objection, thereby, supporting the case of the petitioners in these Civil Revisions.
2.3 In support of the case of the claimants in the said miscellaneous cases, four witnesses were produced. The claimants also produced several documents, which were marked as exhibit Nos. 1-9. On the other hand, the petitioners and the bank produced several documents which were marked as Exhibits 'Ka' to 'Uma' and Exhibit Ka(ka). Thereupon, the Executing Artha Rin Adalat, after hearing the parties, rejected both the Miscellaneous Cases vide orders dated 23-5-2004 taking the view that the claimants or their predecessors in interest purchased the said property from the admitted owner Shekh Mozahar Ali even before creation of interest and title in favour of Mojahar Ali in respect of the said property on the point that the registration in respect of such transfer was not entered in the balam book of the registration office at the time when such transfer took place. According to the executing adalat, although the admitted owner Sheikh Mozahar Ali purchased the said property by registered deed No. 40919, which was executed in his favour on 23-11-1978, the same was recorded in the balam of the Registry Office on 4-11-1981, and, accordingly, during this time in between 23-11-1978 and 4-11-1981, the title of the property did not pass in favour of the said Sheikh Mozahar Ali, and, accordingly, the transfer made by Mozahar Ali was no transfer in the eye of law.
2.4 Being aggrieved by such orders and finding of the Artha Rin Executing Adalat, the claimants preferred appeal before the Court of District Judge, Dhaka, being Miscellaneous Appeal Nos. 16 of 2004 and 15 of 2004. Accordingly, the said miscellaneous appeals were transferred to the First Court of Additional District Judge, Dhaka for hearing and disposal. Thereupon, the said Court, after hearing the parties, allowed both the appeals vide impugned orders dated 2-11-2005 holding the view that the claimants succeeded in establishing their title in respect of the property in question, and, accordingly, the said properties were not liable to be attached in the said execution case. Being aggrieved by the said judgment and orders, the heirs of the admitted owner, as petitioners, have obtained Rules in the aforesaid Civil Revisions.
2.5 Both the Rules are contested by both sets of claimants through learned advocate Mr Md Hamidur Rahman.
3. Submissions:
3.1 Mr Md Ahiya, learned advocate appearing for the petitioners, submits that the petitioners are the admitted heirs of Sheikh Mozahar Ali. Therefore, the property automatically devolved on them on the admitted death of Mozahar Ali. According to him, the petitioners became owners in possession of the said property by way of inherence. By referring to the impugned judgment and orders, learned advocate submits that the impugned judgments passed by the appellate Court are non-speaking judgments and orders and, by the impugned judgments, the appellate Court has mechanically set-aside the judgment of the Artha Rin Executing Adalat which gave judgment in favour of the petitioners taking the view that the transfer in favour of the said claimants of the disputed property was not lawful transfer and such transfer did not pass any title in favour of the claimants. By referring to another observation of the executing adalat as regards publication of sale notice in the newspaper by the proposed purchaser of the land, learned advocate submits that the executing adalat categorically held that when such notice was published, the claimants did not raise any objection against the same, although the claimants were in possession ai the relevant time. Therefore, according to him, the appellate Court having allowed the appeal without controverting the questions of facts and law decided by the executing adalat in favour of the petitioners, the impugned judgments and orders should be set-aside.
3.2 He submits further that the. Miscellaneous Cases filed by the claimants were barred by the proviso to Order XXI, rule 58 of the Code inasmuch as that they intentionally delayed in filing the said Miscellaneous Cases which is apparent from their depositions before the Court below. Therefore, he submits that since the claimants failed to prove their title, possession, and their bonafide interest in claiming the title in the said property or release of the property from attachment at the earlier opportunity, the appellate Court below has committed gross illegality in setting aside the judgment and orders passed by the executing adalat.
3.3 As against above submissions, Mr Md Hamidur Ralunan, learned advocate appearing for both sets of opposite parties, submits that the main issue in this case before the executing adalat was as to when the title of the suit property was passed in favour of the purchaser from the admitted owner Mozahar Ali or whether the title was at all passed in their favour. Therefore, he submits that other collateral issues were unnecessarily discussed by the executing adalat in order to justify the rejection of the said miscellaneous cases.
3.4 By referring to the provisions under Section 47 of the Registration Act, he submits that the title of admitted owner sheikh Mozahar Ali in the property in question passed in favour of the purchasers of the said property on the day he executed the transfer deed. According to him, registration of a title deed being a legal requirement, such registration strengthens such transfer of title, and it is immaterial as to when the said registration got its entry into the balam book of the registration office concerned. In support of his such submission, he has referred to decisions in Ata Ullah vs Custodian Evacuee Property, 16 DLR (SC) 298 and Messrs. Green & White vs Registrar, IS Companies, 15 DLR 492.
3.5 Learned advocate submits that the issue of passing of title from the original admitted owner as decided by the executing adalat is bereft of any legal authority, and, as such, the same should be set-aside immediately even though the said issue has not been categorically addressed by the appellate Court below. By referring to Exhibit-9, namely the inquiry report done by surveyor office, he submits that as per the said inquiry report, the claimants were found in possession of the suit property, but the executing adalat, in a very cursory way, ignored the finding of possession in the said inquiry report.
<u>4. Deliberations, Findings, and Orders of the Court:</u>
<u>4.1 To address the issues raised by the contesting parties, we have examined the impugned judgment and orders passed by the lower appellate Court. It appears that the said judgment has been delivered not in accordance with law inasmuch as that the said judgment did not address the issues on the basis of which the lower executing adalat decided the dispute concerned. The lower appellate Court discussed nothing about the possession of the respective parties. Most importantly, it did not address the issue of execution of transfer deed or as to when the title passes upon such execution and the effect of registration of transfer deed in respect of immovable properties as provided by the relevant provisions of the Registration Act.</u>
4.2 The same mistake, although in similar way, has been done by the executing adalat inasmuch as that it took the view (rightly or wrongly) that the title did not pass at the time of execution of the transfer deed by the admitted owner Sheikh Mozahar Ali on the ground that the registered deeds did not get their place in the balam book of the registration office. However, frustratingly, the lower executing adalat did not cite any authority or law on the basis of which it reached such conclusion, particularly when there are specific provisions of law in this regard as provided by Transfer of Property Act and Registration Act. Therefore, we have no option but to discuss the core issues of this case, namely, as to when the title passed from the admitted owner Sheikh Mozahar Ali in favour of the purchasers by the said deeds.
4.3 As per the claim of the claimants, the admitted owner Sheikh Mozahar Ali became owner in possession of the said property by way of purchase from the admitted transferor Radha Bhallav Mandal, who executed such transfer deed on 23-11-1978 (Exhibit-Ka), which, according to the executing adalat, got its entry in the balam book of the registration office on 4-11-1981. The question raised before the executing adalat was whether the title in the property passed in favour of Sheikh Mozahar Ali on the date of execution and registration of the said transfer deed, namely, on 23-11-1978. In this regard, we may refer to the provisions under Section 8 of the Transfer of Property Act which provides that a transfer takes place forthwith unless a different intention is expressed, or necessarily implied, and such transfer passes forthwith to the transferee all the interest which the transferor is then capable of passing in the property and all the legal incidents thereof.
4.4 It was not the case of the petitioners before the executing adalat that the said transfer deed, by which the admitted owner got title, was a forged transfer deed. The very title of the petitioners before the executing adalat also is based on the said transfer deed by Radha Ballav in favour of Sheikh Mozahar Ali. Therefore, it appears from the judgment of the executing adalat that the whole issue circled around the effect of execution of transfer deed and/or registration thereof.
4.5 As stated above, a transfer of immovable property passes forthwith all the title, interest in the transferor in favour of the transferee as per the provisions of Section 8 of the Transfer of Property Act. Now, the requirement of registration of such transfer deed is requirement of law in order to safeguard such transfer from any future question, and by such registration, the State becomes party to such transfer, and the Legislature has given a kind of protection in favour of such registered transfer by operation of law in that it gets presumption of correctness once it is registered, unless contrary is proved. Section 47 of the Registration Act is very much clear in this regard which provides that a registered document shall operate from the time which it would have commenced to operate, if no registration thereof had been required or made and not from the time of its registration. Therefore, the Legislature has made it clear that since the registration of a transfer deed is a formal requirement, the transfer in fact started to operate at the time when such transfer is made by way of execution of transfer deeds although, at that point of time, the said deed was not registered formally. Now, the Legislature has subsequently made such transfer mandatory even by saying that any transfer without such registration will be void. This statutory requirement of registration of transfer deed in respect of immovable property has been provided only to safeguard the transferor and the transferee from any manipulation or subsequent fraudulent act in respect of such transfer, as because the State becomes witness to such transfer by way of such registration.
4.6 Again, the further formalities as regards certification of such registration and/or endorsement of such registration, as provided by Part X of the Registration Act are also formalities to be complied with by registration office upon such registration of a transfer deed in respect of immovable property. The transferor or transferee has got nothing to do with that. Therefore, it cannot be said that even if a registration is not certified or any delay takes place in the certification of such transfer or entry of such transfer in the balam book of the registration office, the transfer did not take place. On this point, it appears, the executing adalat has committed gross mistake of law, which is apparent from the judgment of the executing adalat. Based on that misconceived idea of law of transfer and registration, the executing adalat proceeded to the extent of holding the view that the admitted owner Mozahar Ali did not get any title in respect of the said property before 4-11-1981, when the said registration as regard his purchase was recorded in the balam book of the registration office. From this misconceived idea, the executing adalat held that the title in respect of the said property did not pass in favour of the said Sheikh Mozahar Ali before 4-11-1981. This view of the executing adalat does not have any basis of law. Rather, it is clearly contrary to the provisions of law as stated above. The subsequent observations of the executing adalat were nothing but to justify his main legal contention as regards transfer of title in favour of the original owner Sheikh Mozahar Ali, particularly, when it is apparent that the executing adalat clearly ignored Exhibit-9 without assigning any reason, wherein the inquiry of the surveyor office found the claimants' possession in the disputed land. This being the position of law and fact, we do not need to deliberate on other collateral issues, which are not very relevant for determining the main issue of transfer of the title. The other contention of the petitioners before the executing adalat as regards the signature of admitted owner Sheikh Mozahar Ali on the transfer deed, by which Mozahar Ali transferred the property in favour of the claimants, also could not be established by them.
4.7 The executing adalat did not even consider that point by assigning reason in the judgment delivered by it. Therefore, since the registered title deeds, by which the claimants purchased disputed properties, namely, Exhibit-2, 3, 5, being registered transferred deeds, they have legal protection in their favour and such protection cannot be taken away by mere statements of anybody that the said documents were false documents, unless the party claiming the same be false adduces sufficient evidence, which is clearly absent in this case.
4.8 Therefore, we are of the view that the claimants in the miscellaneous cases concerned have been able to establish their title in respect of the disputed property, and, accordingly, the executing adalat should have released the said property from the clutches of attachment in view of the provisions under Order XXI, rule 58 of the Code of Civil Procedure.
4.9 Thus, although we are not very happy with the contents of the impugned judgment of the appellate Court below, we agree with the conclusion reached by it in allowing the said appeals. Therefore, we have no option, but to discharge the Rules in these Civil Revisions. 4.10 In the result, the Rules are discharged. Ad interim order, if any, thus stands recalled and vacated. The impugned judgment and orders dated 2-10-2005 passed by the First Court of Additional District Judge, Dhaka in Artha Rin Miscellaneous Appeal Nos. 16 of 2004 and 15 of 2004 are, hereby, affirmed.
Communicate at once.
End.

caseno:
Civil Revision No. 9213 of 1991
Civil Revision No. 87 of 1987
lawyer:
Ms. Salina Akter, with Mr. Uzzal Bhowmick, Advocates ------- For the petitioners
None appears ---------- For the opposite parties
parties:
Md. Abdul Wadud Khan being dead his heirs: Mahmud Nadir Abdullah Khan and others ------- Plaintiff-Respondent-Petitioners
Vs.
Md. Kamrul Islam Khan and others ---------- Defendant-Appellant-O.P.s
full_judgment:
Md. Zakir Hossain, J: 1. At the instance of the petitioners, the Rule was issued by this Court with the following terms: 
“Let the records of the Case be called for and a Rule issue calling upon the opposite parties to show cause as to why the judgment and decree complained of in the petition moved in Court today should not be set aside or such other or further order or orders passed as to this Court may seem fit and proper.” 

2. Facts leading to the issuance of the Rule are inter alia that the predecessor of the instant petitioners being plaintiff filed Other Class Suit No. 405 of 1978 before the Court of the learned Munsif (now Assistant Judge), Naogaon for declaration of title in the suit land as mentioned in the schedule to the plaint. 

3. The plaintiff’s case, in short, is that the suit property was the khas land of the Ex Zaminder. The plaintiff took settlement of the same by dint of amalnama (Exhibit-1) in the year of 1333 B.S. The zaminder instituted the Rent Suit No. 582 of 1951 against the plaintiff for arrears of rent wherein the plaintiff paid up the demand by challan (Exhibit-3). Accordingly, S.A khatian was prepared in the name of the plaintiff and thereafter, the plaintiff used to pay rent to the Government. But unfortunately, at the time of Revisional Settlement Operation, the suit land was recorded in the names of both the plaintiff and the defendants. On the basis of the objection petition filed by the plaintiff, the Revenue Officer corrected the MRR and accordingly, recorded the entire land in the name of the plaintiff. But since the plaintiff lived far away from the suit land, the defendants managed to record their names in the RS khatin along with the name of the plaintiff though the plaintiff is the absolute owner of the suit land. He has exclusive possession therein and the RS record created cloudy over the suit land, therefore, the plaintiff constrained to file the aforesaid suit. The defendant contested the suit by filing joint written statements denying the material allegations set out in the plaint contending inter alia that the suit is not maintainable in its present form. 

4. The defendants’ case is that their father was a Government service holder and he took pattan of the suit land from Brikutsha Estate to this plaintiff as his benamder from his own fund for his own benefit. The plaintiff who was minor had no independent source of income and he did not take pattan and pay rents. During his life time, Naybullah khan possessed the suit land. He died in 1974 leaving behind the plaintiff and the defendants as his legal heirs. The suit land was correctly recorded in the finally published RS khatian. The plaintiff has got no exclusive title and possession in the suit land. And, therefore, the defendant prayed for dismissal of the suit. 

5. On the pleadings, the learned Munsif, Naogaon was pleased to frame the following issues: 
(i) Is the suit maintainable in its present form? 
(ii) Has the plaintiff got any cause of action to file the suit? 
(iii) Has the plaintiff any exclusive right, title and possession in the suit land? 
(iv) To what reliefs, if any, is the plaintiff entitled? 

6. After conclusion of the trial, the learned Munsif was pleased to decree the suit. Challenging the legality and propriety of the judgment and decree of the learned Munsif, the defendant-opposite parties preferred Title Appeal No. 81 of 1984 before the Court of the learned District Judge, Naogaon. Upon hearing, the learned District Judge was pleased to allow the said Title Appeal No. 81 of 1984 and as such, set aside the judgment and decree of the Trial Court. Impugning the judgment and decree of the learned District Judge, the petitioners moved this Court and obtained the aforesaid Rule. 

7. The Civil Revision was originally filed being No. 87 of 1987 at Rangpur Session and later on, it was renumbered as Civil Revision No. 9213 of 1991. 

8. Ms. Salina Akter, the learned Advocate alongwith Mr. Uzzal Bhowmick for the petitioners, submits that the learned Munsif after considering the evidence on record rightly held that the plaintiff is the owner and possessor of the suit land and the learned District Judge turned down the decision of the judgment and decree of the Trial Court holding the view that the original owner of the suit land is Naybullah khan and he purchased the suit land in the name of the plaintiff as benamder in the name of the plaintiff from his own fund. The learned District Judge also held that S.A record was prepared in the name of the plaintiff on the basis of the tenants; ledger of the Ex-land receiver and the plaintiff paid up rent to the Government and S.A stood in his name. The learned District Judge further held that during the revisional settlement operation, the suit land was recorded in the name of the plaintiff and the defendants according to their respective shares. 

9. She refers ratio and obiter of different judgments reported in 49 DLR (AD) 73, 51 DLR (AD) 81, 55 DLR (HCD) 412, 8 BLT (HCD) 171 and 11 BLT (HCD) 26. 

10. None appears to oppose the Rule. 

11. The trial Court after considering the entire materials on record held that the plaintiff has got the suit land by way of settlement and he has been possessing the same by paying rent and SA Operation was duly prepared in the name of the plaintiff, but the contention of the defendants is that their father took settlement of suit land from his own fund in the benami of the plaintiff; therefore, onus lies upon them but they hopelessly failed to discharge the burden of proof that their father took settlement in the name of the plaintiff as his benamder. After considering the evidence on record, the trial Court held that the plaintiff has title and possession in the suit land and accordingly, decreed the suit. It is true that father of the plaintiff and defendants did not challenge the settlement made in favour of the plaintiff during his lifetime. The Appellate Court held that Naybullah Khan was a government service holder and he took settlement of the suit land on 18th Jaistha, 1333 BS in the benami of his eldest son Abdul Khan who was at the time a minor boy of 6/7 years of age without any independent source of income or having any independent fund of his own. It is also stated by the Appellate Court since R.S. Khatian was jointly recorded in the name of the plaintiff and defendants; therefore, Appellate Court held the view the predecessor of the plaintiff Nayeb Ullah took settlement of the suit land showing the plaintiff as his benamdar. 

12. Now the pertinent issue is whether the impugned judgment and decree is liable to be interfered with by this Court. 

13. Heard the submissions advanced by the learned Advocates for the petitioners along with materials on record with care and attention and seriousness as it deserves. I have also meaningfully waded through the legal position critically involved in this case. 

14. It cannot be denied that the benami transaction was custom of the Country and it was recognized as customary law till Land Reforms Ordinance, 1984 was promulgated. In 1882, the practice of benami transaction received legislative recognition under section 81 and 82 of the Trusts Act, 1882. 

15. The principles governing the determination of the question whether a transaction is a benami transaction or not, may be summed up thus: 
i. The burden of showing that a transfer is a benami transaction, lies on the person who asserts that it is such a transaction. 
ii. If it is proved that the purchase money came from a person other than the person in whose favour the property is transferred, the purchase is prima facie assumed to be for the benefit of the person who supplied the purchase money, unless there is evidence to the contrary. 
iii. The true character of the transaction is governed by the intention of the person who has contributed the purchase money. 
iv. The question as to what his intention was, has to be decided on the basis of- 
(a) the surrounding circumstances, 
(b) the relationship of the parties, 
(c) the motives governing their action in bringing about the transaction, and 
(d) their subsequent conduct, etc. 

16. In this case, the onus of establishing that the transaction is benami, is on the defendants, where it is not possible to obtain evidence which conclusively establishes or rebuts the allegation, the case must be dealt with on reasonable probabilities and legal inferences arising from proved or admitted facts. 

17. In case of Nurjahan Begum v. Mahmudur Rahman 34 DLR (AD) 61 traced the history of benami transaction and also the law propounded by the Privy Council for the following conclusions: 
“In a benami transaction source of purchase money is an important criteria (sic) but it is not conclusive. The initial presumption in the case of a transfer concluded by a registered deed is in favour of the person whose name appears as the transferee in the deed, but this presumption is rebuttable. Source of consideration money though an important criteria in a benami transaction but in the absence of an unambiguous ownership consideration of other relevant circumstances become important in a case where ownership is disputed. The disputed question of benami cannot be determined only on the consideration of source of consideration money, and it becomes incumbent for the Court to fall back upon the surrounding circumstances of the transaction, the position of the parties and the relationship to each other. The motive which could govern their actions, but their subsequent conduct including their dealings and the enjoyment of the property become relevant factors for consideration. In the case of Bilas Kunwar vs. Desraj Ranjit Singh (1915) LR 42 1A 202 the Privy Council while adopting the principle an laid down is Gopeekrist Gossain's case, that the criterion in benami cases is the source of money with which the consideration was paid, made an important qualification, in that the source of purchase money is only to be the criterion in the absence of all other relevant circumstances, Among other circumstances possession of the property has been held to be very important. Privy Council in Imambandi Begum vs. Kamleshwari Pershad (1886) LR 13 IA 160 held as under: 
"Where there are benami transactions and the question is who is the real owner, the actual possession or receipt of rents of the property is most important" 

18. In the case of Ram Narain vs. Mohammad Hadi (1898) LR 26 IA 38 the Privy Council laid stress on the factum of possession of the property and the collection of rents. Incidentally, it may be mentioned that in a disputed case of benami, custody of the documents is a relevant factor to be considered. 

19. The Supreme Court of India in Jaydayal Podar vs. Bibi Hazra (1974) 2 SCR 90 had summed up the principles governing determination of benami transaction to which I have respectful approval, in the following words: 
"It is well settled that the burden of proving that a particular sale is benami and the apparent purchaser is not the real owner, always rests on the person asserting it to be so. This burden has to be strictly discharged by adducing legal evidence of a definite character which would either directly prove the fact of benami or establish circumstances unerringly and reasonably raising an inference of that fact. The essence of a benami is the intention of the party or parties concerned; and not unoften such intention is shrouded in a thick veil which cannot be easily pierced through. But such difficulties do not relieve the person asserting the transaction to be benami of any part of the serious onus that rests on him; nor justify the acceptance of mere conjectures or surmises, as a substitute for proof. The reason is, that a deed is a solemn document prepared and executed after considerable deliberation and the person expressly shown as the purchaser or transferee in the deed, starts with the initial presumption in his favour that the apparent state of affairs is the real state of affairs. Though the question, whether a particular sale is benami or not, is largely one of fact, and for determining this question, no absolute formulae or acid tests, uniformly applicable in all situations, can be laid down; yet in weighing the probabilities and for gathering the relevant indicia, the courts are usually guided by these circumstances; (1) the source from which the purchase money came; (2) the nature and possession of the property, after the purchase; (3) motive, if any, for giving the transaction a benami colour, (4) the position of the parties and the relationship, if any between, the claimant and the alleged benamder, (5) the custody of the title deeds after the sale and (6) the conduct of the parties concerned in dealing with the property after the sale." 

20. It appears from the record that the father of the plaintiff; Naybullah Khan took settlement of the suit land in favour of the plaintiff-petitioners in 18 Poush, 1333 B.S and S.A record was prepared in the name of the plaintiff and the plaintiff also paid rent to the Government as well as zamindar. It also appears from the record that the plaintiff’s father; Naybullah Khan left this transitory world on 11.01.1974. During his life time i.e within 46 years, Naybullah Khan did not file any suit for declaration that the plaintiff was his benamder nor he raised any question as to the transaction made by him in favour of the plaintiff. S.A khatian was prepared from 1956 to 1962. At that time Naybullah was alive, but he did not raise objection as to S.A khatian. It also appears that all the original documents were produced from the custody of the plaintiff and these documents were admissible as evidence. It is true that the R.S khatian was prepared in favour the plaintiff-petitioners and the defendants jointly and as such, created cloud over the stainless title of the suit land and therefore, the plaintiff was constrained to file a suit for declaration of title and to make a negative declaration that the defendants are not the owners of the suit land. It also appears that since the plaintiff failed to pay rent to the zaminder, the zaminder started rent suit against the plaintiff for realization of the rent in the year of 1951 being Rent Suit No. 582 of 1951 and the plaintiff paid rent to the zaminder. It also appears that during R.S operation, the plaintiff filed objection against the attestation khatian or field survey (মাঠ জরিপ) operation and upon hearing the objection, which were sustained and accordingly the name of the defendants included in the attested khatian had been struck down; but eventually, in collusion with the concerned officials of survey department, the defendants got their names recorded jointly and therefore, the plaintiff was constrained to file the aforesaid suit. Though, for the sake of argument, it is taken as granted that Naybullah Khan got settlment in favour of the plaintiff but his conduct implies that he took settlement for the benefit and welfare of his son; Md. Abdul Wadud Khan. 

21. P.W-2, Md. Abur Rahman was 62 years old man. He is a cultivator by profession. He also clearly stated that the plaintiff has been possessing the suit land through bargadar and he unequivocally states that he knows the suit land for 40 years. He admitted that he has no land within the contiguous land of the suit land, but his own land is nearby the suit land. He is an independent and reliable witness. His evidence amply supported the possession of the plaintiff and there is no apparent reason to disbelieve his evidence. 

22. P.W-3, Md. Hurmat Ali Mollik clearly spelt out in his evidence that he has been possessing the suit land during last 30 years as the bargadar of the plaintiff. 

23. D.W-2, Sheikh Md. Nazmul Haque is a man of 70 years old. In his evidence, he clearly states that he does not know who cultivates the suit land as bargadar. 

24. D.W-3, Kamal Uddin Tarafdar states that the father of the defendants used to possess the suit land through bargadar. But none of the bargadars was examined. Therefore, they are not competent witnesses and their evidence does not inspire any confidence. 

25. On perusal of the oral and documentary evidences, it appears that as per the Rules of preponderance of evidence, the contention of the plaintiff’s possession is heavy in weight but the learned District Judge on slipshod statement held that the joint possession of the plaintiff and the defendants without sifting the documents in entirety. The original documents are lying with the plaintiff and produced from the custody of the plaintiff and those were admitted as evidence without any objection from the defendants’ side. The burden of showing that the alleged transfer is banami transaction has not been discharged by the defendants’ side. Undisputedly, the father of the defendants in his lifetime did not take any legal action against the transaction nor he filed any suit for declaration that the plaintiff was his benamder. Considering the surrounding circumstances, the relationship between the parties and intention and subsequent conduct of Naybullah Khan, it is as clear as daylight that 94 years ago, Naybyllah Khan took settlement of the suit land for the benefit of his eldest son i.e the plaintiff for the purpose of the welfare of his son which is apparent from the subsequent conduct of the Naybullah Khan that means during his lifetime i.e in the span of 43 years did not take any legal action challenging the legality and propriety of the settlement rent suit, S.A khatian and other acts of possession, therefore, the learned District Judge without considering the ramification of the law of banami transaction from boarder perspective illegally held that since Naybullah Khan took settlement from his on fund, therefore, the transaction was benami transaction. 

26. The learned District Judge failed to appreciate that as soon as R.S record was jointly prepared in the name of the plaintiff and the defendants, the plaintiff was constrained to file the suit for declaration as the joint record of right created cloud over his title in the suit land. Therefore, it can be said that the learned District Judge without considering the materials on record and convoluted question of legal position involved in this case most illegally set aside the finding of the trial Court without assigning cogent reason and most illegally allowed the appeal and as such, the same is liable to be turned down to secure the ends of justice. 

27. My penultimate conclusion is that the presumption that the settlement took in favour of the plaintiff for his benefit has not been rebutted by the defendants adducing cogent and reliable evidence. Accordingly, I find substance in the Rule and therefore, the Rule deserves to be made absolute. 

28. In the result, the Rule is made absolute, however, without passing any order as to costs. The impugned judgment and decree of the Appellate Court is hereby set aside and restored those of the trial Court. 

29. Let a copy of the judgment along with LCRs be transmitted to the Courts below at once.

End.
