Hajera Khan and others	------- Appellants (In both the appeals)
Vs.
Afsaruddin being dead his heirs: 1(a) Rumia Khatun and others 	------- Respondents (In both the appeals)
full_judgment:
Md. Ashfaqul Islam, J: Both the civil appeals by leave are directed against the judgment and order dated 16.10.2012 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 3382 of 1995 (heard analogously with Civil Revision No. 3383 of 1995) making the rules absolute and thereby setting aside the judgment and decree passed in Title Appeal No. 87 of 1989 (heard analogously with Title Appeal No. 86 of 1989), dismissing the appeal and thereby affirming the judgment and decree passed in Title Suit No. 168 of 1984 (heard analogously with Title Suit No. 53 of 1987), decreeing the suit No. 168 of 1984 and dismissing the suit No. 53 of 1987.

The predecessor of the present appellants, Amjad Hossain as the plaintiff, filed Title Suit No. 575 of 1978 against Jashimuddin, the predecessor of the present respondent Nos. 1-5, and others which was subsequently renumbered as Title Suit No. 168 of 1984. The suit sought a declaration of title for the lands described in Schedules 1 and 2, confirmation of possession of the land in Schedule 1, recovery of khas possession of the land in Schedule 2, and a permanent injunction along with mesne profits.

Jashimuddin as plaintiff filed another suit being Title Suit No. 53 of 1987 impleading Amjad Hossain as the defendants regarding the self same suit land.

The case of the plaintiff in Title Suit No. 168 of 1984, in short, was that the lands described in schedule 1 and 2 are the accreted lands of Nuruli Ganga river adjacent to C.S. Plot No.153 owned by Jibunnessa Khatun and others, after accretion while the suit land became fit for cultivation the predecessor of the plaintiff Alauddin Bepari took settlement of the same from its owner 40 years back by giving salami and paying taxes. The suit land was duly recorded in the name of Alauddin Bepari in Plot Nos. 101 and 153. Alauddin Bepari died leaving plaintiff as his heir. The defendants raised objection against the S.A. record of the suit land under section 30 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act but became unsuccessful. The defendants reside near the schedule 2 property and in the first part of Agrahayan 1385 B.S. they forcefully dispossessed the plaintiffs from the schedule 2 property and hence the suit.

The case of the defendants is that the suit land is the accreted land and it is contiguous to Plot Nos. 154, 161 and 162. While the land started accreting gradually Jashimuddin took settlement of 101/2 pakhi of land from the original owner Jibunnessa Khatun by executing a kabuliyat which was registered on 14th Chaitra 1353 B.S. Subsequently Jasimuddin took settlement of 15 pakhi of land more from Jibunnnessa by two patta. Since taking settlement of those lands Jashimuddin possessed the same on payment of rent to the landlord and subsequently to the Government. He constructed his house on a portion of the suit land and possessed the rest through cultivation, all within the knowledge of everyone, including the plaintiffs. During S.A. operation the suit land was wrongly recorded in the name of plaintiffs. The plaintiffs took advantage of the survey staff residing in their house and collusively managed to have the suit land recorded in their names in the S.A. khatian. The defendants had been residing on the suit land for about 30 to 35 years.

During pendency of Title Suit No.168 of 1984 Jasimuddin himself also filed Title Suit No.53 of 1987 in the same Court for declaration of title in the same land and also for correction of record of rights. Both the Title Suit No.168 of 1984 and Title Suit No.53 of 1987 were tried analogously. The trial Court, decreed Title Suit No.168 of 1984 and dismissed Title Suit No.53 of 1987 by the judgment and decree dated 29.06.1989.

Being aggrieved by the decision of the trial Court, the defendants of Title Suit No.168 of 1984 and the plaintiff of Title Suit No.53 of 1987 preferred Title Appeal Nos.86 of 1989 and 87 of 1989 respectively. The appellate Court by the judgment and decree dated 04.04.1995 dismissed both the appeals affirming the judgment and decree of the trial Court.

The heirs of the defendants of Title Suit No. 168 of 1984 and the plaintiff of Title Suit No.53 of 1987 then preferred Civil Revision Nos. 3382 of 1995 and 3383 of 1995 before the High Court Division challenging the judgment and decree of the appellate Court below which upon hearing the parties the High Court Division made both the Rules absolute setting aside the judgment and decree of the lower appellate court decreeing the Title Suit No. 53 of 1987 and dismissing the Title Suit No. 168 of 1984. The heirs of plaintiff of Title Suit No.168 of 1984 and defendants of Title Suit No.53 of 1987 have preferred separate Civil Petitions for Leave to Appeal challenging judgment and order of the High Court Division and obtained leave giving rise to these appeals.

The pith and substance of the submissions pressed to service by the learned Senior Advocate Mr. Farid Ahmed for the appellants is that the High Court Division while making the Rule absolute in both the revisions on setting aside the concurrent findings of both the Courts below gave a finding that both the Courts without discussing the evidence on record decreed Title Suit No.168 of 1984 and dismissed Title Suit No.53 of 1987. This findings of the High Court Division is perverse as because the trial Court as well as the appellate Court on relying on the S.A. and R.S. record of rights, farogs, rent receipts and the oral evidence regarding possession and subsequent dispossession of plaintiff of Title Suit No.168 of 1984 decreed that suit and dismissed Title Suit No. 53 of 1987.

In elaborating his submissions the learned counsel contends that the High Court Division while making the Rule absolute and setting aside the concurrent judgments and decrees of the Courts below, failed to point out the misreading, non-reading or non-consideration of any evidence on record and without reversing the concurrent findings of trial Court and appellate Court made the Rule absolute.

On the other hand Mr. Zainul Abedin, the learned Senior Advocate for the respondents submits the principle not to interfere with concurrent findings of fact is not a cast-iron practice and that the High Court Division in appropriate cases may depart from that principle where there is any violation of any rule of law or procedure or where there have been misreading or non consideration of evidence affecting the ultimate decision of the Courts below. In the instant case the High Court Division rightly interfered with the concurrent findings of fact arrived at by the Courts below. In support of his contention he placed reliance in the decision of Ziaul Hasan Tarafder vs. Mir Osman Ali 73 DLR AD 250.

Now to sculpt a crystalised foundation of the instances where the principle of no interference vis-à-vis the principle of perversity were adopted by the High Court Division and subsequently either endorsed or disapproved by the Appellate Division we can take into account established precedents.

To dispel any iota of ambiguity on the issue let us go through some of those decisions clarifying the same.

In the case of Ziaul Hasan Tarafder (Md.) vs. Mir Osman Ali and Ors 73 DLR AD 250 it was observed: 
“It is contended that the concurrent findings of fact of the Courts below were illegally reversed by the High Court Division although the High Court Division could not point out any misreading or non reading of evidence, oral or documentary.”

In the case of Atiqullah alias Atik Vs. Md Safiquddin being dead his heirs Rashida Begum and others 59 DLR AD 149 this Division observed: 
“The learned Advocate-on-record failed to point out that the consideration of evidence made by the High Court Division in the background of non-consideration and misreading of the evidence by the appellate Court was erroneous in any respect and the said Division was in error in arriving at the finding as to title and possession of plaintiff and thereupon in setting aside the judgment of the appellate Court. In that state of the matter we do not find any substance in the petition.”

In the case of Most. Akiman Nessa Bewa and others Vs. Harez Ali and others 17 BLD AD 36 it was also observed: 
“We find that the High Court Division upon giving cogent reasons found that the plaintiff was not entitled to the benefit of section 13 of the Limitation Act as the pleading in the plaint did not attract the application of the said section. Also we find that the High Court Division in revision rightly interfered with the finding of fact of the lower appellate Court with regard to the genuineness of the bainapatra Ext. 6. We therefore find no ground for interference.

In the case of Promad Chandra Barman vs. Khodeza Khatun Bewa 12 BLC AD 225 it was observed: 
“In the facts and circumstances of the case and in view of our discussion above, we are of the view that the High Court Division without adverting to the findings given by the court of appeal regarding of pattan by Basanta Kumar in favour of the plaintiffs by dakhilas, subsequent execution of unilateral kabuliyats by plaintiffs in favour of Basanta Kumar and possession of the defendants in the suit land reversed those finding on reassessment of the entire evidence. Accordingly, the High Court Division committed error of law in making the Rule absolute, which requires interference by this court.”

In the case of Abul Bakar Siddique (Md) vs. Additional Deputy Commissioner Kurigram and others 48 DLR AD 154 it was observed: 
“The learned Single Judge of the High Court Division having independently assessed the evidence and having found a case of non-consideration of material evidence on record and consequent non-reversal of material findings interfered with the finding of fact. To our mind, the revisional court is competent to interfere in a case of non-consideration of material evidence which is specifically material for the determination of the material issue, namely, the issue of shifting of the school to the new mouza.”

In the case of Khorshed Alam Vs. Amir Sultan Ali Hyder 38 DLR AD 133 it was observed: 
“The learned Single Judge is found to have rightly refused interference with the finding of the courts below which stands on a solid rock.”

Let us now digress into the instant case. Upon gleaning of the decision of the High Court Division with utter surprise we observed that it has misdirected itself without adverting to all the positive findings of the courts below as we have discussed above. The findings of both the Courts below as we have discussed left nothing unsaid about the good title and possession of the plaintiff discarding the feeble and weak case of the defendants. 

Though the learned Senior Advocate Mr. Zainul Abedin, Senior Advocate appearing for the respondents tried to impress upon us basing on the decision of Ziaul Hasan vs. Osman Ali 73 DLR AD 250 that it’s not a cast-iron practice and dogmatic approach that the High Court Division will not interfere with the concurrent findings of Courts below. The decision as cited by the respondent is well founded and the principle laid down therein is an age old one. It has been decided time and again by this Division. As referred to above decision, certainly it’s not a cast-iron practice and dogmatic approach that the High Court Division will not interfere with the concurrent findings of Courts below. Yes, in a proper case as it is propounded in the above decision that High Court Division has ample and unfettered power to interfere with the concurrent findings of the Court below. It can be reiterated that if the decision of the Courts below is a perverse one, no reasons, whatsoever can preclude the High Court Division in interfering with the same. But in the case in hand, no departure of such kind could be traced out upon gleaning the judgments of both the Courts below. Therefore, question of interference by the High Court Division does not arise in this context. It did not at all advert to the points upon which the decision of the Courts below was based. It has travelled in a different direction trying to stretch out the case in favour of the defendants and against the plaintiff which we disapprove. It is not a case in which this Division will endorse merrily the view of the High Court Division contemplating the Judgments of the courts below being perverse. Rather we hold that the High Court Division should have been loath in interfering the concurrent findings.

Further, on the question of limitation, the Courts below held that State Acquisition and Tenancy Act came into force in 1962 but the defendants instituted the Title Suit claiming the suit land in the year 1987 which is hopelessly barred by limitation. The question of limitation goes at the root, we cannot simply understand how it escaped notice of the High Court Division. No deliberation has been given on that point. Moreover, the Amalnama as it has been observed by the Courts below to be fake and fabricated not coming from the real owner was totally ignored and not taken into consideration by the High Court Division. Likewise, there are so many laches and lacunas which in our view, cannot in any case lead us to think that the decision of the High Court Division was a proper judgment of reversal. 

On the conspectus, we find merit in the appeals. Accordingly, both the appeals are allowed. The impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division is set aside, however, without any order as to costs.

End.

case_source: (From the judgment and order dated the 21st day of August, 2008 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No.486 of 1999)
full_judgment:
Jahangir Hossain J. This civil appeal, by leave, is directed against the judgment and order dated the 21st day of August, 2008 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No.486 of 1999 making the Rule absolute. 

2. The relevant facts for disposal of this civil appeal, in short, are that Sam Miah, predecessor of respondent Nos. 1-10 instituted Title Suit No. 47 of 1980 in the Court of Munsif Sadar, Sylhet against the appellants and respondent Nos.11-33 for a declaration that the suit land described in schedule-II to the plaint belonged to the plaintiff in maliki right and the record of rights in respect of the suit land in the names of the predecessors of the defendants is wrong and incorrect and for recovery of khas possession of the suit land described in schedule-III to the plaint. The suit was renumbered as Title Suit No.28 of 1990 on transfer to the Court of Additional Assistant Judge, Circuit Court, Sylhet. During pendency of the suit, Saru Miah died and his heirs, the present plaintiffs were substituted. 

3. The case of the plaintiff, in short, is that the land described in schedule-I of the plaint originally belonged to Mufti Zainuddin and others of Dargah Mahalla, Sylhet in maliki right. Sheikh Selim, father of Saru Miah, original plaintiff, was tenant [chakran] a service under the said landlords. While he [Sheikh Selim] was residing in one of the homesteads of the landlords at Longar Dewri with his family, he took a second wife and went to reside with the 2nd wife at Rajor Goli surrendering the possession of the said homestead in favour of landlords where he had been residing as service tenant. Sam Miah then took settlement of the land described in schedule-I to the plaint from the landlords and while residing there, took his mother with him, gave shelter to his other two brothers named Kantu Miah, predecessor of defendant No.1 and Charu Miah alias Abdul Khalique, predecessor of defendant Nos. 16-24 and also one Rashid Miah, predecessor of defendant Nos.12-16 and another person named Jan Khan. Thereafter, the landlords instituted Title Suit No.80 of 1951 in the 1st Court of Munsif Sadar, Sylhet for declaration of their title in the land of schedule-I of the plaint and recovery of khas possession against Sheikh Selim, Sara Miah and others who had been residing there and got a decree for declaration of title only. Against the said judgment and decree, Sam Miah filed Titie Appeal No.259 of 1953 before the District Judge, but subsequently, compromised the dispute and then by a registered kabala dated 22.09.1954 purchased the right, title and interest of the landlords in the land described in schedule-I to the plaint and continued owning and possessing the same by his right of purchase. While possessing the same, plaintiff Saru Miah transferred 1 (one) powa land in favour of his brother, Charu Miah @ Abdul Khalique out of the land described in schedule-I by registered kabala and also transferred .005 decimal land out of the land described in schedule-I in favour of Tunu Miah, son of his other brother-Kantu. Miah by registered deed of gift dated 08.12.1979. During the field survey of the last survey and operation, settlement the lard described in schedule-1 was recorded in the names of the plaintiff and his brother according to their share, but recently by the first part of Baishakh, 1386 BS, the plaintiff came to know that the land in schedule-II had been wrongly recorded in the names of late Kantu Miah, predecessor of defendant Nos.1-11 and late Rashid Miah, predecessor of defendant Nos.12-14 beyond his knowledge. Kantu Miah and Rashid Miah were very close relatives of the plaintiff and they having no place to live in, sought for temporary shelter to the plaintiff and the plaintiff on compassionate ground allowed them to live in the land described in schedule-III on condition to move therefrom on arrangement of accommodation elsewhere. The plaintiff having learnt about the wrong record of rights of the land described in schedule-II in the names of Kantu Miah and Rashid Miah, demanded to defendant Nos.1-14 for correction of the record of rights and asked them to vacate the land described in schedule-III lastly by the last part of Baishakh, 1386 BS. Said Kantu Miah and Rashid Miah had no right, title and interest whatsoever in the suit land. The wrong record of rights of the Land described in schedule-II to the plaint in the names of Kantu Miah and Rashid Miah has cast cloud over the title of the plaintiff. Hence, the plaintiff instituted the suit. 

4. Defendant Nos. 1 and 11 filed a joint written statement and defendant Nos.2(Ka)-2(Ga) filed another set of written statement and defendant Nos.12 and 13 filed another written statement denying all the material allegations of the plaint. 

5. Defendant Nos.1 and 11 contested the suit contending, inter alia, that the land described in schedule-I originally belonged to Mufti Zainuddin and others in maliki right and Sheikh Selim was the service tenant who used to reside in the scheduled land with his famkly and gave some portion of his land to Rashid Miah to reside therein. After sometime, Zaminders filed Title Suit No.80 of 1951 in the Court of Munsif, Sylhet for declaration of title and recovery of khas possession by evicting Sheikh Selim and others. Sheikh Selim and his son-Chant Miah only contested the suit. In the said suit, the maliki right of the Zaminders was declared, but the prayer for recovery of possession was disallowed. After abolition of the Zamindari system by the operation of State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950, Sheikh Selim became a tenant under the Government in the land described in schedule-I to the plaint and the rent receiving interests of the plaintiff which he purchased from the Zaminders was extinguished by operation of law. The plaintiff acquired no right to the possession of the suit land by his alleged purchase and that the plaintiff used to reside in the land described in schedule-I to the plaint with his father, Sheikh Selim. Thereafter, while possessing the land described in schedule-I, Sheikh Selim died leaving behind two sons named Kantu Miah and plaintiff-Saru Miah, one daughter Malika Bibi and four grandsons and three grand-daughters by his predeceased son, Sheikh Chart Miah @ Abdul Khalique and thus, by inheritance, the plaintiff acquired 1/7th share, Kantu Miah predecessor of defendant Nos. 1 and 11 got 2/7th share, the heirs of Chan: got 2/7th and daughter Malika got 1/7th share in the land described in schedule-1. Rashid Miah, predecessor of defendant Nos.12-14, was residing in a portion of the land described in schedule-1 to the plaint with the permission of Sheikh Selim and during the settlement operation, his name was recorded on the basis of possession though he has no title over the suit land. The record of rights in respect of Rashid Miah is not correct, it should have been recorded in the name of Sheikh Selim, Rashid Miah being a licensee the specific portion of land described in schedule-I under Sheikh Selim. The plaintiff Mliah sold .07 acre of land to Charu Abdul Khalique out of his share in the land described in schedule-I, he has subsisting interest in only to the plaint. 

6. Defendant Nos. 2 (Ka) -2 (Ga) contended that the suit land is recorded in Plot No.4583. Sheikh Selim unlike his predecessor was possessing the suit land un Zaminder, Mufti Zainuddin and others and died leaving behind three sons named Kantu Miah, Saw Miah and Pharo Miah and 3[three] daughters named Monu Shofia Bibi and Alifan Bibi as his heirs who possessed the suit land and accordingly, the entire suit land was recorded in Plot No.4585 in their names. Thereafter, they handed over some portion of the land to Rashid Miah, predecessor of defendant Nos.12-14. Shofia Bibi died leaving behind two daughters named Ayesha Begum-defendant No. 2(Ka) and Champa and one son named Emani Miah as her heirs. Kantu Miah died leaving behind defendant Nos.1-11 as his heirs. Then Tunu Miah died leaving behind Ayesha Bibi, his wife, defendant No.2(Ka), one daughter named Reba Mom [ Minor-defendant No.2(Kha) and one son named Shailaz Miah defendant No.2(Gha) as his heirs who have been in possession of the suit plot. 

7. Defendant Nos. 12-13 that Sheikh Selim and Rashid Miah had title and possession ill the suit land described in schedule-II to the plaint two equal shares and accordingly, the, share of Rashid Miah was rightly recorded in his name in the SA Khatian and While possessing the same, he died leaving behind defendant Nos.12-14 as his heirs and defendant Nos.12 and 13 have been possessing the same. For grabbing the land of these defendants, the plaintiff created false girding the Suit land documents regarding the Suit land.  

8. Al the trial, the plaintiff examined 8[eight] witnesses including plaintiff No. 1[Ka] Rupon Miah as Pw-3 and the defendants examined 5[five] witnesses support of their respective eases. The learned Assistant Judge after framing 7[seven] issues, recording evidence, hearing the arguments of the respective parties and considering the materials on record by the judgment and order dated 31.07.1991 dismissed the suit. 

9. Being aggrieved by the judgment and order dated 31.07.1991 passed by the trial Court, the plaintiff preferred Title Appeal No.133 of 1991 before the learned Additional District and Sessions Judge, Sylhet who having heard the respective parties and considering the materials on record by the judgment and order dated 02.11.1997 dismissed the appeal affirming those of the trial Court. 

10. Being aggrieved by the judgment and order of the Appellate Court, the plaintiff as petitioner filed Civil Revision No.486 of 1999 before the High Court Division. The learned Judge of the High Court Division having heard the respective parties and considering the materials on record by the judgment and order dated 21.08.2008 made the Rule absolute reversing those of the Courts below. 

11. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division, the appellants preferred Civil Appeal No.53 of 2010 arising out of Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 1433 of 2009 before this Division. 

12. Mr. Mrinal Kanti Biswas, learned Advocate, appearing for the appellants, submits that the moot question in this case is whether Sheikh Selim, who was admittedly a service tenant in the land described in schedule-I to the plaint, under Zaminder, Mufti Zainuddin and others, had surrendered the possession of the aforesaid scheduled land in favour of the aforesaid landlords and thereafter, Saru Miah, original plaintiff, had taken settlement of the suit land described in schedule-I to the plaint from the said Zaminders or not. He further submits that the Court of Appeal below, the final Court of facts, on consideration of the evidence, particularly, exhibit-Ka[1], the certified copy of the plaint of Title Suit No.80 of 1951 and exhibit-Kha (1), the certified copy of the judgment of Title Suit No.80 of 1951, held that Sheikh Selim possessed the land described in schedule-I to the plaint as service tenant under the landlords and did not surrender possession thereof in favour of the landlords and that his son, Saru Miah, did not take settlement of the suit land from the Zaminder and the High therefore, Court Division committed serious error in holding that the Appellate Court below gave concurrent findings and affirmed the judgment and decree of the trial Court simply by concurring with the findings of the trial Court without dis-cussing the evidence independently and thereby the High Court Division acted illegally in setting aside the decision of the Court of Appeal below, the final Court of facts and remanded the case to the Court of Appeal below for fresh decision occasioning miscarriage of justice. He further submits that the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division erred to appreciate the concurrent findings of the Court below that Sheikh Selim, who was the service tenant, did not surrender possession of the suit land to his Zaminder, Mufti Zainuddin and others and Saru Miah had not taken settlement of the suit land from the Zaminders is being essentially a finding of facts based on oral as well as documentary evidence is immune from revision since the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division did not spell out any misreading or non-consideration of evidence done by the Court of Appeal below and in that view of the matter acted illegally in making the Rule absolute and sending the case back on remand for fresh decision based upon the evidence on record occasioning miscarriage of justice. 

13. Mr. Md. Motahar Hossain, learned Advocate, appearing on behalf of respondent Nos.1-10, contends that the High Court Division was justified in making the Rule absolute inasmuch as the High Court Division rightly found that the Courts below did not approach the case in proper perspective and both the Courts below were required to find that the plaintiffs had prayed for correction of the record of rights and eviction of some persons from the disputed land described in the said schedule who were claimed to be in permissive possession in the land described in schedule-III to the plaint and the Courts below ought to have decided the owner-ship of the plaintiffs in actual quantum of land. He further contends that the High Court Division, rightly held that the finding of the trial Court has no basis in fact or law since it is evident from the plaint and depositions that the plaintiffs did not pray for evicting anyone from the land described in schedule-II to the plaint an6 for recovery of khas possession. The plaintiffs rather sought for declaration of title along with correction of the record of rights regarding the land described in schedule-II to the plaint and recovery of khas possession of the land described in schedule-III to the plaint by evicting defendant No.1 therefrom. He further submits that the High Court Division was justified in making the Rule absolute inasmuch as the Appellate Court below without discussing the evidence of PWs' and DWs' in light of their pleadings affirmed the judgment and decree of the trial Court below and allowed Cross Objection No.5 of 1992 and, therefore, non-consideration of the oral evidence of the parties in light of their respective cases vitiated the impugned judgment and decree passed by the Courts below. He further contends that the High Court Division was justified in making the Rule absolute inasmuch as both the Courts below misconstrued the pleadings of the parties and the evidence on record and their erroneous findings that the land described in schedule-II to the plaint is possessed by the defendants, and the plaintiffs cannot get the relief of recovery of khas possession without praying for recovery of khas possession of the entire Land described in schedule-II to the plaint are totally baseless and misconceived one and, moreover, the trial Court below also came to the erroneous conclusion that the suit is barred by limitation and that the suit is not duly stamped and, on a clear wrong approach to the cases of the parties, and their respective evidence led the Courts below to arrive at the erroneous conclusion with regard to the plaintiffs' possession over the suit land which has occasioned a serious miscarriage of justice. He further contends that the High Court Division was justified in making the Rule absolute inasmuch as defendant Nos.1 and 11 filed a joint written statement, defendant Nos.2(Ka)-(Ga) filed another joint written statement, and defendant Nos.12 and 13 also filed another joint written statement denying the case of the plain-tiffs but the said defendants did not adduce any evidence in support of their written statements and, furthermore, the Appellate Court below without elaborate consideration of entire evidence, both oral and documentary, held that the plaintiffs have not proved their title in the land described in schedule-II to the plaint, and allowed the cross objection, although the trial Court below came to a clear finding that the plaintiffs have their title over the suit land but no possession was maintained by the plaintiffs and, thus, the Courts below committed an error of law in not holding that the plaintiffs have proved their case. He further contends that the High Court Division was justified in making the Rule absolute inasmuch as PW-2 stated in his deposition that he knows the plaintiff, Sam Miah, and his heirs and he also knows the father of plaintiff, Sam Miah, namely, Sheikha Selim, and he also stated that he knows Sheikh Selim since his childhood, and Pw-3, Rupon Miah, as substituted plaintiff deposed on behalf of the plaintiffs, and he supported the plaintiffs' case, and Pw-4 corroborated the plaintiffs' case. He further contends that Pws'- 2, 3, 4, 5, 7 and 8 corroborated the case of the plaint, but both the trial Court below and the Appellate Court below without considering the evidence of all the Pws' and Dws' dismissed the suit and, thus, non-consideration of the said evidence by the Courts below caused a serious miscarriage of justice. It is further submitted that they High Court Division was justified in making the Rule absolute inasmuch as the trial Court below did not at all discuss the evidence of Pwsf-3, 4, 5, 7 ant 8 regarding the title and possession of the suit land, and the Appellate Court below also did not consider the same. It is further submitted that the High Court Division was justified in making the Rule absolute inasmuch as the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh in Habibullah (Md)-Vs-Sher Ali Khan and others [57 DLR (AD) (2005) 55] held that the High Court Division while exercising its revisional jurisdiction is competent to reverse the judgment and decree of the Courts below when the same has been made either upon misreading or non-consideration of the material evidence causing failure of justice. The High Court Division is also competent to set aside the judgment and decree of the Courts below when the same has been passed on the basis of evidence, which cannot be considered as legal evidence, and had the same been not taken into consideration, the judgment and decree would not have been one as has been made. It is further contended that the High Court Division rightly found that the Appellate Court below ought to have written the impugned judgment and decree upon the independent analysis of fact and law in a comprehensive manner and, as such, there was total non-consideration of evidence by the Appellate Court below as evident from the impugned judgment and decree and, therefore, it is required that the Appellate Court below in passing the fresh judgment and decree on remand shall consider the amendments made in the plaint and find the real substance of the plaint as it contains numerous amendments and, further, consider all relevant evidence and, accordingly, the suit was rightly sent on remand to the Appellate Court below to write out a fresh judgment and decree in light of observations mate by the High Court Division. 

14. Heard the learned Advocates for both the parties and perused the material documents along with other connected papers on record. 

15. The appellants claimed that the Court of Appeal below on perusal of the solenama [exhibit-3] found the solenama was executed by the contesting defendant-appellants and the plaintiff respondents of Title Appeal No.259 of 1953 and only that Sheikh Selim and Charu Miah contested Title Suit No.80 of 1951 and they alone filed the appeal and executed the sohmama and Sam Miah, son of Sheikh Selim was not a party in the solenama and as per terms of the solenama, the title of the land described in schedule-I to the plaint remained with the landlords and possession of the same remained with Sheikh Selim as service tenant and by exhibit-1, the registered sale deed dated 22.09.1954, Saru Miah purchased the rent receiving interests of the superior landlords but did not get possession of the 1st scheduled land which was possessed by Sheikh Selim as service tenant and with the operation of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, Saru Miah's rent receiving interest was extinguished. Sheikh Selim possessed the 1st scheduled land as service tenant under superior landlords and his son-Saru Miah did not take settlement of the said land from the landlords by sale deed dated 22.09.1954. Saru Miah acquired only the rent receiving interests which the land-lords had and with the operation of State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, Saru Miah's rent receiving interests extinguished and Sheikh Selim acquired occupancy tenancy right in the suit land under the Government and on the death of Sheikh Selim, his son-Kantu Miah, Saru Miah, daughter-Malika Bibi and 4[four] grand-sons and 3[three] grand-daughter by his predeceased son-Sheikh Charu @ Abdul Khaleque inherited his property. 

16. The respondents claimed that Sam Miah by a registered deed of sale transferred one powa of land out of the 1st scheduled land to his brother, Charu Miah @ Abdul Khalique and handed over the possession to him. Thereafter, Saru Miah gifted .005 acre of land out the 1st scheduled land to Tunu Miah, son of his other brother named Kantu Miah by a registered deed of gift dated 08.12.1979 and during the field survey in the last settlement operation, the 1st scheduled land was recorded in the names of the plaintiff and his said brother according to their respective share and possession in two different khatiang and thus, the plaintiffs had been under the wrong impression that the record of rights of the land prepared naturally and legally during the field survey would be duly published. However, at same time, during the first part of baishakh, 1386 B.S., the plaintiffs upon enquiry were utterly surprised to know that the record of rights of the land described in schedule-II to the plaint which is a part And parcel of the 1st scheduled land belonged to the plaintiff in its totality, had been changed and wrongly recorded in the names of late Kantu Miah and Rashid Miah without any basis and knowledge of the plaintiff and done in the back of the plaintiff. Said Kantu Miah and Rashid Miah, brother-in-law of Sheikh Selim were close relatives of the plaintiff. Having no place to live in, said Kantu Miah and Rashid Miah sought for temporary shelter from the plaintiff during the time of local survey of the last settlement operation and the plaintiffs out of grace permitted them to reside in the land described in schedule-III to the plaint which is a part of the 2nd scheduled land purely for the time being on temporary basis on condition to move away therefrom after arrangement of their own accommodation elsewhere and while they were residing there on permission, said Kantu Miah and Rashid Miah died leaving benind defendant Nos.1-11 and 12-14 as their legal hers respectively. Since defendant Nos.1-14 were very helpless, the plaintiff merely allowed them to reside in the 3"' scheduled land on condition to vacate the same as soon as they would be able to arrange accommodation elsewhere. Defendant No.2 purchased .01 acre of land out of the 2nd scheduled land on the western side of the land of the 3rd scheduled land. The plaintiff having learnt about the wrong and illegal record of rights of the 2nd scheduled land in the names of Kantu Miah and Rashid Miah demanded to defendant Nos.1-14 for correction of the same record of rights and asked them to vacate the land concerned and remove the structures therefrom. Though they initially agreed to take appropriate step for correction of the record, they refused to take any step later and defendant Nos.1 and 2 additionally refused to vacate the 3rd scheduled land when pressed by the plaintiff for the last time by the last part of baishakh, 1386 B.S. Kantu Miah and Rashid Miah had no title or interest of any kind in any of the lands of the suit property and as such, they recorded the land in their names by influencing the survey officials. The wrong and illegal record of rights in respect of the 2nd scheduled land cast cloud over the title of the plaintiff. 

17. It appears from the judgment and decree of the trial Court that exhibit-1 was the saf-kabala deed whereby Saru Miah, predecessor of the present plaintiffs, owned the suit property described in schedule-I to the plaint because, by that time, there has been an acquisition of rent receiving interests under the ,East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 and the Zaminders remained only as superior rent receiving owner and Sam Miah purchased that entitlement from Mufti Zainuddin [exhibit-1] and at the same time, he had the occupancy right under the Government. It is admitted that the plaintiff sold a quantum of land of .71/2 acre to his younger brother, Charu Miah @ Abdul Khalique. It appears from exhibit sKaly that Sheikh Selim did not continue to stay in the house situated in the scheduled property in Longer Dewari rather after getting married for The second time, he started living with his wife in Rajar Goli, Sylhet and therefore, Sheikh Selim did not earn any right of occupancy under the landlord and so his name could not be recorded in the settlement operation. The trial Court after consideration of the evidence on record came to the conclusion that the plaintiff had occupancy right in the property described in schedule-I to the plaint and predecessor of defendant Nos.1-11/12/13 did not have title to the property described in schedule-II to the plaint by occupancy right and the defendants were in possession of the property described in schedule-II to the plaint and without a prayer for recovery of khas possession the suit is not maintainable. The trial Court also held that the suit was barred by limitation and the valuation of the suit property was not proper. The Appellate Court below without applying judicial mind concurred with the findings of the trial Court regarding dismissal of the suit and disposed of the appeal in the same tune of the trial Court.  

18. It appears from the judgment and order of the High Court Division that the trial Court as well as the Appellate Court below ought to have given their thoughtful findings on the point of limitation on the basis of evidence on record and the trial Court as well as the Appellate Court below ought to have approached the case in proper perspective and were required to find that the plaintiff had prayed for two major reliefs: one is correction of record of rights and another is eviction of some persons from the disputed land described in schedule-III to the plaint who were claimed to be in permissive possession therein. The High Court Division further observed that the Courts below ought to have decided the ownership of the plaintiff in the actual quantum of land which remained with him after transfer. The trial Court found that "বাদিগনের সাক্ষীগনের মৌখিক সাক্ষ্য মতে বিবাদীরা আর্জির ২য় তপসিল বর্ণিত ভূমিতে বর্তমানে দখলকার আছেন। কাজেই আর্জিত ২য় তপসিল বর্ণিত সমুদয় ভূমি হইতে উচ্ছেদের প্রার্থনা ব্যতিত বাদিগনের অত্রাকারের মামলা আইনত চলিতে পারে না।" It is observed by the High Court Division that this finding of the trial Court is not quite substantial because from the 2nd scheduled land, the plaintiff did not pray for evicting any one. He wanted for correction of the record of rights only to the particular quantum of land. It was observed that the Appellate Court below ought to have written the judgment and order on the independent analysis of fact and law in a comprehensive manner. Therefore, it is required that the Appellate Court below in passing the judgment on remand would consider the amendments made in the plaint and find the real sub-stance of the plaint as it contains numerous amendments. 

19. It reveals from the evidence on record that Pw-2 knows plaintiff-Saru Miah and his heirs and he also knows Sheikh Selim, the father of plaintiff-Saru Miah from his boyhood. It appears that, there is no allegation from defendant Nos.1-11 regarding the incorrect record of rights in the name of Saru Miah in 15 decimals of land described in schedule-I and defendant Nos.l-11 did not give any description of non-appearance of the name of Maleka Bibi in the record of rights. They only claimed that Sheikh Selim was the tenant in the 1st scheduled land and he permitted Rashid Miah to reside on 7 decimals of land described in the same schedule and after his death, his heirs had been in possession. It is admitted fact that the Zaminders filed Title Suit No.80 of 1951 in the Court of Munsif, 1st Court, Sylhet against Sheikh Selim for khas possession and eviction of them. The Zaminders obtained a decree in the aforesaid suit, but no order was passed regarding eviction and Sheikh Selim and Charu Miah @ Abdul Khalique contested the suit. It appears that according to exhibit-Ka (1), Sheikh Selim left the suit land and went to Razargoli. It further appears that according to exhibit-1, Saru Miah on 22.09.1954 by a registered deed purchased the scheduled land. He sold one powa land to Charu Miah @ Abdul Khalique and 0½ decimal of land to Tunu, son of Kantu Miah. 

20. Upon perusal of the judgment of the trial Court along with the materials on record, it appears that defendant Nos.1-11 did not object to the incorrect record of rights in the name of Saru Miah in 15 decimals of land described in schedule-1 to the plaint and defencant Nos.16-24, successors of Charu Miah, another son of Sheikh Selim did not object to the claim of the plaintiff by filing written statement. The trial Court held that Rashid Miah did not have title to the land described in schedule-II to the plaint by way of settlement from the superior interest holders and there is no basis of record of rights in his name. The plaintiff and defendant Nos.1-11 admitted that the record of rights in the name of Rashid Miah is incorrect. The trial Court observed that as per the evidence of the plaintiffs witnesses predecessor of defendant Nos.1-11,Kantu Miah, had been in possession of the land described in schedule-II to the plaint with the permission of Sam Miah and there-after, defendant Nos.1-11 have been in possession Of the same with the permission of Saru Miah and the predecessor of defendant Nos.12-13, Rashid Miah, also had been in possession of the land described in schedule-II to the plaint with the permission of Sam Miah. The trial Court, however, did not categorically specify the evidence of those witnesses based on which it reached such finding. The appellate Court also did not specifically appreciate the evidence of the witnesses on record regarding the alleged permissive possession of the predecessor of defendant Nos.1-11, Kantu Miah and thereafter, that of defendant Nos.1-11 and the alleged permissive possession of the predecessor of defendant Nos. l 2-13. It is admitted that the plaintiff transferred 7 decimals of land to his brother Charu Miah. Defendant Nos.1-11 in their written statement stated that like their predecessor Kantu Miah, the heirs of Sheikh Charu got f share of the property of Sheikh Selim described in schedule-I to the plaint by way of inheritance. DW-1, vital witness of defendant Nos.1-11, during cross-examination by the plaintiff side deposed, "চারু মিয়ার ছেলেরা সারু মিয়া হইতে খরিদ সূত্রে নালিশা জমিতে দখলকার আছেন ওয়ারিশসূত্রে নয়"। This significant portion of the material evidence in the deposition of DW-1 is apparently inconsistent with the claim of defendant Nos.1-11 was overlooked both by the trial Court as well as the appellate Court. In the case of Habibullah (Md)-Vs-Sher All Khan and others, reported in 57DLR (AD)(2005)55, it is held that "The High Court Division while exercising its revisional jurisdiction is competent to reverse tile judgment of the Courts below when the sane has been made either upon misreading or non-consideration of the material evidence and the said misreading and non-consideration of the evidence caused failure of justice." In the case of Masjid Kacha Tank, Nahan-Vs-Tuffail Mohammed, AIR 1991 SC 45, it is also held that "the High Court is empowered to interfere with the findings of fact if the findings are perverse or there has been a non-appreciation or non-consideration of the material evidence on record by the Courts below." 

21. The trial Court held that the suit is barred by limitation without appreciating any evidence available on record in this regard and the appellate Court affirmed this erroneous finding without appreciating any evidence available on record in this regard. In the case of Government of Bangladesh-Vs-AKM Abdul Hye and others, 56 DLR(AD)53, it is held that "the law is now well settled that against the wrong record of rights the person whose 'interest is affected by such wrong recording need not file suit questioning legality of the record of rights so prepared and finally published within 6 years from said date or from the date of knowledge of such wrong record of rights, but he is required to file the suit seeking declaration of title within six years from the date the person-in whose name record has been wrongly prepared and finally published raises claim denying his claim on the basis of wrong record." 

22. Upon perusal of the judgment of the trial Court as well as the appellate "Court, it transpires that the findings of the subordinate Courts are not concurrent regarding all the points excepting dismissal of the suit. The trial Court held that the predecessor of the plaintiffs, Saru Miah, had title to the property described in schedule-I to the plaint by occupancy right. Conversely, the appellate Court held that the predecessor of Saru Miah and the predecessor-in-interest of defendant Nos.1-11, Sheikh Selim, had occupancy right in the land described in schedule-I to the plaint and Sam Miah did not have any occupancy right in the same. 

23. The High Court Division in the exercise of its revisional authority should not ordinarily reassess the evidence on record in reversing a finding of fact. In the case or Golam Sarwar (Md) and others-Vs-Md. Liakat Ali and Others reported in SODLR(AD) (1998)67, it was held that "Ordinarily, the High Court Division in the exercise of its revisional authority should not embark upon the function of the lower appellate Court to reassess the evidence on record in reversing the finding of fact. If, however, the High Court Division is satisfied that the lower appellate Court has failed to consider any material evidence in reversing a finding of fact arrived at by the trial Court upon assigning proper reason therefor, the proper course is to send back the case on remand to the appellate Court for rehearing the appeal upon proper assessment of the evidence on record." 

24. In view of the abovementioned facts and circumstances, the High Court Division was justified in making the Rule absolute and, therefore, we do not find any substance to interfere with the judgment and order of the High Court Division. 

25. Therefore, we find no merit in the submissions of the learned Advocate for the appellants and accordingly, the appeal is dismissed without any order as costs. 

End.

full_judgment:
Obaidul Hassan J. Both the Civil Appeals are being disposed of by this common judgment because those arise out of the common judgment and order between the same parties involving common question of law and facts. 

2. Both the Civil Appeals are directed by leave granting order dated 07.08.2016 passed in Civil Petitions for Leave to Appeal No.2789-2790 of 2013 against the judgment and decree dated 29.07.2013 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revisions No.2078-2079 of 1999 making both the Rules absolute reversing the judgment and decree dated 05.04.1999 passed by the learned Additional District Judge, 3rd Court, Sylhet in Title Appeals No.83-84 of 1997 dismissing both the appeals affirming the judgment and decree dated 07.04.1997 passed by the Court of Additional Senior Assistant Judge, Sadar, Sylhet in Title Suit No.155 of 1993 dis-missing the suit and in Title Suit No.74 of 1993 decreeing the suit. 

3. The relevant facts necessary for the disposal of both the civil appeals are that on 12.07.1993 the respondents No.1-2 as plaintiffs instituted Title Suit No.155 of 1993 in the Court of Senior Assistant Judge, Sadar, Sylhet impleading the appellant as main defendant and respondents No.3-9 as proforma defendants praying for declaration of title over the 2nd schedule land and for recovery of Khas possession of the said land upon removing the houses and obstruction there from. 

4. The case of the plaintiffs in Title Suit No.155 of 1993, in a nutshell, is that the land described in 1st schedule of the plaint originally belonged to Katanmoni Nath, son of Shankar Nath, who by a registered Kabala dated 25th Shrabon, 1359 B.S. corresponding to 10.08.1952 transferred northern half portion of the 1st schedule land in favour of Krishnamoni Dey, wife of Surendra Kumar Dey. Said Katanmoni Nath and Krishnamani Dey while in possession of the 1st schedule in equal share the record of right of the said land was correctly prepared in their names. Said Krishnamoni Dey sold her eight Anas share in favour of Samuj Miah, the predecessor of the pro-forma defendants No.2-7 by a registered Kabala dated 10.11.1973 and he had been possessing the same by constructing boundary wall at the eastern, western and northern side of their purchased land and by constructing dwelling house at the west of the said land. Said Katanmoni Nath having been the owner of 2nd schedule land on request of Roshomoy Datta, the husband of the defendant No.1 allowed him to reside at the western part of .01 acres of land out of 2nd schedule land by raising a mud-built but thereon. Thereafter, Katanmoni Nati died on 28th Chaitra 1366 B.S. corresponding to 11.04.1960 leaving behind his wife Kornomoni Nath as the only heir and became the owner of all the properties belonging to Katanmani Nath. Subsequently, Kornomoni Nath again got married with Prashanna Nath and she died on 12th Chaitra 1399 B.S. corresponding to 26.06.1993. Said Karnamani Nath was deprived of enjoying the 2" schedule land since she lost her life interest in the said land after entering into a second marriage. The right, title and interest of Katanmani Nath in the 2nd schedule land devolved upon the plaintiffs as reversionary heirs (brother's daughter's sons of Katanmani Nath) according to Hindu Law. The plaintiffs got mutated their names in respect of the suit land. The husband of the defendant No.1 used to live in a very small portion of the suit land having received per-mission from the plaintiffs. On the demise of the husband of the defendant No.1, the plaintiffs asked the defendant No.1 on several occasions to deliver vacant possession of the land while the defendant No.1 agreed to comply with the said request. Subsequently, the plaintiffs came to know at the middle of April, 1993 that the defendant No.1 being plaintiff instituted Title Suit No.74 of 1993 claiming the suit land as her purchased land. Thereafter, at the last part of April 1993 the plaintiffs again asked the defendant No.1 to vacate the suit land while she refused to do so since she claimed the title of the suit land by way of the alleged sale deed which is false, fraudulent and collusive being the said Kabala is an antedated and void document and on the basis of the alleged Kabala the defendant No.1 instituted Title Suit No.42 of 1992 against two fictitious women, who had no right, title in the suit land and she managed to get the said suit decreed on compromise by practicing fraud, upon the Court and subsequently by creating a new story the defendant No.1 instituted Title Suit No.74 of 1993 against the plaintiffs which cast cloud upon the right, title and interest of the plaintiffs and as such the plaintiffs have filed the suit. 

5. The defendant No.1-appellant contested the Title Suit No.155 of 1993 by filing a Written Statement denying all the material allegations made in the plaint. She con-tended, inter alia, that Katanmoni Nath as owner of the land of plot No.1208 executed a Bainapatra on 2nd Ashar 1367 B.S. in favour of the plaintiff on receiving Tk.50.00 out of the total consideration money of Tk.95.00 and delivered possession of the disputed homestead which is situated at the southern part of plot No.1208 and since then she had been possessing the same. Due to sudden death of Katanmoni Nath no Kabala was executed and registered according to the terms of the aforesaid contract for sale. On the demise of Katanmoni Nath his wife Kornomoni Nath executed a Kabala on 31.01.1963 in favour of the defendant No.1 regarding the land described in the schedule of the Bainapatra executed by her husband Katanmoni Nath. She excavated a tank at the eastern part of the plot No.1208 and converted the western part of the said plot as Bhiti land by earth-filling and constructed two dwelling houses thereon. She had been possessing the same beyond statutory period of limitation. The defendant No.1 filed Title Suit No.42 of 1992 in the Court of the Senior Assistant Judge, Sadar, Sylhet against Kornomani Nath which was decreed on compromise on 21.11.1992. The plot number was wrongly written as 1207 instead of 1208 in the schedule of said Bainapatra and registered Kabala, but from the boundaries delineated in the schedules of the aforesaid two documents it is clear that the land of plot No.1208 was transferred in favour of the defendant No.1. Due to the afore-said mistake of mentioning plot No.1207 in the compromise decree dated 21.11.1992 passed in Title Suit No.42 of 1992 there arose a confusion and as such the defendant No.1 instituted Title Suit No.74 of 1993 to remove such confusion. Kornomoni Nath did not get married for the second time rather she became pregnant by leading immoral life with Prosanna Nath for which her life interest had not been lost. Being a woman of immoral character Kornomoni Nath departed to elsewhere. Krishnamoni Dey sold out the land of plot No.1207 to the defendant No.7 and her husband by a Kabala dated 25th Kartik 1380 B.S. and they had been possessing the land of plot No.1207 since the time of purchase. The plaintiffs brought the suit with a view to harass the defendant No.1 and as such the suit is liable to be dismissed. 

6. On the other hand, the appellant as plaintiff instituted Title Suit No.74 of 1993 in the Court of Senior Assistant Judge, Sadar, Sylhet impleading the respondents No.1-2, Kornomoni Nath and the respondent No.9 as defendants praying for a declaratory decree that the land described within the boundary of the deed dated 31.01.1963 executed in favour of the plaintiff by the defendant No.1 and the land stated in the decree of the Title Suit No.42 of 1992 appertain to the land of plot No.1208 although plot No.1207 was mentioned in the deed dated 31.01.1963 and the Title Suit No.42 of 1992. The averments made in the plaint of Title Suit No.155 of 1993 are identical to the same made in the written statement filed by the defendant No.1 in Title Suit No.155 of 1993. 

7. The defendants No.3 & 4, who are the plaintiffs of Title Suit No.155 of 1993 contested Title Suit No.155 of 1993 by filing a written statement denying all the material averments made in the plaint sup-porting the self-same statements made in the plaint of Title Suit No.155 of 1993. The defendant No.2 also contested the Title Suit No.74 of 1993 by filing a separate written statement although supporting the claim of the defendants No.3 and 4. 

8. Both the Title Suit No. 155 of 1993 and Title Suit No.74 of 1993 were heard analogously by the trial Court. Upon hearing both the suits, the trial Court was pleased to dismiss Title Suit No.155 of 1993 while decreed Title Suit No.74 of 1993 by a single judgment dated 07.04.1997. 

9. Being aggrieved by the judgment and decrees dated 07.04.1997 passed by the trial Court in Title Suit No.155 of 1993 and Title Suit No. 74 of 1993 the respondents No.1 and 2 preferred Title Appeal No.83 of 1997 and Title Appeal No.84 of 1997 respectively before the learned District Judge, Sylhet which were eventually transferred to tie Court of Additional District Judge, 3r Court, Sylhet, who upon final hearing dismissed both the appeals by judgment and decree dated 05.04.1999. 

10. Against the judgment and decree dated 05.04.1999 passed by the appellate Court in Title Appeal No.83 of 1997 and Title Appeal No.84 of 1997 the respondents No.1 and 2 filed Civil Revision No.2078 of 1999 and Civil Revision No.2079 of 1999 respectively before the High Court Division and Rules were issued. 

11. Upon final hearing, the High Court Division was pleased to make both the Rules absolute by judgment and decree dated 29.07.2013. 

12. Being disgruntled with the judgment and decree dated 29.07.2013 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revisions No.2078-2079 of 1999, the appellant filed the Civil Petitions for Leave to Appeal No.2789-2790 of 2013 respectively before this Division and after hearing this Division was pleased to grant leave on 07.08.2016 and hence these appeals. 

13. Mr. A.M. Amin Uddin, learned senior Advocate appearing along with Mr. Didar Alam Kollol, Advocate appearing on behalf of the appellant in both the appeals taking us through the judgment and decree of the High Court Division dated 29.07.2013 passed in Civil Revisions No.2078-2079 of 1999, judgments and decrees of the appellate Court as well as the trial Court, the other materials on record, contends that the High Court Division has committed illegality in totally misconceiving the case of the appellant upon misreading and misconstruing the evidence and materials on record and thereby misdirected beyond the law and facts of the case in passing the erroneous judgment making the Rules absolute occasioning serious miscarriage of justice and as such the impugned judgment and decree is liable to be set aside. The learned Counsel contends further that appellant acquired title and possession in the suit land from the original owner Kotanmoni Nath by way of sale deed dated 31.01.1963. The learned Counsels contend next that Kornomoni Nath never got married for the second time and as such she did not lose her life interest in the suit land, but the High Court Division on mis-conception made the Rules absolute. The learned Counsels argue next that from the Local Investigation Report along with other relevant papers (Exhibits- 6 series) it is found that the land described both in the sale deed dated 31.01.1963 (Exhibit-z) and compromise decree (Exhibit-5(A)) would attract the land of plot No.1208, but the High Court Division ignoring the said documents most illegally made the Rules absolute. The learned Counsels referred to the case of Md. Alkas Ali and others vs. Mansur Ahmed Khan and others reported in 1983 BLD(AD) 126. The learned Counsels contend, in fine, that although the possession of the plaintiff is admitted by the defendants, the High Court Division could not appreciate the matter and most illegally set aside the judgment and degree of the appellate Court as well as the trial Court and as such the judgment and decree of the High Court Division is liable to be set aside. 

14. Per contra, Mr. Surojit Bhattacharjee, learned Counsel appearing on behalf of the respondents No.1 and 2 in both the appeals referring a Catena of case laws reported in 29 DLR (SC) (1977) 137; 16 BLT(AD) 350; 39 DLR(AD) 237; and 4 BLD(AD) 183 contends that due to the second marriage of Komomoni Nath she became divested of the life interest of her husband Katanmoni Nath and the respon-dents No.1 and 2 as reversionary heirs of Katanmoni Nath acquired the suit land, but the trial Court as well as lower appellate Court committed illegality failing to appreciate the said issue while the High Court Division on proper scrutiny made the Rules absolute and as such no interference by this Division with the impugned judgment of the High Court Division is needed and hence both the appeals are liable to be dismissed. 

15. We have perused the judgment and decree dated 29.07.2013 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No.2078 of 1999 and Civil Revision No.2079 of .1999. We have also considered the submissions of the learned Counsels for the appellant and the respondents No.1 and 2 and gone through the judgments and decrees of the appellate Court as well as the trial Court, evidences and other materials on record. 

16. It is admitted that the land of plot No.1208 belonged to Katanmoni Nath while the land of plot No.1207 belonged to Krishnamoni Dey. 17. Needless to say that the plaintiff of Title Suit No.74 of 1993 contested the Title Suit No.155 of 1993 by filing a written statement while the plaintiffs of Title Suit No.155 of 1993 contested Title Suit No.74 of 1993 by filing a written statement. It is apparent from the record that both the Title Suit No.74 of 1993 and Title Suit No.155 of 1993 were tried analogously and the plaintiff of Title Suit No.74 of 1993 produced both oral and documentary evidences as plaintiff in both the suits while the defendants No.3 and 4 in the said suits produced both oral and documentary evidences as defendants in both the suits. 

18. The case of the plaintiff of Title Suit No.74 of 1993 is that Katanmoni Nath being the owner of land of plot No.1208 executed a Bainapatra (contract for sale) on 2nd Ashar 1367 BS. in favour of the plaintiff (Lakshmi Rani Dutta) on receiving Tk.50.00 out of the total consideration money of Tk.95.00 and delivered possession of the said land to her. On the demise of Katanmoni Nath his wife Kornomoni Nath executed a Kabala on 31.01.1963 in favour of the plaintiff regarding the land described in the schedule of the Bainapatra. In the aforesaid Bainapatra and Sale Deed dated 31.01.1963 plot No.1207 was mistakenly written as the location of plot numbers had not been properly identified through investigation on the spot although the land of plot No.1208 was transferred in favour of the plaintiff by way of aforesaid deeds. Katanmoni Nath owned the land situated on the south side and the boundaries specified in the sale deed dated 31.01.1963 would attract the land of plot No.1208. Kornomoni Nath did not get married for the second time rather she became pregnant by leading immoral life with Prosanna Nath on account of which her life interest had not been lost. Being a woman of immoral character Kornomoni Nath departed to elsewhere. 

19. Now let us examine how far the plain-tiff of Title Suit No.74 of 1993 has been able to prove her case. The document on the basis of which the plaintiff claims her title on the suit land is the sale deed dated 31.01.1963 which was exhibited as Exhibit-2, but admittedly plot No.1207 was stated in the said deed. To cure such mistake happened in the above sale deed the plaintiff claims that she instituted Title Suit No.42 of 1992 which was decreed on compromise on 21.11.1992. It also transpires that Kornomoni Nath was the defendant No. I in the Title Suit No.42 of 1992 and she deposed in the said suit in support of the compromise deed. The plaintiff filed the certified copy of the judgment and decree and Solenama (compromise deed) which were exhibited and marked as Exhibit-5 series. From the decree of Title Suit No.42 of 1992 (Exhibit-5(A)) it appears that plot No.1207 along with specific boundaries had been described in the decree although the plaintiff claims that the land described in the schedule of the sale deed dated 31.01.1963 as well as decree of Title Suit No.42 of 1992 (Exhibit-5(A)) are the same and they would indeed attract the land of plot No.1208. To dispel such confusion the plaintiff prayed for local investigation before the court and accordingly a local investigation was held. P.W.6 deposed in support of the Local Investigation Report and the defendants No.3 and 4 cross-examined him, but they could not show any contradiction. On going through the Local Investigation Report together with relevant papers in this regard (Exhibits-6 series) it appears that the land described both in the Exhibits-2 and 5(A) would attract the land of plot No.1208. 

20. It is crystal clear from the foregoing discussion that due to demise of her husband Kornomoni Nath executed Sale Deed (Exhibit-2) in favour of the plaintiff (in Title Suit No.74 of 1993) in compliance with the terms and conditions of Bainamana. Thus, it is proved that the plaintiff acquired title and interest from Katanmoni Nath. But the defendants No.3 and 4 raised a question that the plaintiff could not acquire title by virtue of an unregistered deed. On plain reading of the Sale Deed (Exhibit-2) it is seen that the sale in question was settled at the consideration money of Tk.95.00. According to Section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 the sale of immovable property the value of which is less than 100 taka can be made by an unregistered document. Therefore, the Sale Deed (Exhibit-2) is a valid instrument accruing title to the plain-tiff (In Title Suit No.74 of 1993). 

21. Apart from the above, the plaintiff (In Title Suit No.74 of 1993) examined sever-al witnesses in support of the genuineness of the Sale Deed (Exhibit-2). P.W.2 is the scribe, who identified his signature in the said deed as Exhibit-2(A). P.W.2 stated in his deposition in the following way: 
"লক্ষিরানী দত্ত কর্নমনি নাথকে চিনি। তাহাদের মাধ্যমে দলিল হয়। কর্নমনিকে আমি এ দলিল পড়ে শুনিয়েছি। মর্ম বুঝে ইহাতে আমার ও সাক্ষিগনের সামনে টিপ দিয়েছে। আমি উহা বকলম করেছি।"

22. P.W.3 was also present at the time of execution of the Sale Deed (Exhibit-2), who identified the said Sale Deed. 

23. Regarding possession in the suit land i.e. land of plot No.1208 the plaintiff (In Title Suit No.74 of 1993) examined four witnesses. P.Ws.1, 2, 3 and 5 deposed sup-porting the possession of the plaintiff in the suit land. Although those witnesses were cross-examined by the defendants No.3 and 4, but no contradiction had been made. Moreover, Exhibit-4 (D.P. Khatian) shows that Katanmoni Nath had the possession in respect of the land of plot No.1208. 

24. Adverting to the case of defendants No.3 and 4 (In Title Suit No.74 of 1993), let us first scan the evidences adduced in support of their claim. The defendants No.3 and 4 claim that Katanmoni Nath died on 28th Chaitra 1366 B.S. corresponding to 11.04.1960 leaving behind his wife Kornomoni Nath as the only heir, who became the owner of the land of plot No.1208 belonging to Katanmani Nath. Subsequently, Kornomoni Nath again got married with Proshanna Nath and she died on 12th Chaitra 1399 B.S. corresponding to 26.00.1993. The time Kornomoni Nath got 2nu marriage she became divested-of suit land belonging to Katanmani Nath the said land devolved upon the defendants No.3 and 4 as reversionary heirs (brother's daughter's sons of Katanmani Nath) according to Hindu Law. 

25. The crux of the contention between the plaintiff and the defendants No.3 and 4 (In Title Suit No.74 of 1993) indeed revolves around the question whether due to second marriage Kornomoni Nath lost her life interest in the land of plot No.1208 originally belonged to her husband Katanmoni Nath and the same devolved upon the defendants No.3 and 4 as reversionary heirs. On scrutiny of the record it is evident that the defendants No.3 and 4 could not prove by adducing satisfactory evidence as to the fact that at the time of execution of Sale Deed (Exhibit-2) Kornomoni Nath got married for the second time due to which she lost her life interest in the suit land. The defendants (In Title Suit No.74 of 1993) could not also adduce any document to prove the facts that on the death of Katanmoni Nath his brother Ratan i.e. the predecessor of the defendants No.3 and 4 became the owner the suit land. Rather, it is squarely proved that at the time of execution of the Sale Deed (Exhibit-2) Katanmoni Nath did not lose her life interest in the suit land due to the reason of second marriage or loosing chastity. 

26. The defendants No.3 and 4 (In Title Suit No.74 of 1993) further claim that Katanmoni Nath died on 28th Chaitra 1366 B.S. corresponding to 11.04.1960 while the plaintiffs claim that Katanmoni Nath died on 15th Chaitra 1368 B.S. But there is no iota of evidence available on the record in support of the claim of the defendants whereas the plaintiff adduced the death certificate of Katanmoni Nath which was marked as Exhibit-7. It reveals from Exhibit-7 that Katanmoni Nath died on 15th Chaitra 1368 B.S. 

27. There is another contention between the plaintiff and the defendants No.3 and 4 (In Title Suit No.74 of 1993) regarding the second marriage of the Katanmoni Nath. The defendants No.3 and 4 claim that after the death of Katanmoni Nath his wife Komomoni Nath entered into second marriage with one Proshonno Nath for which she lost her life interest in the suit land while the plaintiff claims that Kornomoni Nath never got married with Proshonno Nath although she used to led immoral life with Proshonno Nath. 

28. D.W.1 stated in his cross-examination that "কর্নমনি নাথ অনুমান ২৭/২৮ বছর আগে ২য় বিয়ে করে।" D. W.1 deposed before the court on 22.03.1997 from which it is logically deduced that Kornomoni Nath entered into second marriage in the year 1969/70. But the alleged Sale Deed (Exhibit-2) was executed by Kornomoni Nath on 31.01.1963 which is too earlier before her second marriage. Thus, even if it is admit-ted for the sake of argument that Kornomoni Nath got married for the second time that did not affect the transfer of suit land in favour of the plaintiff inasmuch said Kornomoni Nath did not lose her life interest in the suit land on 31.01.1963. 

29. Again, D.W.2 stated in her deposition in the following way: 
"আমার মাতার নাম কর্নমনি নাথ। আমার মাতার সাথে বাবার ২য় বিবাহ হয়। আমার মাতার প্রথম স্বামীর নাম ছিল কটন নাথ।"

30. D.W.2 further stated in her cross-examination that " আমার জন্ম সন তারিখ বলিতে পারিবনা। প্রসন্ন নাথের সাথে আমার মাতার বিয়ের কাগজপত্র আছে। তবে কোন সনে বিয়ে হয় বলতে পারিব না। ৪/৫ বছর আগে মারা যায়।”

31. Thus, D. W.2 could not state the year on which her mother Komomoni Nath got married for the second time. 

32. D.W.3 also could not state the year on which Kornomoni Nath entered into second marriage. D.W. 3 stated in her cross-examination in the following way: 
"কর্নশনির সাথে প্রসন্ন নাথের ২য় বিয়ে হয় অনেক আগে। আমি সন তারিখ বলিতে পারিব না। প্রসন্ন নাথের সাথে কর্নমনির বিয়ের সময় প্রসন্ন নাথকে চিনি।"

33. Be that as it may, despite the proposition of second marriage of Komomoni Nath is accepted the same will not affect the title of the plaintiff if the said sale in favour of the plaintiff takes place before losing her life interest in the suit land originally owned by Komomoni Nath got married for the second time. From the foregoing discussion, it has abundantly proved that due to demise of Katanmoni Nath his wife Kornomoni Nath transferred the suit land in favour of plaintiff on 31.01.1963 by way of Exhibit-2 as per the terms and conditions of Bainapatra executed between the plaintiff and Katanmoni Nath while Kornomoni Nath had subsisting life interest on 31.01.1963. 

34. The defendants No.3 and 4 claim further that being the owner suit land Katanmoni Nath on the request of Roshomoy Datta, the husband of the defendant No.1 allowed him to reside at the western part of 01 decimal land raising a mud-built but thereon. 

35. But D.W.1 stated in his cross-examination that "রসময় দত্ত নালিশী জমিতে অনুমতি দখলকার হিসাবে ছিল এই ব্যাপারে আমার কোন ব্যক্তিগত জ্ঞান নাই। তবে আমি মা ও দিদিমা তরপছানী নাথ থেকে নালিশা জমিতে কটনমনি নাথ থেকে রসময় দত্তের অনুমতি দখলকার থাকার কথা শুনেছি। আমার মা বেঁচে আছে। তবে অসুস্থ অবস্থায় আছে। আমার দিদিমা তরপছানী নাথ বেঁচে আছে। রসময় দত্ত কোন মাসের কত তারিখ থেকে নালিশা জমিতে অনুমতি সূত্রে দখলকার হয় তাহা বলতে পারিব না। রসময় দত্ত অনুমতি সূত্রে এস/এল এর দখলে যাওয়ার সময় সত্যেন্দ্র কুমার দে উপস্থিত ছিল এবং তিনি এখনো বেঁচে আছে।..........লক্ষি রানীদত্ত আমাদের কাছ থেকে অনুমতি নিয়ে নালিশা জমি���ে বসবাস করার কথা জবাব বা আরজিতে বলি নাই।"

36. What appears from the above is that D.W. 1 had no firsthand knowledge about the facts of letting Roshomoy Datta the husband of the plaintiff to reside in 01 decimal land of the suit plot as permissive possessor. Even at one stage of his cross-examination D.W.1 admitted that he neither stated in his written statement nor in his plaint about the fact of residing of plaintiff in the suit land as permissive possessor. However, as per the statement made in the cross-examination of D.W.1, the defendants No.3 and 4 could not produce their mother and one Tarafchani Nath to prove the said claim. Although another witness namely Sattyendra. Kumar Dey having examined as D.W.4 deposed sup-porting the fact of permissive possession, he stated in his cross-examination that-
"আমি ২/৩ বছর ধরে গোপাল টিলায় বসবাস করতেছি। ইহার আগে আমি নিখিল/মুকুল দেবনাথের বাড়িতে বসবাস করতাম। প্রায় ১০/১২ বছর আমি নিখিলদেবের বাড়িতে বসবাস করেছি। নিখিলদেবনাথ গং সম্পর্কে আমার ভাতিজা হয়। নিখিলদের সাথে আমার কোন আত্মীয়তা নেই।" 

37. From the above cross-examination it appears that D.W.4 had a good relationship with the defendants No.3 and 4 as he lived 10/12 years in the house of defendants No.3 and 4 although he is not their relative. In such context, D.W.4 appears to be an interested witness and as such his testimony is not safe to be relied on. 

38. The defendant Nos. 3-4 also produced D.W. 5 in support of the claim of permissive possession. Let us see how D.W.5 came to know about the said permissive possession. D.W.5 stated in his examination-in-chief in the following way: 
"আমি যে দিন কটন নাথের বাড়িতে রসময় দত্তের সাথে যাই সেদিন কটন নাথ এক সপ্তাহ পরে যাওয়ার জন্য রসময় দত্তকে বলেছিল। আমি পরে রসময় দত্তের সাথে কটন নাথের কাছে যাই নাই। রসময়দত্ত পরে আমাকে জানায় নলিশা বাড়িতে রসময় দত্তকে অনুমতি সূত্রে থাকতে দেয় এই শর্তে যে, কটননাথ চাইলে জায়গা ছেড়ে দেবেন।"

Subsequently, D.W.5 stated in his cross-examination that "রসময় দত্ত নালিশা বাড়িতে থাকার জন্য অনুমতি নেয়ার সময় ও দখল নেয়ার সময় আমি ছিলাম না।"

39. Thus, D.W.5 claimed to know the fact of permissive possession from the husband of plaintiff although at one stage of his cross-examination he admitted that he was not present at the time of taking possession of 01 decimal land by Roshomoy Datta from Katanmoni Nath as permissive possessor. In the given situation the testimony of D.W.5 regarding permissive possession does not carry any evidentiary value and as such it is not proved that Roshomoy Datta was not a permissive possessor in 01 decimal land of suit plot No.1208. Apart from this, the defendants No.3 and 4 did not claim the plaintiff as illegal possessor in rest 24 decimal land of suit plot No.1208. 

40. At this juncture, let us know what about the relief of the defendants No.3 and 4 in the land of plot No.1207 regarding which the plaintiff does not claim any title. On examination of the plaint of Title Suit No.155 of 1993 it reveals that the defendants No.3 and 4 of Title Suit No.74 of 1993 as plaintiffs in Title Suit No.155 of 1993 further claimed their relief in respect of the land of plot No.1207. 41. On perusal of the plaint of Title Suit No.155 of 1993 it is seen that the plaintiffs (In Title Suit No.155 of 1993) admitted the transfer of land of plot No.7 in favour of the defendant No.7 (In Title Suit No.155 of 1993) namely Samuj Mia. Apart from the above, D. W.1 stated in his deposition in the following way: 
"কৃষ্ণ মনি দেব তাহার অংশ সমুজ মিয়ার কাছে ১৯৭৩ সনে ছাপ কবলা মুলে বিক্রয় করে। আদালতে ১০/১১/৭৩ ইং তারিখের কবলার জাবেদা নকল দাখিল করেছি কিনা মনে নাই। সমুজ মিয়া খরিদের পর খরিদী ভূমির পূর্ব পশ্চিম উত্তর দিকে পাকাওয়াল নির্মাণ করে পশ্চিমাংশে একটি পাকা গৃহ নির্মাণ করে বসবাস করতেছে।”

42. Therefore, admittedly after transfer of the land of plot No.1207 by Krishnamoni Nath in favour of Samuj Mia the defendants No.3 and 4 have no title in the said plot. 

43. It is to be noted that the case laws referred by the learned counsel for the respondents No.1 and 2 have no direct bearing with the facts and circumstances in the cases in hand for which those do not deserve consideration in both appeals. 

44. In the light of the foregoing discussion it is evident that the plaintiff of Title Suit No.74 of 1993 has been able to prove her title and possession in the suit land i.e. on plot No.1208 and as such she is entitled to get the relief as prayed for. On the other hand, the defendants No.3 and 4 (plaintiffs of Title Suit No.155 of 1993) have not been able to prove their title and possession in the suit land. The trial Court as well as the appellate court on proper appreciation of the facts and law lawfully decreed the Title Suit No.74 of 1993 suit and dis-missed the Title Suit No.155 of 1993, but the High Court Division most illegally set aside the judgments and decrees of the trial Court as well as the appellate Court. 

45. In view of the aforesaid reasons, the impugned judgment and decree of the High Court Division warrants interference by this Division. Therefore, we find merit in the submissions of the learned Counsel for the appellant. In the prevailing circumstances, the impugned judgment and decree of the High Court Division cannot stand at all in the eye of law. 

46. Accordingly, both the civil appeals are allowed. 

47. The judgment and decree dated 29.07.2013 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revisions No.2078-2079 of 1999 is hereby set aside. 

End.

Mr. Md. Layequzzaman, Advocate with Mr Ahmed Nowsad Jamil, Advocate instructed by Mr Mohammad Ali, Advocate-on-Record ----- For the Appellants 
For the Respondents ------ None represented
