case_source: (From the judgment and order dated the 31st day of July, 2008 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No.3412 of 2005)
full_judgment:
Jahangir Hossain J. This civil appeal, by leave, is directed against the judgment and order dated the 31" day of July, 2008 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No.3412 of 2005 making the Rule absolute. 

2. The relevant facts for disposal of this civil appeal, in short, are that present appellant as pre-emptor filed Miscellaneous Case No.65 of 1997 for pre-emption of the case land under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 [in brief the Act] in the Court of Assistant Judge, First Court, Kalia, Narail, stating, inter alia, that the preemptor is a co-sharer in the case holding by purchase. Afsaruddin Bhuiyan, father of the pre-emptor and the pre-emptee was owner of 1.10 acre land in the case holding by purchase vide registered deed No.4009 dated 13.05.1970. The pre-emptor also purchased 0.20 acre land-from the case holding by a registered deed dated 17.06.1982 from one Rakib Biswas who purchased the same with other land from the heirs of recorded owners. By this way, the pre-emptor is a co-sharer in the case holding. On the other hand, the pre-emptee is a stranger in the case holding, who purchased the case land from his father, Afsaruddin Bhuiyan vide registered deed No.5416 doted 14.12.1995 at a consideration of taka 12,000.00 beyond the knowledge of the pre-emptor without serving any notice as required under section 89 of the Act. After the death of Afsaruddin, on 01.06.1997, the pre-emptor came to know that his father transferred the case land to the pre-emptee. Then, the pre-emptor obtained certified copy of the said deed on  10.06.1997. He is a cultivator and not owner of more than 10 bigha land. Hence, he filed this pre-emption application. 

3. The pre-emptee contested the case by filing written objection denying all the material allegations contending, inter cilia, that Afsaruddin Bhuiyan, father of the pre-emptee and the pre-emptor, in presence of all of his sons and daughters, transferred 0.98 acre land to the pre-emptee from the case holding out of his 1.10 acre land and after the death of their father, all of his sons and daughters including the preemptor and the pre-emptee became the co-sharers in the case holding by inheritance. The pre-emption application is barred by limitation as the impugned deed was registered on 14.12.1995 and the pre-emption application was filed on 06.08.1997 after statutory period of limitation and he being a co-sharer of the case holding, the pre-emption application is not maintainable. The pre-emptor with a view to having illegal gain filed the pre-emption application and therefore, he prayed for dismissal of the case. 

4. During trial, both the pre-emptor and the pre-emptee examined 3 [three] witnesses each and exhibited relevant papers and documents in support of their respective cases. The learned Assistant Judge after framing issues, recording evidence, hearing the arguments of the respective parties and considering the materials on record by the judgment and order dated 17.10.2001 allowed the pre-emption application. 

5. Being aggrieved by the judgment and order dated 17.1022001. passed by the trial Court, the pre-emptee- purchaser preferred Miscellaneous Appeal No.34 of 2001 before the learned District Judge, Narail and on transfer, the appeal was head by the learned Joint District Judge, 2nd Court, Narail and the learned Joint District Judge after hearing the respective parties and considering the materials on record by the judgment and order dated 23.06.2005 dismissed the appeal affirming those of the trial Court. 

6. Being aggrieved by the judgment and order of the Appellate Court below, the pre-emptee-purchaser as petitioner filed Civil Revision No.3412 of 2005 before the High Court Division. The learned Judge of the High Court Division having heard the respective parties and considering the materials on record by the judgment and order dated 31.07.2008 made the Rule absolute reversing those of the Appellate Court below. 

7. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division, the appellants preferred this civil appeal arising out of Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No.404 of 2009 before this Division. 

8. Mr. Md. Layequzzaman, learned Advocate, appearing for the appellants, submits that the trial Court and the Appellate Court below considered all the material evidence on record in its true per-spective and thereby came to a just, right and lawful conclusion and there is no non-reading or misreading of material evidence on record. According to the settled principles of law, the Appellate Court below is the last and final Court of fats and there is a little scope of the High Court Division to interfere with the finding of fact arrived at by the Appellate Court below. He further submits that at time of the registration of the impugned deed of transfer, the pre-emptee was not a co-sharer in the case holding. Subsequently, after death of his father, the pre-emptee became a co-sharer of the case holding. So there is no scope of its retrospective effect. Therefore, the claim of the pre-emptee as a co-sharer in the case holding is not correct. He further submits that admittedly, no notice was served upon the pre-emptor about the transfer of the case holding and therefore, the High Court Division wrongly shifted the onus upon the pre-emptor that he failed to prove that he had no knowledge about the transfer. He adds that the pre-emption application is not maintainable as it is based on misconception of law, inasmuch, as even if it is assumed that the pre-emptee is a co-sharer in the case holding, he cannot resist pre-emption other than claiming as co-purchaser under sub-section (4) of section 96 of the Act, 1950 and as such, the impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division is bad in Law. 

9. No one appeared on behalf of the respondents to contest the appeal. 

10. Heard the learned Advocate for the appellants and perused the material documents along with other connected papers on record. 

11. It appears from the relevant documents on record that the trial Court held that the case is not barred by limitation as no notice was served upon the pre-emptor about the transfer and pre-emptor filed the petition within four months from the date of knowledge and the pre-emptor is a co-sharer of the case holding. The learned Judge of the Appellate Court below held the same view and affirmed the judgment and order of the trial Court below. It is admitted that Afsaruddin Bhuiyan, father of the pre-emptor-appellant [hereinafter referred to as the appellant] and respondent No.1 on 13.05.1970 purchased the land from two suited khatians. The appellant argued that even if there was more land in the deed of 13.05.1970, his father acquired 98 decimals of land. His father orally gifted him the suit land. He further argued that respondent No.1, deed-holder, on 14.12.1995, secretly got the sale deed executed regarding the whole land of the suited khatians from his father. Though the appellant is the co-sharer by purchase, he was not served notice of the transfer. The appellant by exhibit-2 proved that he is a co-sharer in the suited khatians. Exhibit- 2[ga], jabeda nakal, dated 13.05.1970 produced by the appellant proved that Afsaruddin purchased 1.10 acre land from the suited khatians. The appellant claimed that though 1.10 acre land is alleged to be transferred, the transferable land of the vendor was 98 decimals. His father possessed 98 decimals of land. It is necessary to mention here that the father of the appellant and respondent No.1 purchased 1.10 acre land from 3 plots of those khatians. 

12. It reveals from the judgment and order of the High Court Division that the pre-emptor failed to prove the date of knowledge by adducing reliable evidence and therefore, the case is barred by limitation since it was instituted after 1 [one] year and 8[eight] months from the date of registration of the deed and the pre-emptee being a co-sharer of the case holding, the pre-emption application is not maintainable. 

13. The pre-emptor-appellant claimed that Md. Ekram Hossain Bhuiyan, pre-emptee, disclosed about the impugned deed on 01.06.1997. Then the pre-emptor got certified copy of the impugned deed on 10.06.1997 and filed the pre-emption application on 06.08.1997 which is very much within the limitation from the date of his knowledge. Pws' 2 and 3 are reliable witness who supported the contention of Pw-1. The pre-emptor proved, that he is co-sharer of the case holding by purchase by a registered kabala dated 17.06.1982. Md. Ekram Hossain Bhuiyan, pre-emptee, does not raise any question about the registered kabala dated 17.06.1982 in favour of the pre-emptor and admittedly the pre-emptor is a co-sharer tenant of the case holding and no notice as required under section 89 of the Act wag served upon the pre-emptor. It is further claimed that at the time of registration of the impugned deed of transfer, the pre-emptee was not a co-sharer in the case holding. Subsequently, after death of his father, the pre-emptee became a co-sharer of the case holding, so there is no scope of its retrospective effect. Thus, the claim of the pre-emptee as a co-sharer in the case holding is not correct. It is claimed that the High Court Division in exercise of revisional jurisdiction exceed-ed its jurisdiction in interfering with the findings of facts arrived at by the Court of Appeal below as to the point of limitation in holding that the case is barred by the limitation. It is further claimed that admittedly no notice was served upon the pre-emptor about the transfer of the case holding and therefore, the High Court Division wrongly shifted the onus upon the pre-emptor that he failed to prove that he had no knowledge about the transfer and finally it is claimed that the pre-emption application is not maintainable as the same is based on misconception of law inasmuch as, even if it is assumed that the pre-emptee is a co-sharer in the case holding, he cannot resistr pre-emption other than claiming as co-purchaser under sub-section (4) of section 96 of the Act, 1950. 

14. Respondent No. I argued that the pre-emptee and the pre-emptor are co-sharers in the case jote and as such, the application for pre-emption is not maintainable in the eye of law. Since it is argued that the father of pre-emptor earlier verbally gifted him the case land, the pre-emptor has remedy to challenge the impugned deed by filing a suit for cancellation of deed but not by the pre-emption application under section 96 of the Act. It is further argued that the application for pre-emption is barred by limitation, the impugned deed was registered on 14.12.1995 and the pre-emption case was filed on 06.08.1997, i.e. after one year eight months from the sale of case land. Before sale of the case land, the pre-emptor and the pre-emptee and the vendor were present in a conversation regarding sale of the suit land. It is further argued that Pw-1, Matiar Rahman Bhuiyan, in his deposition deposed that. ....বাবা ইকরামকে দলিল দলিল দেয়। আমার দান মূলে কোন দাবী না। ১৩/০৭/১৯৭০ইং তারিখের তারিখে আমার অংশ কতটুকু অংশ খারিদ করে আমার জানা নেই।.. which proved that the pre-emptor filed the said case only to gain illegally. It is further argued that the pre-emptor did not prove the date of knowledge of the sale for filing pre-emption application by adducing evidence in the case filed after a period of one year eight months from the date of sale and as such, the application for pre-emption is clearly barred by limitation. It is further argued that the pre-emptor was not a co-sharer by purchase, before purchase of the case land through registered kabala dated 14.12.1995. It is further argued that the pre-emptee and the pre-emptor have been possessing the rest 12 decimals of land as co-owners. Atiar Rahman Bhuiyan, brother of OPW1, in his deposition deposed that .... নালিশী জমিসহ ১.১০ একর জমি আমার পিতা খরিদ করে। তার মধ্যে ৯৮ শতক জমি ইকরামেরনিকট বিক্রয় করে। বিক্রয়ের সময় প্রার্থীসহ আমরা সবাই ছিলাম। নালিশী খতিয়ানের বাকী ১২ শতাংশ জমিতে আমরা উত্তরাধীকারসূত্রে অংশ পাই। so the pre-emption application is barred by acquiescence and estoppels. Karim Sheikh, OPW-3, brother-in-law of the pre-emptor and the preemptee, in his deposition deposed that আমার শ্বশুর ১.১০ এক জমি খরিদ করে দখল করিতে তার মধ্যে ৯৮ শতক জমি ইকরামের নিকট বিক্রয় করে। এ বিক্রয় মতিয়ারসহ আমরা জানতাম। .... so the pre-emption appli-cation is barred by acquiescence and estoppels, but the Courts below did not consider this point and illegally allowed the pre-emption application.

15. In the present case, the trial Court as well as the appellate Court below has arrived at concurrent finding that the pre-emption petition is not barred by limitation. But the trial Court as well as the appellate Court did not appreciate the evidence of the witnesses of the petitioner on the point of the date of knowledge of the impugned sale deed though the present pre-emption petition was filed almost 1 year 8 months later from the date of impugned sale deed. The trial Court with-out appreciating the evidence of the witnesses on record in that regard came to a conclusion that though the petitioner deposed some inconsistent statements regarding knowledge of the impugned sale deed, it was not proved that he knew about the impugned sale deed earlier and the pre-emption petition is not time barred since the petitioner filed the petition with-in the prescribed period of limitation. The appellate Court went a step forward and without appreciating the evidence of the witnesses of petitioner on record with respect to the date of knowledge of the impugned sale deed decided that the petition was not time barred since the opposite party did not give notice of the impugned sale to the petitioner and the consent of the petitioner to the impugned sale deed was not proved. Both the Courts below did not take into account the legal proposition that as per section 96(1) of the Act read with sec ions 101 and 103 of the Evidence Act, 1872, the burden of proof as to the date of knowledge of the impugned sale deed is with the petitioner to prove that he has filed the pre-emption petition within 4 months from the date of knowledge of the impugned sale deed. The trial Court as well as the appellate Court should have been very much cautious in addressing the point of limitation. The right of pre-emption being a feeble right requirements of law have to be fully complied with to be entitled to pre-emption. A citizen's right to deal with his property freely, in view of the special statutory provision, bears a clog, that is, subject to right of pre-emption. The statutory provision providing such a right curtailing owner's right to deal with his property must be construed very strictly [Ahmed Hossain and others-Vs-Basharat Ali and others 32 DLR (AD) 54].The claim of pre-emption is a predatory right and that is why, the legislature has imposed conditions for claiming pre-emption, such as, the petition should be made within four months of the service of notice under section 89, or if no notice has been served, within four months of the date of knowledge of the transfer. Even if the pre-emptee does not raise the above point, the requirement of law must be satisfied by the pre-emptor before claiming a right of pre-emption [Habibur Rahman Bhuiyan and others-Vs-Galman Begum and Others, 64 DLR AD page 133]. The petitioner came to Court to enforce a right. A period of limitation is prescribed by the statute for the purpose. The burden lies with him to prove the date of his alleged knowledge and that is within the period of limitation. On a consideration of the language used in section 96(1) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, it further appears that the definite article "the" has been used to qualify "knowledge" occur-ring twice in the section. It, therefore, indicates that "the knowledge" must by definite knowledge. A precise or exact perception of the necessary particulars of a fact is the determinant of "the knowledge" which is essentially a question of fact [Habibur Rahman Khalifa-Vs-Satish Chandra Ghose 29 DLR 178]. When a pre-emptor is coming to the court to exercise his right of preemption, which is essentially a predatory right, after a long lapse of time a heavy duty is cast upon him to prove his alleged knowledge about the impugned sale by most convincing evidence so as to circumvent the bar of limitation [Habibur Rahman alias Md. Habibur Rahman and another-Vs-Mobarak All Rani and others, 50 DLR 193]. 

16. Now, let us proceed to ascertain whether the interference by the High Court Division with the finding of the courts below regarding the point that the petition is not barred by limitation is justified or not. The petitioner stated in the pre-emption petition that he for the first time came to know about the impugned sale deed on 01.06.1997 A.D. corresponding to ১৮ জ্যেষ্ঠ ১৪০৪ বাংলা সাল. The petitioner did rot depose in his examination-in-chief the corresponding Gregorian calendar date when he knew about the peti-impugned sale deed. Though the petitioner PW-1 deposed in his examination-in-chief, "পিতা মারা গেলে ১৪০৪ সালের ১৮ই জ্যেষ্ঠ তর্কিত দলিলের কথা বলে ও দখল ছেড়ে দিতে বলেচ, he deposed during his cross-examination, "১৪০৪ সালে বিক্রয়ের কথা জানি। ১৪০৪ সাল বাংলা না ইংরেজি তা বলিতে পারিনা। বর্তমানে বাংলা কত সাল তা বলিতে পারিনা"। If we go through this portion of the deposition of Pw-1, we find that he failed to prove definitely that he knew occur-about the impugned sale deed for the first time on 18th Jaishtha 1404 BS. Pw-2 deposed in cross-examination, "১৪০৪ সালের জ্যেষ্ঠ মাসে একরাম প্রকাশ করে। আমি বাংলা কোন সালে বিবাহ করি তা স্মরণ নাই। আমার সর্বশেষ সন্তানের জন্ম কত তারিখ তা মনে নাই।" Pw-2 also failed to corroborate the testimony of Pw-1 on the point of the date of knowledge of the impugned sale deed since he did not cate-exergorically mention the date when he exactly heard about the impugned sale deed. Pw-3 deposed, "মতিয়ার আমাকে বলে নালিশী জমি একরাম দলিল করে নেয়। কোন দাগের জমি বা ফাহার নিকট থেকে লিখে নেয় সে সম্পর্কে আমাকে কিছু বলে নাই। কথা শুনে আমি চলে যাই। অন্য কোনো বিষয় আমি জানিনা। কোন তারিখে একরাম বা মতিয়ার বলে তা বিবরণ নেই।" Pw-3 was not told which property or whose property was taken by the Opposite party Ekram. Moreover, Pw-3 did not depose when he heard about the impugned sale deed. on the point of the date of knowledge c the petitioner about the impugned gale deed for the first time, the evidence definite of the petitioner's witnesses is not definite, complete, corroborative and convincing enough to dis-charge his burden of proof. "Knowledge" as referred to in sub-section 1 of section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act means and includes a definite and complete knowledge in order to qualify the petitioner to file an application under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act[Abdul Sattar and another-Vs-Osimuddin and Others, 42 DLR 24).The High Court Division accepted the evidence of OPWs regarding the point that the transfer was within the knowledge of the petitioner since OPW-1, Ekram Hossain, who is also full brother of pre-emptor Motiar Rahman and OPW-2, Atiar Rahman, who is also full brother of pre-emptor Matiar Rahman and OPW-3 Karim Sheikh, Sister's husband of the pre-emptor, all these OPWs testified in one voice that their father late Afsaruddin transferred the case land to the preemptee opposite party by a registered kabala dated 14/12/1995 within full knowledge of all his sons arid daughters including the pre-emptor. The High Court Division while exercising its revisional jurisdiction is competent to reverse the judgment of the courts below when the same has been made either upon mis-reading or non-consideration of the material evidence and the said mis-reading and non-consideration of the evidence caused failure of jus-tice [Habibullah (Md)-Vs-Sher Ali Khan and others, 57 DLR (AD) 55]. The High Court Division is empowered to interfere with the findings of fact if the findings are perverse or there has been a non-appreciation or non-consideration of the material evidence on record by the Courts below [Masjid kacha Tank, Nahan-Vs-Tuffail Mohammed, AIR 1991 SC 455]. 

17. The purchaser opposite party no 1 claims himself to be a co-sharer tenant in the holding by inheritance, and, therefore, he claims that sub-section 10(a) of section 96 of the Act would be a bar to the instant pre-emption proceeding. Let us examine this aspect of the case from the legal per-spective. The purchaser opposite party 
No.1 as Opw-1 deposed, "নালিশী জমিসহ ১.১০ একর জমি আমার পিতা ১৯৭০ সালে খরিদ করে দখল করিত। বাবা এর পরবর্তীতে ৯৮ শতক জমি ১৪/১২/৯৫ তারিখে রেজিঃ কবলামূলে আমার নিকট বিক্রয় করে। বক্রি ১২ শতক জমি ভোগ দখলকালে বাবা মারা গেলে আমরা সবাই উত্তরাধিকার লাভ করি। সেই হিসাবে আমি ও প্রার্থী শরীক।" It transpires from this portion of the deposition of the opposite party No.1 that the impugned deed was registered on 14/12/95 and the opposite party No.1, after his father's death, became a co-sharer tenant in the holding by inheritance subsequent to the registration of the impugned deed No.5416 dated 14/12/95. At the date of registration of the impugned deed No.5416 dated 14/12/95 opposite party No.1, Md. Ekram Hossen, was not a co-sharer tenant in the holding by inheritance. It is now a well settled principle of law that the cause of action under section 96 of the State Acquisition and' Tenancy Act accrues on the date of the registration of the deed of sale, when registration is compulsory [Ayesha Khatun (Musammat)- Vs-Musammat Jahanara Begum and others, 43 DLR (AD)9). The right of pre-emption accrued to the pre-emptor is not affected by the subsequent acquisition of co-sharership by the pre-emptee [Abdul Baten-Vs-Abdul Latif Sheikh and others, 45 DLR (AD) 26]. One who acquires co-sharership subsequent to the dare of notice of transfer or one who becomes a co-sharer in the holding on a date later to the date of presentation of the deed of transfer for registration and sought to be pre-empted is not competent to oppose pre-emption [Fatema Khatun and others-Vs-Abdul Quddus 58 DLR (AD)110]. From this perspective of the case, we hole that the impugned sale to the pre-emptee is not protected from pre-emption under sub-section 10(a) of section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950. The High Court Division probably did not analyze this aspect of this case. However, this finding does not have any impact upon the decision of the case since the petition is barred by limitation. 

18. In view of the above mentioned facts, circumstances and legal position, we are of the view that the High Court Division was justified to interfere with the finding of the Courts below that the petition is not barred by limitation and, therefore, was justified in making the Rule absolute. 

19. Therefore, we find no merit in the sub-missions of the learned Advocate for the appellant and accordingly, the appeal is dismissed without any order as costs. 

End.

full_judgment:
Obaidul Hassan J. This Civil Appeal by leave granting order dated 02.06.2016 in Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No.2934 of 2012 is directed against the judgment and decree dated 21.05.2012 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No.4805 of 2003 disposing of the Rule reversing the judgment and decree dated 03.07.2003 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, 2nd Court, Lakshmipur in Civil Appeal No.49 of 1993 dismissing the appeal affirming the judgment and decree dated 28.06.1993 passed by the Court of Assistant Judge, Additional Court, Lakshmipur Sadar, Lakshmipur in Civil Suit No.123 of 1991 decreeing the suit. 

2. The relevant facts necessary for disposal of this Civil Appeal are that the appellant as plaintiff filed Title Suit No.123 of 1991 against the respondents for declaration of title in the suit land. The case of the plaintiff, in a nutshell, is that one Ram Chandra Dey got settlement of the suit land vide N.H.C.C. Settlement Case No.216 of 1941-42 and executed Kabuliyat in favour of the government and accordingly the same was accepted and Khatian No.860 was opened in the name of said Ram Chandra Dey. While possessing and enjoying the suit land said Ram Chandra Dey died leaving behind Chinta Haran Dey as only son. Chinta Haran Dey sold out the suit land to the plaintiff by a registered sale deed No.20095 dated 27.12.1984 and handed over possession of the same to the plaintiff. The plaintiff had been possessing and enjoying the suit land by cultivation with the knowledge of the defendants and other people. The defendants have no right, title and possession in the suit land since then. The plain-tiff was informed that the suit land was recorded in the name of vendor of the plaintiff and the deed would be written accordingly. Thereafter the plaintiff came to know that during Diara Survey the suit land was not recorded in the name of vendor of the plaintiff rather the same wrongly recorded in the name of the predecessor of the defendants No.1-11, Abid Ali and others and in the name of the defendants No.12 and 13, which cast doubt cloud on the title of the plaintiff. The plaintiff on 12.02.1989 sent one Siraj (her nephew) to the concerned Tahsil Office to pay rent of the suit lana and came to know from said Siraj about the wrong record of the suit land in the name of defendant, thereafter, the plain-tiff collected the certified copy of the Khatian and learnt properly about the wrong record of the suit land. Hence the plaintiff filed the suit for declaration of title. 

3. The defendant No.12-respondent No.1 contested the suit by filing a written statement contending, inter alia, that the defendant No.12 is the owner of the suit land measuring 4.20 acres along with other non-suit land. One Ram Chandra Dey got settlement of the said land vide N.H.S.C. No.216 of 1941-42 and accordingly the Kabuliyat was executed in the name of Ram Chandra Dey and Khatian No.860 was recorded in his name. Ram Chandra Dey gave settlement of the suit land to the father of the defendant No.12 at his proposal and subsequently Ram Chandra Dey executed Patta dated 12th Baishakh, 1385 B.S. and handed over possession of the suit land to the father of the defendant No.12. The father of the defendant No.12 used to possess the suit land on his behalf and thereafter the defendant No.12 used to possess the same through Bargadar. The defendant No.12 is sole owner of the suit land under the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. During the Diara survey the defendant No.12 was in belief that Diara khatian regarding the suit land was correctly recorded in his name, but after receiving the summons of the suit and copy of Diara Khatian No.333 the defendant came to know that only 5(five) annas share out of 16(sixteen) annas of the suit land recorded in the name of defendant No.12. The husband of the plaintiff namely Abdul Khaleque was the clerk and posted at Diara operation office at Ramgati and the defendant No.13, Abdur Rahim was the peon of the said office and they in connivance with each other taking the privilege of being the employee of Diara Office got illegally recorded the rest portion of the suit land in the name of the defendant No.13 Abdur Rahim and father, brother and other sister of said Abdul Khaleque although they have no right, title or possession of the suit land. Ram Chandra Dey had no son namely Chinta Haran Dey, but the plaintiff created the forged deed by showing a fictitious person. The valuation of the land was Tk.1,00,000.00 at the time of alleged transfer of the suit land, but the plaintiff created a forged deed stating the valuation of the suit land at Tk.5,000.00 only. The husband of the plaintiff is witness of the so-called deed and Diara plot was not mentioned in the said deed and the possession of the suit land was never handed over to the plaintiff. Ram Chandra Dey left the country and went to India and he never came back to this country and the cause of action of the suit land did not arise on 16.02.1989. The defendant No.12 has been possessing and enjoying the total suit land of plot No.1336 including the non-suit land for more than 12 years and as such the suit is liable to be dismissed. 

4. During the trial of the case, the trial Court framed as many as five issues for disposal of the suit. The plaintiff examined five witnesses as P.Ws.1-5 while the defendants No.1 and 2 examined three witnesses as D.Ws.1-3. Both parties adduced documentary evidences in support of their respective case. 

5. The trial Court on completion of the trial decreed the suit by judgment and decree dated 28.06.1993. Being aggrieved with the judgment of the trial Court the defendant No.12 preferred Civil Appeal No.49 of 1993 before the learned District Judge, Lakshmipur and on transfer the said appeal was heard and disposed of by the learned Joint District Judge, 2nd Court, Lakshmipur, who upon hearing dismissed the same by judgment and decree dated 19.06.2003 affirming the judgment and decree of the trial Court. 

6. Thereafter, the defendant No.12 filed Civil Revision No.4805 of 2003 before the High Court Division against the judgment and decree dated 19.06.2003 passed by the lower appellate Court and Rule was issued. Upon final hearing, the High Court Division was pleased to dispose of the Rule by judgment and decree dated 21.05.2012 thereby set aside the judgments of both the lower appellate Court and trial Court while declared the suit land as vested property directing the plaintiff and the defendant to hand over the suit land in favour of the Deputy Commissioner, Lakshmipur. 

7. Being disgruntled with the judgment and decree dated 21.05.2012 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No.4805 of 2003 the plaintiff-appellant preferred the Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No.2934 of 2012 before this Division and after hearing this Division was pleased to grant leave on 02.06.2016 and hence the instant appeal. 

8. Mr. Shaheed Alam, the learned senior Counsel appearing on behalf of the appellant taking us through the judgment and decree of the High Court Division dated 21.05.2012 passed in Civil Revision No.4805 of 2003, judgments and decrees of the appellate Court as well as trial Court, the other materials on record, contends that the High Court Division has committed illegality in totally misconceiving the case of the appellant upon misreading and misconstruing the evidence and materials on record and thereby misdirected beyond the law and facts of the case in passing the erroneous judgment disposing of the Rule occasioning serious miscarriage of justice and as such the impugned judgment and decree is liable to be set aside. The learned Counsel argues next that appellant's vendor's father died in Bangladesh in 1960 and death certificate was filed and the name of appellant's vendor was available in the voter lost and the respondent No.1 could not prove his Patta but the High Court Division without discussing these aspects made out a third case that the suit land was vested property which has no basis and as such the impugned judgment is liable to be set aside. The learned senior-Counsel contends next that it is settled law that a revisional Court cannot set aside the concurrent findings of the trial Court and appellate court unless there is misreading and non-readings of facts but the High Court Division without taking into consideration of the settled law most illegally passed the impugned judgment reversing the judgments and decrees of the lower appellate Court, as well as the trial Court and as such the impugned judgment and decree of the High Court Division is liable to be set aside. 

9. On the other hand, none appears on behalf of the respondent to contest the appeal. 

10. We have perused the impugned judgment and decree dated 21.05.2012 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No.4805 of 2003. We have also considered the submissions of the learned counsels for the appellant and gone through the judgments and decrees of the lower appellate Court as well as the trial Court, evidences and other materials on record. 

11. It is admitted that Ram Chandra Dey was the owner of suit land by taking settlement from the government. From the record the plaintiff appears to claim that Ram Chandra Dey died leaving Chinta Haran Dey as the only son who transferred the suit land to the plaintiff by registered sale deed No.20095 dated 27.12.1984 and the plaintiff had been possessing the same since the time it was purchased. But during the Diara survey me suit land was wrongly recorded in the name of the defendants and their predecessors. 

12. However, the defendant No.12-respondent No.1 claims that Ram Chandra Dey transferred the suit land in favour of the defendant by way of Patta dated 3rd Baishak 1359 B.S. and he had been possessing the suit land since then. Despite the total Patta land was recorded in the name of defendant No.12 in draft survey during the Diara operation, but final Diara Khatian of the said land was wrongly published in the name of the plaintiff's father-in-law and defendant No.13. The defendant learnt about the said wrong record on receipt of summons in the instant suit. During the Pakistan period Ram Chandra Dey left the country and resided in India permanently and never came back to the country. Ram Chandra Dey had no son named Chinta Haran Dey, but the plaintiff created the alleged sale deed by false personation of Chinta Haran Dey. 

13. On scrutiny of the record, it is seen that the plaintiff filed the registered sale deed No.20095 dated 27.12.1984 which was marked as Exhibit-2. The said sale deed being a registered deed executed by the successor of the original owner generally does not put any hindrance to pass title to the vendee i.e. plaintiff. Yet the main contention between the plaintiff and the defendant No.12 is whether the vendor namely Chinta Haran Dey is son of Ram Chandra Dey and the aforesaid sale deed was executed fraudulently with false personation. 

14. The plaintiff examined Chinta Haran Dey as P.W.5, who stated in his deposition that "আমার নাম চিন্তাহরণ দে। বাবার নাম রাম চন্দ্র দে। গ্রাম-নুর সোনাপুর পূর্বে আমাদের বাড়ী অমরপুর ছিল। নুর সোনাপুর গ্রামে ভোটার তালিকায় আমার এবং ছেলে ৪ জন এর নাম আছে। ২৩১-২৩৫ নং ক্রমিকে আমাদের নামগুলো আছে।"

15. The said voter list was exhibited and marked as Exhibit-7 from which it transpires that the name of Chinta Haran Dey and his four sons were registered in serial Nos.231-235 in the voter list of Nur Sonapur village and in serial No.231 it was particularly written the name of Chinta Haran Dey, son of Ram Chandra Dey. In the given circumstances, it is proved beyond doubt that Ram Chandra Dey had a son named Chinta Haran Dey. 

16. From the Exhibit-6 i.e. certified copy of the death register it appears that Ram Chandra Dey died in Bangladesh on 25.09.1960 at Omarpur, Police Station-Sudharam, District-Noakhali and the information of his death was registered on 17.10.1960. P.W.5 stated in his cross-examination that they had two houses and his father-in-law's house at Omarpur was merged in the river erosion, thereafter his father built house at Sonapur. P.W.5 was cross-examined by the defendant No.12, but no discrepancy was made. Apart from this, P.W.3 deposed that at the time of execution of sale deed (Exhibit-2) he was present. This witness identified his signature in the said deed as Exhibit-2(Ka). P.W.3 was cross-examined by the defendant No.12 but no contradiction could have been shown. Thus, P.Ws.1, 3 and 5 deposed coherently supporting the title of the plaintiff in the suit land. 

17. In view of the discussion made above, it is abundantly clear that Ram Chandra Dey never left the country for India and he died in the country leaving Chinta Haran Dey as the only son due to which the sale deed No.20095 dated 27.12.1984 (Exhibit-2) executed by Chinta Haran Dey is genuine and the plaintiff accrued legal title in the suit land by virtue of the said sale deed. 

18. On the other hand, the defendant No.12 claims his title on the footing that Ram Chandra Dey gave settlement of the suit land in his favour at Tk.80.00 as Salami and accordingly Diara Khatian No.333 was finally prepared in his name. The defendant No.12 filed unregistered Patta deed (Exhibit-Ka) in support of his claim. But regarding the authenticity of Exhibit-Ka the appellate Court observed in the following: 
"প্রদ: 'ক' সম্পর্কে বাদী পক্ষের বিজ্ঞ কৌশুলী জাল জালিয়াতির অভিযোগ নিম্নাদালতে করেছেন। আপীল শুনানীকালে বাদী রেসপনডেন্ট পক্ষের বিজ্ঞ কৌশুলী (প্রদঃক) এর উপর আদালতের দৃষ্টি আকর্ষণ করেন। তিনি বলেন যে, এক রুপিয়া আট আনার একটি পুরাতন কার্টিজ সংগ্রহ করে জালিয়াতীর মাধ্যমে বিবাদীপক্ষ এ পাট্টা সৃষ্টি করেছেন। স্ট্যাম্পের উপরিভাগের প্রতি আদালতের বিশেষ দৃষ্টি আকর্ষণ করে বলেন, এতে ইংরেজী বিভিন্ন তথ্য লিখা ছিল। বিবাদীপক্ষ ঐ লিখা মুছে ফেলে, ধুয়ে ফেলে পরবর্তী এ পাট্টা লিখেছেন। শিন একটি আতশী কাঁচ সরবরাহ করেছেন। এতে দেখ যায় যে, ইংরেজীতে দুই লাইন লিখা ছিল যা মুছে ফেলা হয়েছে। কিন্তু মেগনিফাইন গ্লাস দিয়ে এ লিখার অস্তিত্ব এখনো দেখা যায়। রেসপনডেন্ট পক্ষের বিজ্ঞ কৌশুলীর মতে বিাদী পক্ষের জালিয়াতী স্পষ্টভাবে প্রমাণিত হয়েছে।”

19. Regarding the Patta of defendant No.12 the trial court observed as follows: 
" প্রদর্শনী-পাট্টা (ক) দলিলটি ২ ফর্দে সম্পাদিত। প্রথম ফৰ্দ্দে ১.৫০ টাকার ব্রিটিশ আমলের ষ্ট্যাম্প এবং দ্বিতীয় ফদ্দটি একটি রেপ কাগজ। সাধারণ দৃষ্টিতে উক্ত ফৰ্দ্দ দুইটি একই সময়ে নহে বলিয়া প্রতীয়মান হয় অর্থাৎ স্ট্যাম্পটি অতি পুরাতন এবং রেপটি তুলনামূলকভাবে পুরাতন কাগজ। স্ট্যাম্প এর ১ম ফদ্দটি তিন বারে চার টুকরা এবং প্রত্যেকটি ভাজে ছেড়া। কিন্তু দ্বিতীয় ফৰ্দ্দের রেপটি তিন ভাজে চার টুকরা কিন্তু কোন ভাজে ছেড়া নহে। এখানে লক্ষণীয় বিষয় হলো পিছনের পেটি ভাজের মধ্যে না ছিড়িয়া ভিতরের ষ্ট্যাম্প ফৰ্দ্দটি ভাজে ভাজে ছিড়ে যাওয়ার প্রেক্ষিতে যুক্তিসংগত কোন কারণ বিবাদী পক্ষের বিজ্ঞ কৌশুলীকে আদালত কর্তৃক জিজ্ঞাসা করার সন্তোষজনক বক্তব্য উপস্থাপন করিতে পারে নাই এবং উক্ত পাট্টা লিখা ইদানিংকার বলিয়া প্রতীয়মান হয়।"

20. Given the aforesaid observation of the lower appellate Court and the trial Court it is crystal clear that the alleged Patta (Exhibit-Ka) is a fabricated one which was created by the defendant No.12 fraudulently showing one Ram Chandra Dey as the vendor. 

21. Again, the defendant No.12 as D.W.1 stated in his cross-examination that he has no personal information about the Patta (Exhibit-Ka) and he did not know when the stamp was purchased. That apart, there are four witnesses in the Patta (Exhibit-Ka), but the defendant No.12 could neither produce any of the said witnesses nor the scribe of the Patta to prove the genuineness of Patta. The defendant also could not show any reason for not producing the witnesses stated in Patta before the Court. But the High Court Division without controverting the concurrent findings of the lower appellate Court and the trial Court disposed of the Rule by the impugned judgment. 

22. In the given backdrop, it is abundantly proved that Patta (Exhibit-Ka) adduced by the defendant No.12 is a false and fabricated document which did not confer a valid title on the defendant No.12, hence we are of the view that the defendant No.12 has not acquired any valid title on the basis of the said Patta. 

23. At this juncture, let us examine whether the plaintiff has been able to prove her possession in the suit land. On scrutiny of the record the plaintiff appears to claim that she possessed the suit land through one Jabi Ullah appointing him as Bargadar Said Jobi Ullah was examined as P.W.2, who deposed supporting the said claim of the plaintiff. P.W.4 also deposed supporting the possession of the plaintiff through her Bargadar Jobi Ullah. Therefore, we hold that the plaintiff has been able to prove her possession in the suit land. 

24. On the other hand, the defendant No.12 as D.W.1 stated in his deposition that after settlement his father cultivated the suit land and upon his demise the defendant No.12 got cultivated the suit land through Bargadar Defendant No.12 as D.W.1 stated in his cross-examination that his father got cultivated the suit land for last 20/21 years through one Abdul Quaiyum. Thereafter, the defendant appointed Abdus Sahid and Abdur Rahim as Bargadar in equal share for the period of 1973-74. The suit land is one piece in one plot. Abdus Sahid built house on the suit land 4/5 years after the year 1973. While D.Ws.2-3 stated in their depositions that Abdus Sahid and Abdur Rahim got Barga of the suit land since the year 1970. 

25. From the record it is seen that during appeal hearing the defendant No.12 filed 4(four) ground rent receipts in the lower appellate court and there were signatures of Ram Chandra on those receipts but on comparing those signature with the one in Patta the discrepancy is patent. On the other hand, the defendant No.12 stated in his written statement that he could not find the ground rent receipts of the suit land and could not file those in the trial Court. So, even for the sake of argument it is admitted that the defendant No.12 finding the ground rent receipts of the suit land filed those at the stage of appeal hearing, but on examination of those there is discrepancy of signature of Ram Chandra as stated in the preceding discussion. Therefore, those ground rent receipts do not carry any evidentiary value. 

26. Moreover, on scrutiny of the record there appears to be serious contradiction among the depositions of all D.Ws regarding the possession of the defendant No.12 and the identification of the same. In the premises above, we find that the possession of the defendant No.12 in the suit land is not proved. 

27. In view of the discussion made above, the title and possession of the plaintiff in the suit land is proved without controversy and the trial Court on proper appreciation of the relevant facts decreed the suit and the lower appellate Court also finding no anomaly upheld the judgment of the trial Court. 

28. On going through the impugned judgment and decree of the High Court Division it appears that the High Court Division reversed the judgments and decrees of the appellate Court as well as the trial Court without controverting the concurrent findings and observation made by those Courts. It is settled law that the appellate Court is the last Court of facts and in revisional jurisdiction, the High Court Division can only exercise its power if there is misreading and non- reading of evidence occasioning failure of justice. But the High Court Division while passing the impugned judgment could not show any lawful ground for its interference with the judgments of the lower appellate Court as well as the .trial Court. Rather, the High Court Division made out a third case which caused a serious miscarriage of justice. In view of the aforesaid reasons, the impugned judgment and decree of the High Court Division war-rants interference by this Division. We find merit in the submissions of the learned senior Counsel for the appellant. In the prevailing circumstances, the impugned judgment and decree of the High Court Division can-not stand at all in the eye of law. 

29. Accordingly, the instant Civil Appeal is allowed. 

30. The judgment and decree dated 21.05.2012 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 4805 of 2003 is set aside. 

End.
