case_source: (From the judgment and order dated 3rd day of July, 2014 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 3904 of 2007 and Civil Revision No. 4265 of 2007 respectively)
full_judgment:
M. Enayetur Rahim J. These 02(two) appeals, by leave are directed against the same judgment and order dated 03rd July, 2014 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No.3904 of 2007 and Civil Revision No.4265 of 2007 respectively making the Rule absolute. 

2. Since both the appeals have arisen out of the same property and parties are all most same and as such the appeals were heard analogously and being disposed of by this common judgment. 

Facts of the Civil Appeal No.436 of 2017: 
3. The present appellant as plaintiff instituted Other Class Suit No.33 of 1984 in the Court of Subordinate Judge, First Court, Mymensingh for declaration that the judgment and decree dated 27.11.1974 and 10.12.1974 respectively passed by the Munsif, 2nd Court, Sadar, Mymensingh in Other Class Suit No.86 of 1974 is null and void and also for cancellation of the registered deed No.11174 dated 14.07.1976 executed and registered through Court in Other Class Execution Case No.02 of 1976 and also for declaration of Title and recovery of possession in respect of the immovable property described in the schedule to the plaint. 

4. In the plaint it is averred, inter alia, that the suit land was owned by one Poranchand Churuleya and he used to run his jute business therein. He left for India in 1965 during the war between India and Pakistan. As a result, the suit land was declared as an enemy property by Gazette Notification under section 182 of the Defence of Pakistan Rules. Thereafter, the suit property was vested upon the Additional, Custodian of Enemy Property and he possessed the suit property through tenants. After the independence of Bangladesh, the suit property was newly named as special property. The Secretary, Ministry of Jute sold the said property on behalf of the Government to the plaintiff by a deed of sale bearing No.19943 dated 29.06.1974. The plaintiff possessed the suit land by opening a jute purchase center and through tenants since then. The Head Office of the plaintiff published a tender notice to sell the suit property and accepted the tender of the highest bidder. On 30.65.1981 defendant No.1 (present respondent No.1) unlawfully entered into the suit property. The plaintiff was 'informed for the first time upon receiving summons on 21.04.1982 that defendant No.1 filed Other Class Suit No. 390 of 1981 before the Court of 2nd Munsif, Mymensingh for perpetual injunction. In that suit defendant No.1 claimed the suit land on the strength of the impugned decree and registered deed. The Additional custodian of Enemy Property was not made party in that suit. Defendant No.1 obtained the impugned decree by practicing fraud for not implicating the additional custodian as a party. The plaintiff could have contested the suit, if he had been informed and notified. The defendant has no title and possession in the suit land and the plaintiff is in possession by way of purchase. If the impugned decree is in existence, the plaintiff will suffer irreparable loss. Hence, the suit. 

5. Defendant Nos.1 and 6 contested the suit by filing two separate written statements denying the material allegations made in the plaint. The contention in the written statements of defendant Nos.1 and 6 is that, the suit land was owned by Begraj Churuleya and R.O.R. Khatain also stood in his name. Begraj Churuleya offered to sell the land to defendant No.1 and he accepted the offer and accordingly he executed a bainapatra on 23.09.1963 and delivered possession of the suit land in favour of defendant No. l. Due to non-execution of Kabala, defendant No.1 filed Other Class Suit No.86 of 1974 for specific performance of contract. The suit was decreed on 27.11.1974. Defendant No.4 (Government of Bangladesh) of the instant suit also filed Other Class Suit No.388 of 1975 against defendant No.1 for setting aside the decree passed in Other Class Suit No.86 of 1974. The suit was dismissed on contest by the judgment and decree dated 31.05.1979 (decree signed on 07.06.1979). The plaintiff of that suit, i.e. Government filed Other Appeal No.206 of 1979 before the District Judge, Mymensingh against the said decree, and the appeal was also dismissed on 07.04.1981. The suit property was not declared as enemy property and the Government had no right to sell the said property. Defendant No.1 sold the suit property through two sale deeds dated 19.05.1984 and 21.05.1984 to defendant No.6 Feruja Begum, who has been possessing the suit property. Poran Chand was not the owner of suit property and there was no jute business and godown on the suit property. The plaintiff has no right and title in the suit land and the suit is liable to be dismissed. 

6. After hearing the parties and upon considering the evidence and materials on record, the then Subordinate Judge, First Court, Mymensingh, by his judgment and decree dated 28.02.1999 dismissed the suit. On appeal, by the plaintiff the Other Class Appeal No.114 of 1999 was allowed and the judgment and decree passed by the trial court was set aside. 

7. Being aggrieved, the defendants preferred Civil Revision No.390 of 2007 before the High Court Division and Rule was made absolute. Against the said judgment and order the plaintiff preferred civil petition for leave to appeal No.1 522 of 2015 before this Division, upon which leave was granted. 

Facts of Civil Appeal No.438 of 2017. 
8. The predecessor of the respondent Nos.1-8 as plaintiffs instituted Other Class Suit No.390 of 1982 the Court of Munsif, 2nd Court, Mymensingh for perpetual injunction in respect of suit property. 

9. Eventually, the said suit was transferred to the Court of Subordinate Judge, Mymensingh and renumbered as Other Class Suit No.12 of 1990. 

10. The plaintiffs contended, inter alia, that the suit land was owned by Begraj Churuleya and R.O.R. khatian was recorded in his name. Accordingly, he proposed to sell the land to the plaintiff and the plaintiff accepted the proposal and a bainapatra was executed on 23.09.1963 and possession of the suit land was delivered in favour of the plaintiff. Due to non-execution of kabala and failure to register the same by Begraj Churuleya, the plaintiff and others filed Other Class Suit No.86 of 1974 for specific performance of contract. The suit was decreed on 27.11.1974 and pursuant to the said decree in Execution Case No.2 of 1976, the plaintiff got deed of sale on 14.07.1976 through court. The Government of Bangladesh and Deputy Director of special property Division of the Ministry of Industry filed other suit No.388 of 1975 against the plaintiff for setting aside the decree passed in Other Class Suit No.86 of 1974. The suit was dismissed on contest by judgment and decree dated 31.05.1979. The plaintiffs of that suit filed other Appeal No.206 of 1979 before the District Judge, Mymensingh against the decree, and the appeal was also disallowed on 07.04.1981. There are two parts of holding No.107 and the disputed land was situated in the southern part of that holding. There is a jute godown in the Northern part of holding No.107. Defendant No.1 is in possession of that godown as lessee under the Government. The Government published as auction notice in the Daily Ittefaq to sell the suit land and Defendant No.1 participated in the said auction and that was accepted by Defendant No.2 on 25.08.1981. The plot number, Khatian number and area of the land were not mentioned in that auction notice. Only holding No.107 was mentioned in that notice. The plaintiff was informed from the employee of Defendant No.1 that defendant No.1 will dispossess the plaintiff because the suit land is a part of holding No. 107. The plaintiff will suffer irreparable loss, if Defendant No.1 dispossesses the plaintiff in connivance with other defendants. Hence plaintiff filed the suit. 

11. Defendant No.2 (Jute Trading Corporation) the present appellant con-tested the suit by filing a written statement denying the materials statement made in the plaint. It is contended, inter alia that, Poranchand Churuleya was the actual owner of the suit land and Poranchand Churuleya left this country in the year 1965 during India-Pakistan War. As a result, the suit land was declared as enemy property by Gazette Notification under section 182 of the Defence of Pakistan Rules. After the independence of Bangladesh the suit property was newly named as special property. The Government sold the said property to the contesting Defendant by a deed of sale bearing No.19943 dated 29.06.1974. The Defendant is in possession since then. Poranchand Churuleya neither sold the suit property nor did he execute any bainapatra. Though the plaintiff got a sale deed through court, but the deed is not effective upon the Defendant. The plaintiffs have no right and title in the disputed land and the suit is liable to be dismissed. The trial court dismissed the suit. Plaintiff preferred other Appeal No.104 of 1999 before the District Judge, Mymensingh, which was eventually heard by the Additional District and Sessions Judge, 2nd Court, Mymensingh and the appeal was dis-missed. Thereafter, plaintiff filed Civil Revision No.4265 of 2007 before the High Court Division and Rule was made absolute and thereby the suit was decreed. The defendant, present appellant preferred civil petition for leave to appeal No.1212 of 2016 before this Division and leave was granted. 

Submission on behalf of the appellants (in both the appeals): 
12. Mr. Sk. Md. Morshed, learned Additional Attorney General, appearing for the appellant in both the appeal submits that the courts bellow having concurrently found that the witness of the defendant is not a competent witness in view of the provision of Section 120 of the Evidence Act as he was deposed in the suit as an employee of the plaintiff without any power of attorney, but the learned judge of the High Court Division erred in law by making the Rule absolute without reversing those findings. 

13. He further submits that the appellate court upon considering the documents found that the defendant failed to produce bianapatra in support of his claim, thus the claim of acquiring title through bainapatra is not tenable in law, but the learned judge of the High Court Division erred in law by making the Rule absolute without setting aside those findings. By a Gazette Notification of 1967, the suit property having been vested upon the Jute Board, but in the Other Class Suit No.86 of 1974 or the subsequent Other Class Suit No.388 of 1975, the plaintiff was not impleaded in those suits, as such the present suit is maintainable by the plaintiff but the learned judge of the High Court Division erred in law by making the Rule absolute with a erroneous finding that in view of the earlier decree the present suit is not maintainable. 

14. Learned Additional Attorney General further submits that the appellate court being the final court of fact arrived at a finding that the defendant by practicing fraud upon the court has obtained decree in Other Class Suit. No.86 of 1974 but the learned judge of the High Court Division erred in law by making the Rule absolute without reversing those findings. 

Submission on behalf of the Respondents (in both the appeals): 
15. Mr. Probir Neogi, learned Senior Advocate with Mr. Minhajul Hoque Chowdhury, the learned Advocate appearing for the respondents in both the appeals submits that P. W. 1 was examined with leave of the trial court for adducing oral evidence on behalf of the plaintiff in Other Class Suit No.12 of 1990, all documents were exhibited by P.W-1 and he was duly cross-examined by the defendant at the time of trial and as such the evidence of P.W-1 could not be taken away on a mere technicality and as such the High Court Division rightly make the Rule absolute. 

16. Mr. Neogi further submits that the predecessor of respondents acquired title over the suit land by a deed of purchase being No.11174 dated 14.07.1976 executed and registered through Court by virtue of the judgment and decree passed in Other Class Suit No.86 of 1974 and there-after they took possession through Court vide Execution Case No.02 of 1976 and admittedly they are in possession of the suit land since 1976 and the title and possession of the predecessor of respondents was confirmed by the trial court in Other Class Suit No.388 of 1975 which was affirmed by the appellate court in Other Class Appeal No.206 of 1979 and considering those aspects bainapatra has lost its effect after execution of the deed of sale No.11174 dated 14.07.1976 and such the impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division is sustainable in law. 

17. Mr. Neogi further submits that the Title of the predecessor of the respondents was declared by a competent Court in Other Class Suit go.388 of 1975 which was filed by the predecessor of the present appellant and the said judgment was affirmed in Other Class Appeal No.206 of 1979 and that vital aspect was discussed elaborately by the High Court Division in the impugned judgment and the High Court Division righty hold that the instant suit is barred by the principle of res-judicata. Other Class Suit No.86 of 1974 was filed on 10.05.1974 and the Jute Trading Corporation claimed title of the suit land from the Government by a deed of purchase being no.19943 dated 29.06.1974 and considering the said aspect, the Jute Trading Corporation was neither proper nor necessary party of the said suit. 

18. Mr. Neogi further submits that the Jute Trading Corporation is claiming title of the suit property through Government, who filed Other Class Suit No.388 of 1975 against the plaintiff of that suit for setting aside the judgment and decree passed in Other Class Suit No.86 of 1974 and the said suit was dismissed on contest and the said judgment and decree was affirmed in Other Appeal No. 206 of 1979 and as such all findings and observations of that suit are binding upon the present appellant. 

19. Mr. Neogi lastly also submits that it was decided in Other Class Suit No.388 of 1975 and other Class Appeal No.206 of 1979 that the suit land of the instant suit is different from the land claimed by the appellant and that finding is final and binding upon the parties of that suit and their successors in interest; but both the courts below dismissed the suit without considering that vital aspects of law which was reversed by the High Curt Division lawfully and as such the impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division is sustainable in law. The predecessor of present respondents Firoja Begum mutated her name in S.A Khatian no.646 and paid rent regularly; Government acquired 13 decimals of land out of 25.50 decimals of land. from Firoja Khatum for Shombhugonj Sarak Bridge Project; vide L.A Case No.21/A(88-89); Firoja Begum filed Arbitration Case No.214 of 1989 in the Court of Arbitration Court, Mymensingh for proper compensation and she got the award of Tk.6,30,00/- by order dated 17.01.1999 and considering those aspects the original plaintiff has been recognized as tenant of the Government for the suit land; but both courts below dismissed the suit which was rightly reversed by the High Court Division. 

20. Heard the learned Advocates for the respective parties, perused the impugned judgment passed by the High Court Division as well as the judgment passed by the courts below, the evidence and other materials available on record. 

21. It transpires from the impugned judgment that the High Court Division dis-charged the rule on (Civil Revision No.1522 of 2015) holding that the plain-tiffs (present appellant) of Other Class Suit Na.33 of 1984 is barred by the principal of res-judicata. 

22. In this particular case Bangladesh Jute Trading Corporation as plaintiff filed the above suit for a declaration that the judgment and decree dated 27.11.1974 and decree signed on 10.12.1974 passed by the learned Munsif, 2nd Court, (Sadar) Mymensingh in O.C. Suit No.86 of 1974 is null and void and also for cancellation of the deed No.11174 dated 14.07.1976 executed and registered through court in Execution Case No.02 of 1976 and also for declaration of title and recovery of khas possession. 

23. It is the case of the plaintiff-appellant that the defendant of the said suit obtained the alleged decree for specific performance of contract ex-parte and got the deed execution on 14.07.1976 through Court. The said decree was fraudulent one. 

24. Having regard to the fact that the Government of Bangladesh and the Deputy Director, Special Properties Cell under the Ministry of Industries  Government of Bangladesh challenging the said ex-parte decree instituted other class suit No.388 of 1975 for setting aside the same. The said suit was dismissed on contest by the judgment and decree dated 31.05.1979 (decree signed on 07.06.1979) passed by the Munsif, 2nd Court, Sadar, Mymensingh and against the said judgment and decree the Government of Bangladesh and the Deputy Director, Special Property (Cell) under the Ministry of Industries preferred Other Appeal No.206 of 1979 before the District Judge, Mymensingh and upon hearing the said appeal, that was also dismissed by the judgment and decree dated 07.04.1981 (decree signed on 18.04.1981). Thereafter, no steps were taken by the Government against the judgment and decree. 

25. After long laps of time the Bangladesh Jute Trading Corporation, a Government Organization, the present appellant as a plaintiff filed Title Suit No.33 of 1984 challenging the judgment and decree passed in Other Class Suit No.86 of 1974 which was challenged by the Government in Other Class Suit No.388 of 1974. 

26. In the instant case the pertinent issue is that when previous Government instituted Other Class Suit No.388 of 1974 challenging the ex-parte decree passed in Other Class Suit No.86 of 1974 which was dis-missed and subsequently affirmed by the appellate court and the Government did not move before the higher forum, in such situation whether the present suit is maintainable or not. 

27. It is pertinent to mention here that Bangladesh Jute Corporation Ordinance, 1985 has been repealed by the Bangladesh Jute Corporation (Repeal Act 1993) and the asset and liability of the said corporation has been vested in the Government. 

28. Having considered the admitted fact that the other Class Stilt No.388 of 1974 filed by the Government. The Deputy Director, Special Property Cell under the Ministry of Industries, Government of Bangladesh was dismissed and thus on the same issue the suit filed by the Jute Trading Corporation, which has no existence at resent is not maintainable and the High Court Division as well as the trial Court upon elaborate discussion rightly observed that the suit is hit by the principal of res-judicata. 

29. It should be borne in mind that principle of res-judicata is intended not only to prevent a new decision, but also to prevent a new investigation so that the same per-son(s) cannot be harassed again and again in various proceedings upon the same question or issue. 

30. Section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure provides that no court shall try any suit or issue in which the matter directly and substantially in issue in a former suit between the same parties or between parties under whom they or any of them claim, litigating under the same title and the court has finally decided the matter. 

31. In the case of Syed Md. Shah Jalal Nure Alam and others Vs. Salimullah Chowdhury & others, 10 MLR(AD) 90; Rasheda Begum Vs. M.M. Nurussafa and others, 9 MLR(AD) 294; it has been decided by this Division that once an issue has been finally decided, it cannot be re-agitated between the same parties. 

32. It is admitted position that the predecessor of respondent's got possession of the suit land in execution of decree in Execution Case No. 02 of 1976 and the defendant's have been possessing and enjoying suit by paying rent to the Government and mutation has already been done. Further the Jute Trading Corporation, plaintiff of Other Class Suit No.33 of 1984 filed the said suit for recovery of possession in respect of the possession of immovable property, which proves the possession of the defendants. 

33. In view of the above, the High Court Division did not commit any error in making the Rule absolute in Civil Revision No.4265 of 2007 and thereby decreeing the Other Class Suit No.12 of 1990 for perpetual injunction. 

34. Thus, we do not find any merit in both the appeals. 

35. Accordingly, the both appeals are dis-missed without any order as to cost. 

End.

caseno: Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No.2870 of 2022
lawyer:
Mr. A. M Aminuddin, Attorney General with Mr Mohammad Saiful Alam, Assistant Attorney General, instructed by Mr Md. Helal Amin, Advocate-on-Record ------ For the Petitioners 
Mr M Sayed Ahmed, Senior Advocate with Mr. Mohammad Bakir Uddin Bhuiyan, Advocate instructed by Mr Zainul Abedin, Advocate-on-Record -------- for the Respondent
parties:
The Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh, represented by the Secretary, Ministry of Home Affairs, Bangladesh Secretariat Ramna, Dhaka-1000 and others --------- Petitioners
Vs.
Md. Abdul Bari --------- Respondent
case_source: (From the judgment and order dated the 16th day of September, 2021 passed by the High Court Division in Writ Petition No.10367 of 2017)
full_judgment:
Jahangir Hossain J. Delay of 337 days in filing this civil petition for leave to appeal is condoned. 

2. This civil petition for leave to appeal is directed against the judgment and order dated the 16th day of September, 2021 passed by the High Court Division in Writ Petition No.10367 of 2017 making the Rule absolute. 

3. The relevant facts for disposal of this petition, in brief, are that Md. Abdul Bari, writ-petitioner, joined the Police Department as Sub-Inspector of Police, on 20.12.1972 and thereafter, he was posted for training at Sardah Police Training Academy, Rajshahi. After completion of his training for a period of 6[six] months, he was posted in Kotwali Police Station, Mymensingh and continued his service as Sub-Inspector in the aforesaid Police Station. He discharged his duties at various Police Stations and was also posted as Officer-in-charge in Mohonganj Police Station, Mymensingh and from that Police Station, he was again transferred to the Police Line, Mymensingh. 

4. The Chief Martial Law Administrator [CMLA] declared Martial Law Order No. IX published in Bangladesh Gazette on Tuesday, April 6, 1982 and by dint of the Ordinance, he was dismissed from his service. Hence, he moved the High Court Division. 

5. No affidavit-in-opposition was filed by the writ-respondents to controvert the statements made in the writ petition. 

6. Upon hearing the parties, the learned Judges of the High Court Division made the Rule absolute directing the writ-respondents to pay the service benefits to the writ-petitioner to which he is entitled to upto the date on which he reached the age of superannuation, which he would have received, but for the unlawful dismissal. 

7. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the judgment and order dated 16.09.2021 passed by the High Court Division, the writ-respondents preferred this civil petition for leave to appeal before this Court. 

8. Mr. A. M. Aminuddin, learned Attorney General, appearing for the leave petitioners, submits that the High Court Division erred in law directing the writ-respondents to pay the service benefits which he is entitled to upto the date on which he reached the age of superannuation. He further submits that the High Court Division committed an error by ignoring the part of the ratio of Siddique Ahmed-Vs-Bangladesh, reported in 65 DLR (AD) 8 wherein it is stated that "Besides, all orders made, acts and things done, actions and proceedings taken and trials concluded, during the aforesaid period which are past and closed, are condoned on the age old maxim "salus populi est suprema lex", but provisionally. He further submits that the High Court Division committed an error without considering the impact of the judgment on public administration as it would create administrative anarchy and chaos in running the State. He adds that since the judgment and order would encourage others during the impugned period to come up with their rights to be established after a long 40[forty] years gap which would certainly put the incumbent Government under administrative pressure. He further adds that the High Court Division committed an error of law directing the writ-respondents to pay the service benefits to the writ-petitioner to which he is entitled to upto the date on which he reached the age of superannuation, which he would have received, but for the unlawful dismissal. He also added that if other claimants arise like the writ-petitioner, then on the basis of the impugned judgment and order, they all would seek financial benefit from the Government, then the Government would be under tremendous pressure to make up those amounts which would create economic anarchy in the Government and thus, the judgment and order dated 16.09.2021 is bad in law and hence, not tenable in the eye of law. 

9. Per Contra, Mr. M. Sayed Ahmed, Senior Advocate, appearing on behalf of the respondent, by supporting the impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division, contends that no legal procedures were maintained in dismissing the respondent by the authority and no show cause notice was served upon him before his dismissal. He further contends that the respondent was deprived of getting due monthly salary as well as service benefits after dismissal and the respondent was left empty handed and was forced to undergo to face this catastrophe. He further con-tends that by the judgment and order of the Appellate Division, human rights, fundamental rights, civil liberties, high ideal democracy etc. were protected and established and as such, the dismissal that was done under cover of order by the Martial Law Authority in 1982 was manifestly illegal and against fundamental rights. He finally contends that the respondent was dismissed under the regime of Martial Law without assigning any reason thereof, and simply, the dismissal order dated 23.12.1982 was forwarded to him, where-in, it appears that 74 Police Officers and employees have been removed from service without showing reason as referred to Memo No.P14M-61/82(1) MHA(Police-1)/1203 dated 23.12.1982. 

10. Heard the submissions of the learned Advocates for both the parties and perused the impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division along with connected documents on record. 

11. The claim of the writ-respondent-petitioners is that the Chief Martial Law Administrator was of opinion that the removal of a number of police personnel was necessary in the interest of Government. Therefore, in exercise of the powers conferred by Martial Law Order No.IX, the Chief Martial Law Administrator dismissed a good number of police personnel along with the writ-petitioner from the service with effect from 1st October, 1982. Against the afore-mentioned order, the respondent named Md. Abdul Hai as petitioner filed Writ Petition No.10367 of 2017 before the High Court Division challenging the letter under Memo No.P14M -61 /82(I)MHA (Police-I)/1203 dated 23.12.1982 issued by the Chief Martial Law Administrator, Ministry of Home Affairs, Police Section-I Martial Law Order No.IX dismissing the respondent from service with effect from the 1st day of October, 1982. It is stated that the learned Judges of the High Court Division failed to consider the impact of the judgment and order on public administration, and therefore, it would create administrative anarchy and chaos in running the State. It is also stated that the judgment and order of the High Court Division would encourage others who were prejudiced during the impugned period to come up with their rights to be established after a long 40 [forty] years gap which would put the incumbent Government under Administrate pressure. 

12. The contention of the respondent is that he is a freedom fighter and his retirement age is 60[sixty] years in the government service. He obtained training from Sarda Police Training Academy joining his service as freedom fighter. It is con-tended that had there been no martial law in the country, he would continue his respective job till retirement and would enjoy all emoluments and financial benefit per month and also their promotions would be considered according to entitlement and as a result of such catastrophe, the writ-petitioner has been deprived of all such benefits. It is enunciated that as per provision of Article 58(4) of the Constitution, all actions taken must be expressed to have been taken in the name of the President, but during the Martial Law, actions were done and all executive actions were taken in the name of the Chief Martial Administrator, which is also ultra vires the Constitution and as such, the respondent deserves to get all an-ear benefits and notional promotion, with actual pecuniary benefits, upto the date 13.12.2008 on which he would have reached the age of retirement otherwise the respondent would be highly prejudiced. 

13. The High Court Division observed that Latter No.P14M-61/82(1)MHA(Pol ice-1)11203 dated. 23.12.1982 passed by the Chief Martial Law Administrator is declared to have been made without any lawful authority and is of no legal effect. The learned Judges of the High Court Division directed the writ-respondents to pay the service benefits to the writ-petitioner to which he is entitled to upto the date on which he reached the age of superannuation, which he would have received, but for the unlawful dismissal. 

14. In the case of Miss Asma Jilani -Vs- the Government of the Punjab and another PLD 1972 SC 139 Pakistan Supreme court condoned all transactions that took place during Martial Law period as being past and closed transactions since no useful purpose can be served by re-opening them. In the case of Sind High Court Bar Association-Vs-Federation of Pakistan PLD 2009 SC 879, Supreme Court of Pakistan held that on the principle of past and closed transactions, only those acts which were required to be done for the ordinary orderly running of the state could be protected. In that case, it was also held that only such past and closed transactions could have been protected, which were otherwise not illegal at the relevant time, and rights, privileges, obligations or liabilities had been acquired, accrued or incurred, or any investigation, legal proceeding or remedy in respect of any such right, privilege, obligation, liability, penalty, forfeiture or punishment had taken place. 

15. In the case of Khondker Delmar Hossain and others-Vs-Bangladesh Italian Marble Works Ltd. and others [18 BLT (AD) 2010 page 329], all executive acts, things and deeds done and actions taken during the period from the 15th August, 1975 to the 9th April, 1979 which were past and closed and all routine works done during the above period which even the lawful government could have done were condoned by the Appellate Division. In the case of Siddique Ahmed-Vs-Government of Bangladesh and others, reported in 65 DLR (AD) 8, the Appellate Division provisionally condoned the orders, acts, actions, transactions, proceedings etc. that took place during the period of Martial Law from 24 March 1982 to 11 November 1986 as past and closed transactions on the age old maxim 'salus populi est suprema lex' on the ground of their practical impact on the overall administration of the country. In this case it was also decided that since the condonations of orders, acts, actions and proceedings etc. are allowed only provisionally, the court, if moved, can in a proper case, look into the allegations on a case to case basis. The High Court Division did not separately assign well founded reasoning for its decision in the instant case rather delivered judgment comparing the facts, circumstances and decisions of the writ petition No.696 of 2010 and Writ Petition No.421 of 2012 with those of the instant case. The administrative action that was taken against the respondent vide Memo No.P14M-61/82(1)MHA(Police-1)/1203 dated 23.12.1982 in the context of the circumstances prevailing at that time appears to be a past and closed transaction and there-fore, it should not have been mechanically re-opened after around 35 years. The re-opening of past and closed transaction on general basis is against the mandate of the judgment delivered in Siddique Ahmed-Vs-Government of Bangladesh (supra) and has the utmost likelihood of quagmire in the smooth running of the administration. The High Court Division did not consider this aspect of the case and thereby, made error of law in making the Rule absolute. 

16. Having considered all the aspects and discussions made above, we are constrained to hold that the writ-petition filed by the writ-petitioner was not maintainable. Therefore, we find merit in the present leave petition. However, it is better to dispose of the same without granting leave as the writ petition was not maintainable. 

17. Accordingly, this petition is disposed of. The judgment and order dated 16.09.2021 passed by the High Court Division is, hereby, set aside. 

End.

lawyer:
Ms. Sayeda Nasrin, Advocate instructed by Syed Mahbubar Rahman, Advocate-on-Record. ------ For the Appellant 
Mr. Shahidul Inslam, Advocate instructed by Mr. Zainul Abedin, Advocate-on-Record -------- For Respondent No.1 
For Respondent No. 1 --------- None represented
parties:
Proddut Kumar Das ------- Appellant
Vs.
A Rashid Howlader and others --------- Respondents
case_source: (From the judgment and decree dated the 27th day of April, 2015 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 2077 of 2006)
full_judgment:
Jahangir Hossain J. This civil appeal, by leave, is directed against the judgment and decree dated the 27" day of April, 2015 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 2077 of 2006 making the Rule absolute. 

2. The facts, relevant for disposal of this civil appeal, in short, are that the plaintiffs [hereinafter referred to as the appellants] instituted Title Suit No.43 of 1993 in the Court Assistant Judge, Amtoli, Borguna for declaration of the title and recovery of khas possession stating, inter alia, that the suit land originally belonged to one Abdus Sattar and others. The suit land was sold in auction and the same was purchased by plaintiff No.3 on 30.06.1986 who sold out 6 decimals of land to plaintiff No.1 on 14.02.1987 by registered deed. Plaintiff Nos.1 and 3 have been possessing the same by mutating their names in the khatian and paying rent to the Government. Plaintiff No.2 took settlement of 10 decimals of land from plot Nos.921 and 934 recorded in khas khatian No.1 registered by kabuliat dated 12.11.1986 from the Government. In this way, the plaintiffs became the owners of 22 decimals of land. On the 11th day of Falgoon, 1396 B.S. defendant No.1 dispossessed the plaintiffs from the suit land. The plaintiffs requested defendant No.1 to vacate the land, but he did not pay any heed. Hence, the plaintiffs instituted the suit. 

3. Defendant No.1 contested the suit by filing written statement denying the material allegation contending, inter alia, that the suit land appertaining to PS Khatian No.4 of Mouza-Amtoli originally belonged to one Zaminder Zadunath Saha Chowdhury and others who settled 1.81 acres of land to their tenants and kept 1.47 acres of land in their khas possession. One Sukh Lai Saha and others were the owners of the land of PS Khatin No.7 and they settled 2.93 acres of land to the tenants and kept 2.59 acres of land in their khas possession. Zadunath Saha and others through their Naeb Shailendra Nath Sahaettled the land to one Tazem Ali Howlader, the predecessor of defendant No.l. Shailendra Nath executed a salami receipt on 5 Baishakh, 1359 BS on behalf of the Zamindars receiving taka 100 as salami from Tazem Ali Howladar. Tazem All Howlader erected dwelling homestead and planted trees etc in the said land. In this way, his father had been a tenant under the Zamindar with regard to 66 decimals of land including the disputed land and thereafter, on 15.01.1960 his father orally gifted him the disputed land by delivering possession. Defendant No.1 has been possessing the disputed land since 1960. During revisional survey 1.87 acres of land of PS khatian Nos.4, 7, and 12 including the 66 decimals of land which were given pattan to his father Tazem Ali Howladar was wrongly recorded in Hal Plot No.934 of Khatian No.1 in the name of Government. The plaintiffs have had no right, title, interest and possession in the suit land. 

4. During trial, plaintiff No.3 examined himself with two other witnesses and defendant No.1 examined himself with two other witnesses. They produced documents which are marked as exhibit Nos. 1-7 series and exhibit Nos. Ka' series-'Cha'-series. 

5. The learned Judge of the trial Court framed six issues and heard both the parties and decreed the suit. 

6. Against the judgment and decree of the trial Court, the defendant-respondents preferred Title Appeal No.19 of 2004 before the District Judge, Barguna. The appeal was transferred to the Joint District Judge, 2nd Court, Barguna who heard appeal and affirmed the judgment and decree of the Subordinate Court. 

7. Being aggrieved by the judgment and decree of the Court of Appeal below, defendant-Abdur Rashid Howlader, preferred Civil. Revision No.2077 of 2006 before the High Court Division. The learned Judge of the Single Bench of the High Court Division by the impugned judgment and order made the Rule absolute setting aside the judgment and decree of the Appellate Court. 

8. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division, the plaintiff-appellant filed the instant civil appeal arisen out of Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No.2738 of 2015. 

9. Ms. Sayeda Nasrin, learned Advocate, appearing for the appellant, submits that the suit land was recorded in the name of the Government under khas khatian No.1 during SA operation and it vested in the Government and thereafter, the Government settled the suit land in favour of plaintiff Nos.1 and 2 by registered kabuliat vide Certificate Case No.827 of 1980-81 and Lease Case No.02 of AM-1985-86 and thereafter, they mutated their names and paid rent to the Government for the suit land. She further submits that the appellant got settlement of the suit land from the Government by registered kabuliat and got physical possession from the Government and this fact was proved by the plaintiffs by producing both documentary and oral evidence. She further submits that both the Courts below con-currently found the title and possession of the plaintiffs in the suit land pursuant to the settlement case and certificate case and delivery of possession was given by the Government and the concurrent findings of fact as arrived at by both the Courts below are based on material evidence on record. It is finally submitted that there was no misreading or non-consideration of the material evidence on record and the concurrent findings of fact of both the Courts below cannot be interfered by the High Court Division in revisional jurisdiction. 

10. Per contra, Mr. Shahidul Islam, learned Advocate, appearing on behalf of respondent No.1, contends that the plaintiff-appellant totally failed to prove his title and possession in the suit land within 12 years of institution of the suit. He further contends that the fact of settlement allegedly granted by the Additional Deputy Commissioner, Barguna in favour of the plaintiffs father vide exhibit-2[Certified copy of Kabuliat dated 12.11.1986] having not proved and allegedly having granted settlement for an unspecified area of .07 decimals out of 1.87 acres of land of Plot No.934, the suit for declaration of title and recovery of khas possession was not tenable in Law. He adds that exhibit-3[Certified copy of Boinama of Certificate Case No.827 of 1980-81 and dakhalnama] cannot be construed to be a document of handing over possession in favour of the plaintiff upon an unspecified 07 decimals of land out of 1.87 acres of land when the defendants' two storied dwelling house has been constructed upon a part of Plot No.934. He further contends that Pw-1, in his cross-examination, deposed that 'আমাদের settlement দেয়ার অর্থ দখল দেয়া। যে তারেখেই settlement দেয়া সেই তারিখেই Surveyor আমাদের মেপে জমি বুঝিয়ে দিয়ে আসে।' It is an evidence on oath which clearly disclosed that the plaintiffs have instituted the suit for recovery of khas possession followed by dispossession being out of possession and was not maintainable. He further contends that the evidence adduced by Dw-1 proved it beyond doubt that the defendant has been possessing his homestead, constructed upon a part of the suit plot continuously since 1960. He finally contends that there is no evidence in support of handing over possession in favour of the plaintiffs in the suit land within period from 30.06.1986 to 14.02.1987 and the settlement from the Government dated 12.11.1986 having not proved, the evidence on record proved it beyond doubt that the plaintiffs instituted the suit being out of possession. 

11. Heard the contentions of learned Advocates for both the parties and perused the relevant materials and other connected papers along with the judgment and decree of the high Court Division on record. 

12. The claim of the plaintiff-appellants is that they are the owners of the land by Nilam purchase and by purchasing with consideration money vide registered kabala and kabuliyat from the owners of the land, i.e. from the Government as khas land lease and they possessed the land. Devastating Tornedo and flood washed away their house, so the land remained vacant. When WAPDA cut mud from there, a ditch was made therein where the defendant erected houses illegally, forcibly dispossessing the plaintiffs from 'Ka' scheduled land on 11 Falgoon, 1396 BS. A local salish was held wherein the defendants admitted that they would hand over possession. The land in question has properly been recorded in the name of the plaintiffs when the defendant has failed to mutate his name and his rather also failed to mutate his name in the disputed khatian. The plaintiffs claimed that they have been able to prove their right, title and interest in the suit land by producing parchas, boinama, dakhalnama, kabuliyat, rent receipts which are public documents. In support of their contention, they cited the cases: Brahma Nand Puri-Vs-Neki Puri, reported in AIR1965SC1506 and Vijay Pullarwar-Vs-Shri Hanuman Deostan, (2019)11SCC718. 

13. On the other hand, the defendant-respondents claim that their predecessor, Tazem Ali Hawlader got pattan of 39 decimals of land of P.S. Plot No.42 under P.S. Khatian No.4 and 27 decimals of land of P.S. Plot No.42 under P.S. Khatian No.7, i.e. total 66 decimals of land from Lakhmikol Barobari Estate through a Naeb on 5 Baishak, 1359 vide printed receipt of the Estate for taka 100'00 as appropriate salami and got dakhila on 15.08.1960 BS by paying taka 26 as rent. Said Tazem Ali Hawlader gifted the said land orally to defendant No.1 and since then he has been possessing the land erecting house and planting trees and digging a pond nursing fish therein. The plaintiffs have got no title and possession in the suit land. In deposition, defendant No.1 also stated that his father on 15'" January, 1960 orally gifted him 66 decimals of land. At that time, all the heirs of his father were present. The cyclone blown on April, 1961 destroyed his homestead and he re-built the same by his own expense. 

14. Defendant No.1 also claimed that during Revisional Survey operation, 26 decimals of land of P.S.Khatian Nos.4, 7 and 12 is neither recorded in the name of any landlord nor in any other name at all, but recorded in the names of Amrita Lal, Abdul Aziz and others, Kali Bilash and Keshab Lal and others in S.A. Khatian Nos.22/261/411 and 427 correctly. 1'87 acres of land of PS Khatian Nos.4, 7 and 12 including the 66 decimals of land which were given pattan to his father, Tazem Ali Hawlader wrongly recorded in Hal Plot No.934 of Khatian No. 1 in the name of Government. Having taken the opportunity of the wrong record, the Revenue Officer of Amtali Upazila declared for pattan on 01.11.1393 B.S. and to save the possession of defendant No.1, he filed Title Suit No. 34 of 1987 in the Court of Senior Assistant Judge and on transfer, it was renumbered as Title Suit No.8 of 1992 which was heard and dis-missed on 15.08.1992 by the learned Assistant Judge, Bamna Upazila, Borguna. Against the judgment and order, defendant No.1 preferred Title Appeal No.56 of 1992 in the Court of District Judge, Borguna which is still pending. 

15. The claim of title and possession to the suit land has two dimensions. The plain-tiffs claim title and possession followed by dispossession from the suit land, on the basis of auction purchase, boinama, dhakhalnama, sale deed and lease from the Government in pursuance of settlement case and kabuliayat. Conversely, defendant No.1 claims title and possession to the suit land on the basis of Salami receipt, rent receipts and oral gift from his father Tazem Ali Hawlader. The burden of proof as per Sections 101 and 102 of the Evidence Act, 1872 primarily rests upon the plaintiffs to prove their claims. Rules 1 and 2 of Order-XVIII of the Civil Procedure Code, 1908 also provides that the plaintiff has right to begin and shall produce his evidence in support of the issues which he is bound to prove. 
Thereafter, the other party shall produce his evidence. 

16. On perusal of the documents on record, it appears that 12 decimals of land of Plot No.935 of SA Khatian No.789 under Amtalimouza belong to Abdus Sattar, Birendra Bijoy Das and others. The aforesaid land was auctioned on 30.06.1986 and plaintiff No. 3 purchased the same. On 14.02.1987, plaintiff No.3 by a registered deed of sale transferred six decimals of land of Plot No.935 to plain-tiff No. l. Plaintiff Nos.3 and 1 mutated their names. Bijendra Bijoy Das, father of plaintiff No.3 achieved pattan of 3 decimals of land of Plot No.921 and 7 decimals of land of Plot No.934 in total 10 decimals of land from khas khatian No.1 of the Government through Settlement Case No.2(Am) of 1985-86. A Kabuliyat deed was registered on 12.11.1986 after having salami of taka 1750 and a new khatian No. 1326 was created in the name of Birendra Bijoy Das. The plaintiffs exhibited original parcha of SA khatian No.1326, certified copy of Kabuliyat dated 12.1.1.1986, the boinama and dakhalnama of certificate case No. 827(Am) of 1980-81, DCR of payment of salami taka 1.750 dated 10.11.1986, certified copy of SA Khatian No.789 and certified copies of order sheet of Settlement Case No.2(Am)/ 85-86.In the instant suit, the plaintiffs have produced documentary evidence, most of which are public in nature, regarding their title to the suit land. They also produced documentary evidence dhakhalnama and rent receipts in support of their possession to the suit land before dispossession. Simultaneously, they produced oral evidence in support of their title and possession followed by dispossession from the suit land. It appears that Pw-1 consistently deposed in support of the plaint that they took possession of the suit land in accordance with certificate case, boinama, dakhalnama, sale deed, and kabuliyat but on 23'02/1990 corresponding to 11 Falgoon, 1396 B.E. Defendant No.1 dispossessed them from the suit lard by force. Pw-1 did not depose contrary to his statement during cross-examination. Pw-2 and Pw-3 duly corroborated the testimony of Pw-1 regarding the plaintiffs' title and possession (before dispossession) to the suit land. It appears that Pw-2 materially corroborated the testimony of Pw-1 to the effect that on 11 Falgoon, 1396 B.S. defendant No.1 dispossessed the plaintiffs from the suit land. Likewise, Pw-3 substantially corroborated the testimony of Pw-1 that during 1396 B.S. defendant no 1 dispossessed the plaintiffs from the suit land. It appears that the plaintiffs have primarily been able to prove their title and possession (before dispossession) to the suit land and they have discharged their initial burden of proof. Now it is the turn of defendant No.1 to discharge his onus of proof. In terms of Section 102 of the Evidence act, 1872, the initial onus to prove its claim is always on the plaintiff and if he discharges that onus and makes out a case which entitles him to a relief, the onus shifts to the defendant to prove these circumstances, if any, which would disentitle the plaintiff to the same [Bharat Alumnium Co.-V- Maharashtra Alumnium Co., 2009 DLT 489]. In a suit for possession based on title once the plaintiff has been able to create a high degree of probability so as to shift the onus on the defendant, it is for the defendant to discharge his onus and in the absence thereof, the burden of proof lying on the plaintiff shall be held to have been discharged so as to amount to proof of the plaintiffs title [R. V. E. Venkatachala Gounder -V- Arulmigu Viswesaraswaini and V. P. Temple, AIR 2003 SC 4548]. Let us have an overview of the defendant's case to see defendant No.1 has been able to discharge his onus of proof. 

17. The disputed land is presently situated at Amtali Upazila of Borguna District which was formerly included in the subdivision of Patuakhali. Defendant No.1 in support of his title to the suit land produced an unregistered salami receipt dated 5 Baishakh, 1359. BS and Dakhila dated 15.08.1360 BS. The trial Court and the Appellate Court were of the view that at date of execution of the salami receipts on 5 Baishakh, 1359 BS corresponding to 18th April 1952 AD Zamindari system was not prevalent because of the coming into force of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 (hereinafter referred to as the SAT Act) and, therefore, Zamindars had no right to give pattan of their land at that time. But the High Court Division took a different view on the point of coming into force of Part-V of the SAT Act stating that Part-V of this Act came into force in the Sub-Division of Patuakhali on 5th August, 1954 AD. The view taken by the High Court Division on the point of coming into force of Part-V of the SAT Act appears to be correct since Part-V of the SAT Act came into force in entire area of Patuakhali Sub-Division of the District of Bakcrganj with effect from the date of publication of the notification in the Dacca Gazette, vide Notification No.9918-LR., date 8th July 1954, published in the Decca Gazette, date 5th August, 1954, Part-I, p. 890 (SAT ACT DLR by Obaidul Huq Chowdhury, Fifth Edition-2015, page 242- 243].Hence, in the Subdivision of Patuakhali Zamindars had right to give pattan of their land by receiving salami before 5th August, 1954. But the question pertaining to this case is whether Naeb Shailendra Nath Saha executing the salami receipt on behalf of the Zamindars gave the same to the father of defendant No.1, Tazem Ali Hawlader and delivered possession of the suit land to him or not? The salami receipts and rent receipts were marked as exhibits with objection. Salami receipt and dakhila are private documents and those will not be admissible in evidence as genuine documents on the mere production of the same. The genuineness of the salami receipt has to be determined in the light of the facts and circumstances of the instant case. The Appellate Court held that the salami receipt/lease document is not genuine itself since it is rubbed and has cut marks and the back page of it is covered by white paper. This view of the Appellate Court regarding the title document of defendant No.1 seems to be based on proper appreciation of the documentary evidence on record in the light of the facts and circumstances of the instant case. In the case of Ajufannessa @ AjiBibi and others-Vs-Safar Miah and others, 30 D.L.R (AD) 41 it was held that "A private document can-not be taken notice of and marked as an Exhibit without any formal proof, unless the requirement of such proof is waived by the opposing party. The marking of the said document as an exhibit may, however, give rise to a belief that it bears the writing or signature of a person, as has been deposed to by the witness who proves the said document. The question as to whether the document is a genuine one or it represents the true state of affairs is a question of fact which is to be decided by the Court concerned in the light of the facts and circumstances of the case. There is no legal presumption which the Court is bound to make in respect of such a document. There is no such law as requires a Court to presume that a rent receipt purported to be granted by a landlord in favour of a certain person is genuine and what has been written in such a rent receipt are true. In this case, both of the courts of fact have decided the question of genuineness of the disputed rent receipts in the light of the facts and circumstances of the case and have also examined their various features with reference to the surrounding facts and came to the definite finding as to their spurious character. Such a finding is binding upon the High Court in a Second Appeal unless it could be shown that the said finding had been vitiated by an error of law or procedure which had affected the merits of the case." The ratio of this case was again reiterated in the case of Md. Jashimuddins Kanchan -Vs- Md. Ali Ashraf (42 DLR (AD) 289]. The High Court Division did not reverse this finding of the Appellate Court that the genuineness of the salami receipt is highly doubtful. Since the tide document of the father of defendant No.1 is highly doubtful, subsequent transfer of the same property to defendant No.1 by oral gift is also doubtful. Defendant No.1 claimed that during 1961 his house at the disputed land was destroyed by cyclone for which he repaired the same with his own expense. But he deposed,  “১৯৬১ সালে আমি ৬ষ্ঠ শ্রেণীতে পড়তাম। তখন আমার ব্যক্তিগত আয়ের উৎস ছিলনা।" This portion of the deposition of Dv-1 suggests that the claim of defendant No.1 regarding his possession of the suit property from 1960 onward is apparently baseless. It appears that father of defendant No.1 and thereafter, defendant No.1 did not take any time worthy step whatsoever for correction of the record of rights. The possession of the defendant No.1 in the suit land cannot be traced back to any valid title whereas the possession (before dispossession) of the plaintiffs in the suit land can be traced back to valid title which coupled with attending facts and circumstances reasonably gives rise to the presumption that the plaintiffs were dispossessed from the suit land by defendant No.1 by force. 

19. Upon perusal of the Judgment of the High Court Division it appears that the High Court Division on erroneous belief decided the case keeping in view of section-9 of the Specific Relief Act, 1877. But the pleadings of the parties clearly indicate that this case is brought under section-8 of the Specific Relief Act, 1877 read with Article 142 of schedule-1 to the Limitation Act, 1908 and, therefore, the plaintiffs case file the suit for recovery of possession within 12 years from the date of dispossession. The finding by the High Court Division to the effect that the notice by the government to defendant No.1 to vacate possession cast a substantial doubt in believing the plaintiffs' case does not seem to be correct since possession of defendant No.1 can never be adverse to the government without defendant No. 1 is 60 years continuous adverse possession as per article 149 of schedule-1 of the Limitation Act, 1908 which is absent in the present case. 18. The trial Court as well as the Appellate Court arrived at concurrent finding that the plaintiffs have been able to prove their title and possession following by dispossession from the suit land. It appears that the findings of the trial court as well as the Appellate Court are based on the proper appreciation of evidence on record both oral and documentary. It is well settled position in law that under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure, the High Court cannot re-appreciate the evidence and cannot set aside the concurrent findings of the Courts below by taking a different view of the evidence. The High Court is empowered only to interfere with the findings of fact if the findings are per-verse or there has been a non-appreciation or non-consideration of the material evidence on record by the Courts below. Simply because another view of the evidence may be taken is no ground by the High Court to interfere in its revisional jurisdiction [Masjid Kacha Tank, Nahan-Vs-Tuffail Mohammed, AIR 1991 SC 455]. The civil cases are decided on the basis of preponderance of probability. Civil cases are decided on the basis of pre-ponderance of evidence while in a criminal case the entire burden lies on the prosecution and proof beyond reasonable doubt has to be given [Vishnu Dutt Sharma-V-Daya Sapra 13 SCC (2009) page 729]. In view of the facts, circumstances and proposition of law discussed above, we are of the view that the preponderance of probability regarding title and possession (before dispossession) of the plaintiffs to the suit land is clearly in favour of the plaintiffs and, therefore, the High Court Division made serious error of law in making the rule absolute which occasioned failure of justice. 

20. The present appeal is allowed without any order as to costs. 

21. Accordingly, the judgment and order dated 27.04.2015 passed by the High Court Division is, hereby, set aside. 

End.

Mrs. Samira Tarannum Rabeya, DAG instructed by Mr Md. Helal Amin, Advocate-on-Record ------- For the Appellant

Vs.
Tenu Miah Tofader and others ------- Respondents
case_source: (From the judgment and order dated 13.02.2008 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 4626 of 2004)
full_judgment:
Md. Ashfaqul Islam J. This civil appeal by leave is directed against the judgment and order dated 13.02.2008 passed by a single Bench of the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 4626 of 2004 making the Rule absolute. 

2. The present respondent and 24 others as plaintiffs instituted Title Suit No. 4 of 1998 in the court of Senior Assistant Judge, Balalgonj, Sylhet for declaration of title in respect of land of the 1st schedule of the plaint being the part of the 2nd schedule land. 

3. The facts of the original suit in brief are that the 1st and 2nd schedule land of the plaint attracts Taluk No. 367804 Monihar Khan, Thak Survey Chok No. 113 and Taluk No. 36514 Rushon Mohammad, Thak Survey Chok No 113 and the predecessors of the plaintiff and pro-forma defendants Monohar Khan and Rushon Mohammad were the Talukders and owners of the aforesaid two taluks and as such, they were in possession in the suit land as their home-stead land and subsequently they died leaving behind heirs and the plaintiffs and pro-forma defendants are not in exclusive possession in the 1st and 2nd schedule land of the plaint. That the 1st Schedule land of the plaint is the drain type of land and all the waters of the 2nd schedule land passes through the 1st schedule 4trAt1fft and in the rainy season the plaintiffs and the pro-forma defendants cross the 1st schedule land by boat and thus, they use their homestead land which are now situated in both the sides of the 1st schedule land. That at the time of last settlement and survey operation the 1st schedule land of the plaint wrongly recorded in the name of the Government as omit-V. That the plaintiffs could not know earlier regarding the aforesaid wrong record. That in the middle part of the March, 1998 defendant Nos. 1 and 2 raised a claim asserting that the 1st schedule land of the plaint is the land of the Government and they wanted to demarcate and separate the 1st schedule land from the 2nd schedule land of the plaint then the plaintiff started searching to trace out the real problem and they collected the mouza map and came to know that the 1st schedule land has been recorded in the name of the Government. Then the plaintiffs finding no other alternative filed the suit and they prayed that the suit should be decreed. 

4. The defendant Nos. 1 and 3, government contested the suit contending that the suit filed by the plaintiffs is not maintainable, barred by limitation, estoppel, waiver and acquiescence. That the 1st schedule land of the plaint is the khas land of the Government and as such, S.A. record has rightly been prepared the name of the Government as গোপাট type of land. That the 1st schedule land of the plaint is being used by the local people as a গোপাট and the aforesaid 1st schedule land is the only way of the local people through which they go to the nearest Haor. That the plaintiffs and proforma defendants have or had no right, title and interest in the 1" schedule land of the plaint. And they are trying to grab the 1st schedule land and as such, on behalf of the local people one Kazi Mokbul Hossain filed an application before the defendants for demarcating and separating the same from the 2nd schedule land of the plaint. That on 06.05.1998 a date was fixed for demarcation of the same but due to non-cooperation of the plaintiffs the date was shifted and on 20.05.1998 it was fixed for demarcation but the plaintiff created obstruction hence the 1st schedule land of the plaint has not yet been demarcated. The defendants therefore, prayed the suit to be dismissed. 

5. On conclusion of the trial, the learned Senior Assistant Judge, balalgonj, Sylhet by his judgment and order dated 24.11.2002 decreed the suit in part. 

6. Against the said decision the defendants as appellant filed Title Appeal No. 51 of 2003 before the additional district Judge, 1st court, Sylhet and the appellate court reversed the judgment of the trial court by dismissing the suit. 

7. Feeling aggrieved by the judgment of the court of appeal below the plaintiffs preferred Civil Revision No. 4626 of 2004 before the High Court Division and the High Court Division by the impugned judgment and order dated 13.02.2008 made the Rule absolute reversing the decision of the lower appellate court by setting aside the judgment passed by it and restored the decision of the trial court. 

8. Thereafter, the defendants preferred Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 1061 of 2008 before this Division and obtained leave giving rise to this appeal. 

9. Leave was granted to consider the point whether the High Court Division was justified in holding that the land in question is a government land and misdirected itself in reversing the lower appellate court's decision on an erroneous findings. 

10. Mrs. Samira Tarannum Rabeya, the learned Deputy Attorney General, has submitted that the learned additional district judge having came to the finding on a consideration of the evidence and the circumstances of the case that the 1st schedule land of the plaint is the khas land of the government and as such S.A record had rightly prepared in the name of the government as গোপাট type of land. That the schedule of the plaint is being used by the local people as গোপাট and aforesaid 1st schedule land is only way of the local people by which they go to nearest Haor. The plaintiffs and proforma defendants have or had no right title and interest in the 1st schedule land of the pliant. The land in question, as she submits, as it would borne by the evidence on record and was exhibited and reflected in the report of the inquiry commission, is not only a government land but a khal treating the same, as khas land and the high Court Division ought to have considered in its findings and decision upon adverting the same and thus occasioned an error of law causing failure of justice. 

11. No one represents the respondents. 

12. Heard the learned Advocate for the appellant. Perused the papers/documents contained in the paper book. 

13. Admittedly, the suit for deceleration which was filed before the trial court was decreed in part declaring plaintiffs right, title and interest over 0.27 acre of land from taluk No. 36514 appertaining to Daag No. 1035 of the 1st schedule of land. On the contrary it is the positive findings of the lower appellate court that the land in question has been recorded in the S.A record in the name of the government as গোপাট. The relevant portion of the judgment passed by the lower appellate court on this score is quoted below: 
কেননা স্বীকৃত মতে নাঃ জমি এস, এ রেকর্ডে সরকারের নামে গোপাট উল্লেখে রেকর্ড হওয়া সত্ত্বেও ১৯৯৮ সনের কথিত কাল্পনিক cause of action উল্লেখে অত্র মোকদ্দমা আনায়ন করা হইয়াছে। অথচ বাদী নাঃ জমি তাহার বাড়ীর চতুসীমানার বারখালা মর্মে নিজ ভূমি বলিয়া দাবী করেন।

বিবাদী আপীলকারী সরকার পক্ষে দাখিলী মৌজা ম্যাপগুলি হইতেও দেখা যায় যে, নাঃ গোপাটটি শুধু বাদীর বাড়ীর চতুঃসীমানা ঘিরে নাই, বরং উহা মৌজা ম্যাপটিকে আড়া- আড়ি ভাবে মধ্যখান দিয়া ক্রস করিয়া বহুদুর পর্যন্ত গিয়াছে। তেমনি উভয় পক্ষের দাখিলী এস, এ রেকর্ডের খতিয়ানেও নাঃ ভূমি গোপাট হিসাবে যথাক্রমে মৌজা সাহেবাগ (জে,এল, নং ১৬০) এর ২৫টি দাগ এবং মৌজা শরীফ নগর (জে,এল, নং ১৭১) এর ১১টি দাগ জুড়িয়া নালিশী গোপাটটি অবস্থিত।

14. Nowhere in the judgment of trial court we could find a positive assertion or clarification why a property that has been recorded after a long laps of time as গোপাট turned into a বারখালা. There is no evidence except advocate commissioner report having no positive assertion to that effect and which also cannot be treated as a substantive or a conclusive evidence. The Court is required to consider such report in the light of other evidence that may be given by the contesting parties. But in the instant case, as it has been well founded by the court of appeal being the last court of fact that point this of issue could not be disproved by the trial court. 

15. Further as to the record of rights it is to be quoted profitably Section 144(A) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act which was inserted after, Section 144 of the Act by East Pakistan ordinance VIII of 1967. Section 144A Provides: 
"144A. Every entry in a record-of-rights prepared or revised under section 144 shall be evidence of the matter referred to in such entry, and shall be presumed to be correct until it is proved by evidence to be incorrect." 

16. If we glean the said provision it transpires that a finally published record of rights revised under Section 144(A) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act has a presumption of correctness and that presumption continues till it is otherwise rebutted by a reliable evidence. This proposition of law is well settled. The oldest record of rights being the cadastral survey prepared under section 103(B)(5) of the Bengal Tenancy Act (Act No. VIII of 1885) also got a high presumptive value as to correctness of entries therein as it has also been enjoined under section 144(A) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. Of course this is a rebuttable peace of presumption, if it has been so rebutted by evidence. Since the entry of the land in question as per the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act recorded in the name of the government as গোপাট land, in the absence of any positive evidence oral and documentary onus was upon the plaintiff to discharge the presumption proving the same to be wrongly recorded in the record of rights bereft of which title and interest cannot vest upon the plaintiff. The case of Government of Bangladesh vs. A.K.M Abdul Hye 56 DLR AD 53 is an authority on this issue. The decision of High Court Division is totally devoid of consideration of all these settled principles of law adversely reversing the lower appellate court's judgment committing a palpable wrong which required to be intervened by this Division. 

17. In view of the above, we find merit in the appeal. 

18. Accordingly, the appeal is allowed. 

19. The judgment and order dated 13.02.2008 passed by the High Court Division is hereby set aside and the suit is dismissed. 

End.

case_source: (From the judgment and order dated the 5th day of July, 2015 passed by the High Court Division in Writ Petition No.3995 of 2014)
full_judgment:
Jahangir Hossain J. Delay of 1070 days under section 5 of the Limitation Act, 1908 in filing the instant civil petition for leave to appeal is hereby condoned. 

2. This civil petition for leave to appeal is directed against the judgment and order dated the 5th day of July, 2015 passed by the High Court Division in Writ petition No.3995 of 2014 making the Rule Nisi absolute. 

3. The relevant facts for disposal of this petition, in brief; are that the writ-petitioners are law abiding citizens of Bangladesh. They are highly qualified educationist and they have honours' and masters' degree. The writ-petitioners are teaching staffs of Jarip Biswas Degree College, Bagutia, Shailakupa, Jhenaidaha. They have been serving in the said college with their utmost sincerity and since the day of their joining the college, they have been teaching to the highest satisfaction of the authority. All of them have been passing miserable life without having the government portion of salary from the Government in the form of Monthly Payment Order [in brief, MPO]. They were appointed to the college in compliance with all the legal requirements for appointment and their names were duly forwarded to writ-respondent Nos.1 and 2 for release of MPO of the writ-petitioners under rule 13 of the Policy, 1995, but the concerned authority did not pay heed to their prayer. Hence, they moved before the High Court Division. 

4. Writ-respondent No.2 filed an affidavit-in-opposition contending, inter alai, that the writ-petitioners are not entitled to get salaries under Monthly Payment Order as per existing directives and guidelines as provided in "বেসরকারী কলেজ শিক্ষক কর্মচারীর বেতনের সরকারী অংশ ও জনবল কাঠামো, ১৯৯৫"। It is further contended that as per regulation 1(5) of the "বেসরকারি ডিগ্রী কলেজ অধিভূক্ত, ২০০০", the writ-petitioners are not entitled to get any salary under MPO.

5. However, the High Court Division after hearing the parties and on perusal of the materials on record, made the Rule absolute by its judgment and order dated 05.07.2015. 

6. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the aforesaid judgment and order dated 05.07.2015, the respondents to the writ petition as leave petitioners filed the instant civil petition for leave to appeal before this Division to seek redress. 

7. Mr. Amit Das Gupta, learned Deputy Attorney General, appearing on behalf of the petitioners, submits that under the provisions of the Jonobal Kathamo of Non-Government Teachers, 2010 [as amended in 2013] in section 11(10), it is clearly mentioned that if any teacher is appointed beyond the permitted limit of MPO enlistment, the institution appointing their approved limit themselves would bear the salary and other benefits from its own fund. Thus, the institution appointing teacher in excess of their statutory power being sole responsible would contain all the expenses in maintaining the excess teacher. He further submits that enlistment in MPO scheme is a policy matter and no order of mandamus can be demanded in the policy matter of the government. In a landmark decision of Civil Appeal No.115-136 of 2013, the Appellate Division in deciding the appeal filed by the Government decided that the judgments should be maintained particularly in no case. The writ-petitioners cannot claim enrolment in the form of MPO. In violation of the staffing pattern which is a policy of the government and against such policy matter no writ petition is maintainable. He finally submits that the appointment of 3rd teacher was decided by the Appellate Division in a landmark judgment wherein it was clarified the issue. 

8. Per contra, Mr. Raghib Rouf Chowdhury, Advocate, appearing on behalf of present respondent Nos. 1-2, contends that the High Court Division having examined all the papers and documents on record and hearing the parties, rightly passed the impugned judgment and order making the Rule absolute. Since there is no illegality in passing the judgment and order of the High Court Division, no question arises for interference by this Division. 

9. Heard the contentions of the learned Advocates of both the parties and perused the materials on record along with impugned judgment and order passed by the High Court Division. 

10. The claim of the writ-petitioners is that it is enumerated in clause 5 of the circular dated 19.09.2002 that the teaching staffs of a degree college for every subject shall be at least three and in the college, there are three teachers for each subject including the writ-petitioners out of whom two are getting their salaries under MPO, but the writ-petitioners are not getting it for the illegal, arbitrary actions of the writ-respondents. The writ-petitioners further claimed that the appointments of them have been made in compliance with all the legal requirements and they have accrued a legal right to get their salaries from the Government in the form of MPO. They also claimed that their names were duly forwarded to writ-respondent Nos.1 and 2 for release of the MPO of them under rule 13 of the policy, 1995. 

11. On the contrary, the claim of the government, i.e. the present petitioners is that granting MPO is the policy decision of the government. The factual aspects brought out by the writ-petitioners cannot be considered in the nature of mandamds. It is obvious that sanction of Monthly Payment. Order depends on the decision of the Government. There is no enforceable right of any person in the law to get entitlement of MPO or its enhancement because it has financial involvement in meeting up the same. 

12. In the case of Government of Bangladesh and others-vs-Md. Nazrul Islam and others, reported in 27 BLT (AD)167, this Division also observed that "In the case in hand the petitioners did not allege that the writ respondents have violated any legal right of them. The granting of M.P.O. is the policy decision of the Government. Therefore, the petitioners could not claim the same as of right. This Division is of the view that teachers and staffs of the Non-Government School and College could not claim the M.P.G. as a matter of right and as such, direction could not be given unless infringement of legal right or violation of law.' 

13. It has been enshrined in office order bearing Memo No.37.00.000.074.002. 001.2014 (part-1) 353 dated 28.08.2018 that 
“বেসরকারী শিক্ষা প্রতিষ্ঠান (স্কুল, কলেজ, মাদ্রাসা ও কারিগরি শিক্ষা প্রতিষ্ঠানসমূহ) এর শিক্ষক-কর্মচারীদের বেতন-ভাতাদির সরকারি অংশ প্রদান এবং জনবল কাঠামো সম্পর্কিত নির্দেশিকা-২০১০ (৪ ফ্রেব্রুয়ারি, ২০১০ তারিখে জারিকৃত) জারির পূর্বে বিশ্ববিদ্যালয় কর্তৃক ডিগ্রিস্তরে বিষয় অধিভুক্ত এবং ০৪.০২.২০১০ তারিখের পূর্বে প্রচলিত বিধি মোতাবেক নিয়োগপ্রাপ্ত তৃতীয় শিক্ষকগণকে জনবল কাঠামোর শর্তাদি পূরণ সাপেক্ষে এম.পি.ও. ভূক্ত করার সিদ্ধান্ত গ্রহণ করা হয়েছে।"

14. Having gone through the office order bearing Memo No.37.00.000.074.002. 001.2014 (part-1) 353 dated 28.08.2018 issued by the Ministry of Education that the government took decision that the 3rd teachers appointed according to the existing rules before 2010 subject to the fulfillment of the conditions of the Jonobal Kathamo, would get the salary of the government portion of MPO. 

15. However, it is a disputed question of fact against which the writ-petition in the form of mandamus is not maintainable. The writ-petitioners did not also come with clean hands before the Court of law. 

16. Having considered all the aspects and discussions made above, we are constrained to hold that the writ-petition filed by the writ-petitioners was not maintainable. Therefore, we find merit in the present leave petition. However, it is better to dispose of the same without granting leave as the writ petition was not maintainable. 

17. Accordingly, this petition is disposed of the judgment and order dated 05.07.2015 of the High Court Division is, hereby, set aside. However, the authority may consider the case of the writ-petitioner in the light of the order dated 28.08.2018. 

End.
